explanation:
The tree runs instability, then ECG, then pattern. ST depression confined to V1-V3, especially with a tall R wave in V1-V2, is the mirror image of posterior ST elevation, so the pathway sends the patient to the posterior leads before anything else. ACC/AHA 2025 (Table 3) says to record V7-V9 when there is isolated ST depression of at least 0.5 mm in V1-V3; ST elevation of at least 0.5 mm in V7-V9 (at least 1 mm in men under 40, from the 4th Universal Definition of MI) makes it a posterior STEMI, and he joins the STEMI timing branch (primary PCI, FMC-to-device 90 minutes or less). If V7-V9 are negative, he moves to the hs-cTn and NSTE-ACS branch. Trap: treating ST depression in V1-V3 as ordinary NSTE-ACS (missed occlusion), or lysing ST depression without proving a posterior STEMI (COR 3: Harm).

**References:** PERKI 2024 §1.5.2.1, §3.2.1 · PNPK 2026 Bab III.B.4.a, Bab III.C.2.b · ESC 2023 §3.2, §5.1, §5.2.1 · ACC/AHA 2025 §3.1.2, §5.2.1

options.text: Give tenecteplase now, because ST depression in V1-V3 is a STEMI equivalent
options.why_wrong: The pathway confirms a posterior STEMI on V7-V9 before choosing reperfusion, and at a PCI-capable hospital the reperfusion would be primary PCI, not fibrinolysis. Fibrinolysis for ST depression alone is harmful (ACC/AHA 2025 COR 3: Harm).

options.text: Treat as NSTE-ACS and repeat hs-cTn at 1-2 hours before deciding on reperfusion
options.why_wrong: This skips the posterior-lead check. Isolated ST depression in V1-V3 is the one ST-depression pattern that may be a STEMI in disguise, and reperfusion is decided on the ECG, never on troponin.

options.text: Record posterior leads V7-V9 and look for ST elevation of at least 0.5 mm (at least 1 mm in men under 40)
Early invasive angiography within 24 hours as high-risk NSTE-ACS
options.why_wrong: The NSTE-ACS timing ladder only applies once a STEMI, including a posterior STEMI, has been excluded. The posterior leads come first.

stem: A 61-year-old man has had 90 minutes of ongoing central chest pain and is seen at a PCI-capable hospital. BP 132/80 mmHg, HR 84, lungs clear. The 12-lead ECG shows 2 mm horizontal ST depression in V1-V3 with a tall R wave in V2 and no ST elevation in any lead. Following the decision pathway shown, what is the next step?

explanation:
The STEMI time branch splits at 12 hours, 12-24 hours and more than 24 hours. Here the guidelines diverge. ESC 2023: a routine primary PCI strategy should be considered in late presenters 12-48 hours after onset (IIa B); routine PCI of an occluded infarct artery is not recommended in asymptomatic patients presenting after 48 hours (III A). ACC/AHA 2025: PPCI at 12-24 hours is reasonable (2a B-NR); after 24 hours it is reasonable only with ongoing ischaemia, acute HF, haemodynamic instability or life-threatening arrhythmia (2a C-LD); in a stable patient with a totally occluded infarct artery after 24 hours it should not be performed (3: No benefit, B-R; OAT trial). At 30 hours, stable and pain-free, she sits inside the ESC window but outside the ACC/AHA one. Either way she gets full secondary prevention and an assessment of LVEF and residual ischaemia. Trap: carrying the 'regardless of time' rule for shock over to a stable late presenter.

**References:** PERKI 2024 §3.2.1.2 · ESC 2023 §5.2.1.1 · ACC/AHA 2025 §5.2.1

options.text: Both ESC 2023 and ACC/AHA 2025 recommend fibrinolysis, because primary PCI is only indicated within 12 hours
options.why_wrong: The benefit of fibrinolysis beyond 12 hours is not established. Late presenters are judged on PCI timing, ongoing ischaemia and stability, not switched to lysis.

options.text: ESC 2023 would still consider a routine primary PCI strategy (late window up to 48 hours, IIa B), whereas ACC/AHA 2025 advises against PCI of a totally occluded infarct artery in a stable patient more than 24 hours after onset (3: No benefit)
Both guidelines recommend emergency PCI, because time from onset never limits revascularization in STEMI
options.why_wrong: Revascularization irrespective of time applies to cardiogenic shock or haemodynamic instability. She is stable and pain-free.

options.text: ACC/AHA 2025 is the more permissive guideline: it extends routine primary PCI to 48 hours, while ESC 2023 stops at 24 hours
options.why_wrong: This reverses the two. ESC 2023 considers routine primary PCI at 12-48 hours (IIa B); ACC/AHA 2025 calls PPCI reasonable at 12-24 hours (2a B-NR) and, beyond 24 hours, only with ongoing ischaemia, acute HF, instability or a life-threatening arrhythmia (2a C-LD).

stem: A 57-year-old woman presents 30 hours after the onset of chest pain. The ECG shows inferior ST elevation. She is now pain-free, BP 128/76 mmHg, with no heart failure and no arrhythmia on monitoring. Which statement about primary PCI correctly reflects the two guidelines?

explanation:
This is the pharmaco-invasive pathway that matters most in regional hospitals: STEMI under 12 hours, expected PPCI delay over 120 minutes and no contraindication, so a fibrin-specific lytic is given and transfer starts at once. The tree then asks at 60-90 minutes whether reperfusion succeeded. Failure is defined (ACC/AHA 2025 Sec 5.3.2) as less than 50% ST resolution in anterior leads or less than 70% in inferior leads, persistent pain, or haemodynamic or electrical instability. Failure leads to immediate angiography with rescue PCI (ACC/AHA 2025 COR 1, B-R; ESC 2023 I A). Success leads to routine angiography 2-24 hours after lysis (ACC/AHA 2025 COR 1, B-R; ESC 2023 I A). Trap: waiting for the routine 2-24 hour slot, or re-lysing, when the ECG and symptoms already show failure.

**References:** PERKI 2024 §3.2.2 · PNPK 2026 Bab III.C.2.b · ESC 2023 §5.3 · ACC/AHA 2025 §5.3

options.text: Immediate coronary angiography with rescue PCI
Repeat the fibrinolytic dose and reassess in 60 minutes
options.why_wrong: Repeat fibrinolysis is inferior to rescue PCI (REACT).

options.text: Continue the transfer for routine angiography 2-24 hours after fibrinolysis
options.why_wrong: The 2-24 hour pharmaco-invasive window is for successful reperfusion. Less than 50% ST resolution in the anterior leads with ongoing pain is failed fibrinolysis.

options.text: Observe: ST resolution of 30% shows that reperfusion has occurred
options.why_wrong: The threshold is at least 50% resolution in anterior leads (70% in inferior leads), together with relief of pain and stability. 30% with persisting pain is failure.

source: ESC 2023 §5.3; ACC/AHA 2025 §5.3; PERKI 2024 §3.2.2; PNPK 2026 Bab III.C.2.b
stem: A 49-year-old man with an anterior STEMI of 3 hours' duration arrives at a district hospital without a cath lab; the nearest PCI centre is more than 2 hours away. He has no contraindication to fibrinolysis, receives tenecteplase and transfer is started. At 75 minutes he still has chest pain and the ST elevation in V2-V4 has fallen by only 30%. What is the most appropriate next step?

explanation: Warm and wet with normal BP is the 'cardiac' fluid-accumulation profile, treated with an IV loop diuretic at 1-2 times the usual oral daily dose (20-40 mg IV if diuretic-naive). The response is checked early: a spot urinary sodium at about 2 hours is typically adequate if above 50-70 mmol/L, and urine output in the first 6 hours is typically adequate if above 100-150 mL/h. Both of his values are below these, so the loop dose is doubled. If the response is still poor, ESC 2026 says a short course of IV acetazolamide or oral hydrochlorothiazide should be considered (IIa, B1). An SGLT2 inhibitor is then started in hospital once he is stable (ESC 2026 I, B1). Trap: leaving an inadequate diuretic dose running for a day, or reaching for an inotrope in a warm patient.

options.text: Continue the same dose and reassess the response after 24 hours
options.why_wrong: The ESC algorithm checks the response early (urinary sodium at about 2 hours, urine output over 6 hours) precisely so that a poor response is escalated the same day.

options.text: Start IV dobutamine to improve renal perfusion
options.why_wrong: He is warm with adequate BP. Routine inotropes without hypoperfusion add arrhythmia and mortality risk without benefit.

options.text: Stop the loop diuretic and switch to IV nitroglycerin alone
options.why_wrong: A nitrate suits the hypertensive 'vascular' warm-wet profile (ESC 2021: may be considered when SBP >110 mmHg, IIb). This normotensive patient with fluid accumulation needs effective diuresis.

options.text: Double the IV loop diuretic dose; if the response is still poor, add acetazolamide or a thiazide

stem: A 70-year-old man with HFrEF is admitted warm and wet, BP 118/72 mmHg. His usual oral dose is furosemide 40 mg daily and he is given 80 mg IV. At 2 hours the spot urinary sodium is 35 mmol/L, and urine output over the first 6 hours averages 60 mL/h. Using the ESC diuretic algorithm, what is the next step?

explanation:
In the acute HF pathway, after HF is confirmed, the next step is to look for a precipitant that needs its own treatment (CHAMPIT); 'C', an acute coronary syndrome, is treated as very-high-risk ACS. ESC 2023 lists ACS-related acute heart failure among the very-high-risk NSTE-ACS criteria, together with haemodynamic instability or shock, recurrent or refractory pain, life-threatening arrhythmia, mechanical complications and recurrent dynamic ST/T changes. Any one of these means an immediate invasive strategy, within 2 hours (I, C). Congestion is treated in parallel. Trap: stopping at 'NSTEMI = high risk = within 24 hours' and missing the criterion that upgrades her.

**References:** PERKI 2024 §2.1.2 · ESC 2023 §5.2.2 · ACC/AHA 2025 §6.1

options.text: Within 24 hours, because a confirmed NSTEMI is a high-risk criterion
options.why_wrong: NSTEMI alone puts her in the high-risk group (angiography within 24 hours), but ACS-related acute heart failure moves her up to very high risk.

options.text: Immediately (within 2 hours), because ACS-related acute heart failure is a very-high-risk criterion
Before discharge, after non-invasive testing, once the oedema has resolved
options.why_wrong: A selective invasive strategy is for patients without high-risk criteria. She has a very-high-risk one.

options.text: Give fibrinolysis now, then angiography 2-24 hours later
options.why_wrong: Fibrinolysis has no role in NSTE-ACS.

stem: A 66-year-old woman is admitted with NSTEMI (rising hs-cTn, ST depression in V4-V6). Six hours later she develops acute pulmonary oedema; BP 135/80 mmHg, warm peripheries. IV furosemide and a nitrate are started. When should coronary angiography be performed (ESC 2023)?

explanation: Device decisions come after at least 3 months of optimised therapy, and the review step splits patients by LVEF and QRS. With LVEF 35% or less, sinus rhythm and LBBB with QRS of 150 ms or more, CRT is recommended (ESC 2021 I A; ACC/AHA 2022 COR 1). The weaker tiers in ESC 2021 are: LBBB 130-149 ms, should be considered (IIa); non-LBBB 150 ms or more, should be considered (IIa); non-LBBB 130-149 ms, may be considered (IIb). Below 130 ms CRT is not indicated, and the question becomes a primary-prevention ICD (ischaemic I A, non-ischaemic IIa A). Trap: treating 'wide QRS' as one category. Morphology (LBBB or not) and the 150 ms cut-off decide the class.

options.text: LVEF 33%, sinus rhythm, LBBB with QRS 138 ms
options.why_wrong: LBBB with QRS 130-149 ms: CRT should be considered (IIa), not class I.

options.text: LVEF 30%, sinus rhythm, RBBB with QRS 155 ms
options.why_wrong: Non-LBBB morphology with QRS of 150 ms or more: CRT should be considered (IIa).

options.text: LVEF 28%, sinus rhythm, QRS 105 ms
options.why_wrong: With QRS under 130 ms CRT is not indicated (unless there is a pacing indication); this patient is assessed for a primary-prevention ICD instead.

options.text: LVEF 40%, sinus rhythm, LBBB with QRS 165 ms
options.why_wrong: CRT needs LVEF of 35% or less. At 40% the pathway moves to the add-on drug decisions.

options.text: LVEF 32%, sinus rhythm, LBBB with QRS 152 ms

stem: Five patients with symptomatic HFrEF have each had at least 3 months of optimised foundational therapy. Which one has a class I indication for CRT under ESC 2021?

explanation: The first node of the chronic HF tree asks for the LVEF, and the answer depends on the framework. The 2021 universal definition, ESC 2021/2023 and ACC/AHA 2022 use HFrEF 40% or less, HFmrEF 41-49% and HFpEF 50% or more, plus HFimpEF. ESC 2026 keeps only two phenotypes, with HFrEF below 50%. In HFmrEF the SGLT2 inhibitor has the strongest support (ESC 2023 focused update I A; ACC/AHA 2022 2a); ACEi/ARB/ARNI, beta-blocker and MRA are weaker (ESC 2021 IIb; ACC/AHA 2022 2b). ESC 2026 itself notes that no large RCT has tested beta-blockers or ACEi/ARNI/ARB only in LVEF 41-49%, and some drugs keep their own LVEF limits (digoxin 40% or less, vericiguat below 45%). Trap: answering without saying which framework you are using. An LVEF of 45% is HFmrEF in one guideline and HFrEF in another.

options.text: He has HFpEF under every current framework, so beta-blockers have no role as HF therapy
options.why_wrong: HFpEF starts at LVEF 50% in all frameworks. 45% is HFmrEF (2021 universal definition, ESC 2021/2023, ACC/AHA 2022) or HFrEF (ESC 2026).

options.text: He has HFmrEF under ESC 2026, which keeps the 41-49% category
options.why_wrong: ESC 2026 removed HFmrEF and uses two phenotypes: HFrEF below 50% and HFpEF at 50% or more.

options.text: He has HFmrEF under ACC/AHA 2022 and ESC 2021/2023 but HFrEF under ESC 2026; the best-supported drug class at this LVEF in the older frameworks is the SGLT2 inhibitor (ESC 2023 I A; ACC/AHA 2022 2a)
He has HF with improved EF, because his LVEF is above 40%
options.why_wrong: HFimpEF needs a previous LVEF of 40% or less with a rise of at least 10 points to above 40%. No earlier low EF is documented.

stem: A 63-year-old man has symptomatic heart failure with a raised NT-proBNP and an LVEF of 45% on two echocardiograms; there is no previous LVEF measurement. Which statement about his classification is correct?

explanation: Stable AF with no pre-excitation goes to AF-CARE; the 'A' step is stroke prevention. First check for the two VKA-only groups (mechanical valve, moderate-to-severe MS): she has neither. Then score CHA2DS2-VA: CHF 1, hypertension 1, age 75 or over 2, diabetes 1, stroke/TIA/thromboembolism 2, vascular disease 1, age 65-74 1. She scores 1 + 1 + 1 = 3. ESC 2024: 2 or more means OAC recommended, preferably a DOAC at the correct label dose. Under ACC/AHA 2023 her CHA2DS2-VASc of 4 (3 or more in a woman) also gives COR 1, so the two guidelines agree here. Trap: adding the old point for female sex, or substituting aspirin.

options.text: CHA2DS2-VA 3: oral anticoagulation is recommended, preferably a DOAC
CHA2DS2-VA 4: oral anticoagulation is recommended, preferably a DOAC
options.why_wrong: Female sex no longer scores in CHA2DS2-VA (ESC 2024 removed it). 4 is her CHA2DS2-VASc.

options.text: CHA2DS2-VA 2: oral anticoagulation should be considered
options.why_wrong: Age 65-74 (1) + hypertension (1) + diabetes (1) = 3. A score of 2 or more means OAC is recommended, not merely considered.

options.text: CHA2DS2-VA 3: aspirin is an acceptable alternative with a lower bleeding risk
options.why_wrong: Aspirin is not an effective substitute for oral anticoagulation in AF stroke prevention.

options.text: CHA2DS2-VA 3: warfarin is preferred over a DOAC
options.why_wrong: DOACs are preferred over VKA except with a mechanical valve or moderate-to-severe mitral stenosis, and she has neither.

stem: A 72-year-old woman with paroxysmal AF has hypertension and type 2 diabetes. She has no heart failure, no prior stroke or TIA, no vascular disease, no mechanical valve and no mitral stenosis. Using the ESC 2024 score shown in the pathway, what is her stroke-risk score and the recommendation?

explanation: The stroke-prevention node checks the valve before the score. With a mechanical heart valve or moderate-to-severe mitral stenosis the answer is a VKA, not a DOAC: RE-ALIGN showed harm with dabigatran in mechanical valves, and INVICTUS showed a VKA was better than rivaroxaban in rheumatic AF. Only patients outside these two groups are anticoagulated by CHA2DS2-VA (ESC 2024) or CHA2DS2-VASc (ACC/AHA 2023). Rheumatic MS with AF is common in Indonesian exam vignettes. Trap: applying the score, or the 'DOAC preferred' rule, to rheumatic MS.

options.text: No anticoagulation, because her CHA2DS2-VA score is 0
options.why_wrong: Moderate-to-severe mitral stenosis with AF is anticoagulated with a VKA whatever the score.

options.text: Rivaroxaban, because DOACs are preferred over warfarin in AF
options.why_wrong: In rheumatic AF a VKA was better than rivaroxaban (INVICTUS). Both ESC 2024 and ACC/AHA 2023 exclude moderate-to-severe MS from the 'DOAC preferred' recommendation.

options.text: Aspirin 100 mg daily
options.why_wrong: Aspirin is not effective stroke prevention in AF.

options.text: Warfarin (a vitamin K antagonist), whatever the score

stem: A 34-year-old woman with rheumatic mitral stenosis (mitral valve area 1.2 cm²) develops atrial fibrillation. She has no other risk factors, so her CHA2DS2-VA score is 0. What is the appropriate stroke prevention?

explanation: In the 'R' step of AF-CARE, a planned cardioversion depends on how long the AF has lasted and whether the patient is anticoagulated. ESC 2024 shortened the window for cardioversion without prior OAC or TOE to 24 hours of known duration; ACC/AHA 2023 keeps 48 hours. Beyond the window, or if the duration is unknown, either give 3 weeks of effective anticoagulation or do a TOE-guided early cardioversion. After any cardioversion, continue OAC for at least 4 weeks and then decide long-term OAC by the stroke-risk score. For recent-onset AF in stable patients, ESC 2024 also suggests considering a wait-and-see approach (rate control, with spontaneous conversion often within 48 hours). Trap: quoting the 48-hour rule in a question that names ESC 2024.

options.text: Cardiovert today without imaging, because the episode is within the 48-hour safe window
options.why_wrong: 48 hours is the ACC/AHA 2023 window. ESC 2024 shortened it to 24 hours, so under ESC this 30-hour episode needs a TOE or 3 weeks of anticoagulation first.

options.text: Either transoesophageal echo to exclude left atrial thrombus before cardioversion, or 3 weeks of effective anticoagulation first; then anticoagulation for at least 4 weeks afterwards
Cardiovert today; anticoagulation is not needed afterwards if sinus rhythm is restored
options.why_wrong: OAC continues for at least 4 weeks after cardioversion, then long term according to the stroke-risk score, not according to the rhythm.

options.text: Cardioversion is contraindicated; rate control is the only option
options.why_wrong: Rhythm control remains open once LA thrombus has been excluded by TOE or after 3 weeks of effective OAC.

stem: A 55-year-old man with no structural heart disease has symptomatic AF that, by a clear history, began 30 hours ago. He is haemodynamically stable and not on anticoagulation, and he would like cardioversion today. Under ESC 2024, which plan is correct?

explanation: The pathway asks three questions in order: stable or not, QRS narrow or wide, regular or not. A stable, regular, narrow tachycardia gets vagal manoeuvres first (the modified Valsalva roughly doubles success), then adenosine (AHA 2025 COR 1, B-R for both; ESC 2019 adenosine 6-18 mg I B). Record a strip during the push. Termination means AV-node-dependent re-entry (AVNRT or AVRT), and recurrent episodes go to ablation. If transient AV block reveals flutter waves or atrial tachycardia, adenosine has made the diagnosis. If it has no effect, use IV diltiazem/verapamil or a beta-blocker, then cardioversion. Trap: a technically poor adenosine injection, or jumping to cardioversion in a stable patient.

options.text: Synchronized cardioversion under sedation
options.why_wrong: Cardioversion is first-line only for an unstable patient, or after vagal manoeuvres and drugs have failed.

options.text: IV verapamil as the first drug
options.why_wrong: IV diltiazem or verapamil (AHA 2025 2a) is the step after adenosine has had no effect.

options.text: Adenosine 6 mg by rapid IV push with a saline flush (then 12 mg if needed), recording a rhythm strip
Adenosine 6 mg injected slowly over 1-2 minutes through a hand vein
options.why_wrong: Adenosine acts for only seconds. A slow injection through a distal cannula fails; give a rapid push with a flush through a proximal vein.

stem: A 27-year-old woman has sudden palpitations. The ECG shows a regular narrow-complex tachycardia at 190 bpm. BP 112/70 mmHg, she is alert and has no chest pain. A modified Valsalva manoeuvre has not terminated it. Following the pathway shown, what is the next step?

explanation: Wide, irregular and very fast with QRS complexes of changing shape (different degrees of fusion) means pre-excited AF in WPW until proven otherwise. In the tachycardia pathway this is the 'irregular wide' branch, and in the AF pathway it is checked before AF-CARE. All AV-nodal blockers are avoided: adenosine, verapamil/diltiazem, beta-blockers, digoxin and IV amiodarone. A stable patient gets procainamide or ibutilide (ESC 2019 SVT) or elective electrical cardioversion; an unstable one gets electrical cardioversion. Definitive treatment is ablation of the accessory pathway (high risk if the shortest pre-excited RR interval is 250 ms or less). Trap: amiodarone feels 'safe' for a wide-complex tachycardia, but not in pre-excited AF.

options.text: IV adenosine 6 mg to slow the rate and reveal the rhythm
options.why_wrong: In an irregularly irregular wide-complex tachycardia, adenosine is COR 3: Harm (AHA 2025). Blocking the AV node pushes conduction down the accessory pathway and can cause VF.

options.text: IV verapamil
options.why_wrong: An AV-nodal blocker in pre-excited AF can precipitate VF; verapamil and diltiazem are also COR 3: Harm in any wide-complex tachycardia.

options.text: IV amiodarone
options.why_wrong: IV amiodarone is on the pathway's list of drugs to avoid in pre-excited AF, alongside adenosine, verapamil/diltiazem, beta-blockers and digoxin.

options.text: IV procainamide (or ibutilide), or elective electrical cardioversion; then refer for accessory-pathway ablation
IV digoxin plus a beta-blocker for rate control
options.why_wrong: Both are AV-nodal blockers and can accelerate accessory-pathway conduction in pre-excited AF.

stem: A 23-year-old man has had palpitations for an hour. The ECG shows an irregular, very fast (up to 260 bpm) broad-complex tachycardia in which the QRS shape varies from beat to beat. BP 116/74 mmHg, he is alert. What is the most appropriate treatment?

explanation: The initial evaluation is history, examination with supine and standing BP, and a 12-lead ECG, and here it gives the diagnosis. ESC 2018 defines orthostatic hypotension as a sustained fall in SBP of at least 20 mmHg, or in DBP of at least 10 mmHg, or a fall in SBP to below 90 mmHg on standing. A 22 mmHg systolic fall with reproduced symptoms is enough. Management: remove or reduce the offending drugs (here an alpha-blocker, a thiazide and a vasodilator), correct volume, then use non-drug measures (hydration and salt, counter-pressure manoeuvres, compression, head-up tilt sleeping) and, if needed, midodrine or fludrocortisone. Trap: requiring both systolic and diastolic criteria.

options.text: Orthostatic hypotension: the systolic fall of 22 mmHg meets the definition on its own
Not orthostatic hypotension: the diastolic fall is only 6 mmHg, and both criteria must be met
options.why_wrong: The criteria are alternatives: a systolic fall of at least 20 mmHg OR a diastolic fall of at least 10 mmHg OR systolic BP falling below 90 mmHg.

options.text: Not orthostatic hypotension: standing systolic BP stays above 90 mmHg
options.why_wrong: A standing SBP below 90 mmHg is one of three alternative criteria, not a requirement.

options.text: Inconclusive: a tilt-table test is needed before the diagnosis can be made
options.why_wrong: Tilt testing helps when the active-standing test is negative. This test is positive and reproduces his symptoms.

stem: A 76-year-old man taking amlodipine, doxazosin and hydrochlorothiazide reports two faints shortly after getting out of bed. Supine BP is 142/80 mmHg; after 3 minutes of standing it is 120/74 mmHg and he feels light-headed. The ECG is normal. Using the ESC 2018 definition in the pathway, how should the standing test be interpreted?

explanation: After the initial evaluation the cause is uncertain, so the patient is risk-stratified. Syncope during exertion is a high-risk feature (ESC 2018), which means early intensive evaluation, not discharge. In the exertional branch, echocardiography comes first to exclude AS or obstructive HCM, then exercise testing (ESC 2018). The differential is AS, HCM, an anomalous coronary artery, CPVT and long QT type 1; in a young athlete also ARVC (CT coronary angiography or cardiac MRI). Trap: the 'healthy athlete, normal ECG, must be vasovagal' reflex, and the timing detail (during versus after exercise).

options.text: Reassure and discharge: syncope in a fit young athlete is usually vasovagal
options.why_wrong: Syncope during exertion is cardiac until proven otherwise; it is a high-risk feature. Syncope after exertion is the pattern that is more often reflex.

options.text: Brain CT and EEG to exclude a seizure
options.why_wrong: Low yield. The story is syncope, and brief jerks during syncope do not mean epilepsy.

options.text: Echocardiography first to exclude outflow obstruction, then exercise testing; think of HCM, an anomalous coronary artery, CPVT and long QT type 1
An exercise stress test today, before any imaging
options.why_wrong: ESC 2018 performs exercise testing in exertional syncope after echocardiography has excluded severe outflow obstruction.

stem: A 19-year-old footballer collapses in the middle of a sprint and recovers fully within 30 seconds. There was no prodrome. Examination and the resting 12-lead ECG are normal. What is the most appropriate next step?

explanation: Stable, so the pathway asks for the rhythm. A constant PR with suddenly dropped beats and a wide QRS is Mobitz II, usually in the His-Purkinje system. For Mobitz II, 2:1, high-grade and complete block, the next node asks about a reversible or physiological cause or an acute MI. Reversible: correct it and observe (temporary pacing if unstable), and pace if the block persists; block on AV-nodal drugs often unmasks intrinsic disease. Acute MI: revascularize and wait, because many blocks recover (ESC 2021: at least 5 days before a permanent pacemaker). Neither: permanent pacing regardless of symptoms (ACC/AHA/HRS 2018 COR 1; ESC 2021). Trap: borrowing the sinus-node rule ('symptoms decide') for infra-Hisian AV block.

options.text: Whether her symptoms have been shown to correlate with the slow rate
options.why_wrong: Symptom-rhythm correlation is the deciding question in sinus node dysfunction and in first-degree or Mobitz I block. Acquired Mobitz II that is not reversible is paced regardless of symptoms.

options.text: Whether there is a reversible or physiological cause (drugs, hyperkalaemia, Lyme carditis, hypothyroidism) or an acute myocardial infarction
Whether her heart rate is below 40 bpm while awake
options.why_wrong: No heart-rate threshold decides pacing in Mobitz II; the level of the block does.

options.text: Whether the block improves after IV atropine
options.why_wrong: Mobitz II is usually infra-Hisian, so atropine often has no effect; the response does not decide permanent pacing.

stem: A 74-year-old woman is referred with dizziness. She is haemodynamically stable. The rhythm strip shows a constant PR interval of 170 ms with intermittent non-conducted P waves, and the QRS is 130 ms. Following the pathway shown, which question must be answered before permanent pacing is decided?

explanation: Unstable bradycardia (hypotension, confusion) starts with atropine 1 mg IV, repeated every 3-5 minutes to 3 mg, with pacing pads on. The wide escape rhythm shows the block is below the AV node, where atropine often fails, so failure leads straight on: transcutaneous pacing, or dopamine 5-20 mcg/kg/min or adrenaline 2-10 mcg/min, while temporary transvenous pacing is arranged (ACC/AHA/HRS 2018: reasonable for persistent unstable bradycardia refractory to drugs). Confirm mechanical capture by a pulse, not by electrical spikes. Then look for reversible causes (drugs, hyperkalaemia, acute MI). Acquired complete heart block that is not reversible needs a permanent pacemaker regardless of symptoms. Trap: persisting with atropine in infra-Hisian block.

options.text: Wait for further atropine doses, up to 3 mg, to take effect before considering pacing
options.why_wrong: Atropine often fails in infra-Hisian block (wide escape) and must not delay pacing in an unstable patient.

options.text: Implant a permanent pacemaker before any temporary measure
options.why_wrong: He is unstable now. Bridge with transcutaneous pacing or a chronotropic infusion and arrange temporary transvenous pacing; the permanent device follows once he is stable and reversible causes have been checked.

options.text: IV amiodarone to stabilise the escape rhythm
options.why_wrong: Antiarrhythmics are among the reversible causes of bradycardia, not a treatment for it.

options.text: Transcutaneous pacing (confirming mechanical capture with a pulse) or a dopamine or adrenaline infusion as a bridge, and arrange temporary transvenous pacing

stem: A 79-year-old man is brought in confused, BP 72/40 mmHg, HR 32. The ECG shows complete heart block with a wide-QRS escape rhythm. Pacing pads are on and atropine 1 mg IV has had no effect. What is the most appropriate next step?

explanation: At the severe-BP node (180/110 mmHg or more by ESC, above 180/120 mmHg by ACC/AHA) the next question is whether there is new or worsening acute hypertension-mediated organ damage: ACS, pulmonary oedema, dissection, encephalopathy, stroke, AKI, retinal haemorrhages or papilloedema, pre-eclampsia, thrombotic microangiopathy. He has none, so this is severe hypertension (AHA/ACC 2025; formerly 'hypertensive urgency'), not an emergency. Management: start, restart or intensify oral therapy, check adherence and triggers (pain, NSAIDs, stimulants), and recheck within days. Trap: treating the number instead of the organ damage. Rapid lowering harms.

options.text: Restart and intensify oral therapy, address adherence, and review within days
Sublingual nifedipine to bring the BP down quickly
options.why_wrong: A rapid fall can cause stroke or MI when autoregulation has shifted. Sublingual nifedipine and IV boluses are not used.

options.text: Admit for IV labetalol, lowering BP by 25% in the first hour
options.why_wrong: That regimen is for a hypertensive emergency, which requires new or worsening acute organ damage. He has none.

options.text: IV esmolol and nitroprusside to reach SBP below 120 mmHg within an hour
options.why_wrong: SBP below 120 mmHg in the first hour is the target for aortic dissection only.

stem: A 58-year-old man who stopped his antihypertensives 2 weeks ago has a BP of 208/122 mmHg on repeated readings and a mild headache. He has no chest pain, breathlessness or neurological deficit; fundoscopy shows no haemorrhages or papilloedema; ECG, troponin, creatinine and urinalysis are normal. What is the best management?

explanation: She is on the three-drug combination (RAS blocker + CCB + thiazide-like diuretic) at maximum tolerated doses, so the next node asks whether pseudo-resistance has been excluded. ESC 2024 defines resistant hypertension as BP of 140/90 mmHg or more despite lifestyle measures and maximum tolerated doses of a diuretic, RAS blocker and CCB, confirmed out of office, with pseudo-resistance excluded. That means checking cuff size and technique, white-coat effect (ABPM or HBPM), adherence, interfering drugs (NSAIDs, oral contraceptives, decongestants, steroids, liquorice), and salt and alcohol intake. Only then: spironolactone as the fourth drug (ESC 2024 IIa), screening for primary aldosteronism (AHA/ACC 2025 COR 1) and referral. Trap: labelling hypertension 'resistant' on office readings while an NSAID is on board.

options.text: Add spironolactone as the fourth drug
options.why_wrong: Spironolactone is for true resistant hypertension, which can be diagnosed only after pseudo-resistance has been excluded. Here there is an NSAID and no out-of-office confirmation.

options.text: Refer for renal denervation
options.why_wrong: Renal denervation may be considered (ESC 2024 IIb) in true resistant hypertension, in experienced centres. She has not reached that point.

options.text: Exclude pseudo-resistance: confirm with home or ambulatory BP, check cuff size, technique and adherence, and stop the NSAID
Replace the calcium-channel blocker with a beta-blocker
options.why_wrong: Beta-blockers are not first-line for uncomplicated hypertension, and swapping drugs does not address the reasons for apparent resistance.

stem: A 62-year-old woman's office BP is 158/96 mmHg despite a single-pill combination of perindopril, amlodipine and indapamide at maximum doses. She takes ibuprofen most days for knee pain. Following the pathway shown, what should be done next?

explanation: Stable patient, so the pathway goes to clinical probability. Wells 4 or less ('PE unlikely') leads to D-dimer, and a D-dimer below the cut-off excludes PE. ESC 2019 recommends an age-adjusted cut-off after 50 years (age × 10 µg/L, IIa B) to raise specificity in older patients. For an 82-year-old the cut-off is 820 µg/L, so 650 µg/L excludes PE and no anticoagulation is needed; she should be reassessed if symptoms persist. CTPA would be used if the D-dimer were above 820, or straight away if probability were high (Wells above 4), when a D-dimer cannot exclude PE. Trap: applying the fixed 500 µg/L cut-off to an elderly patient, which leads to unnecessary CT scans.

options.text: The D-dimer is positive (above 500 µg/L): proceed to CTPA
options.why_wrong: Over the age of 50 the age-adjusted cut-off applies: age × 10 = 820 µg/L for her (ESC 2019 IIa B). 650 is below it.

options.text: The D-dimer is below her age-adjusted cut-off of 820 µg/L, so PE is excluded without imaging
D-dimer should not be used at her age; go straight to CTPA
options.why_wrong: D-dimer is skipped when clinical probability is high. Age is the reason to adjust the cut-off, not to abandon the test.

options.text: Apply PERC first, and anticoagulate if any PERC item is positive
options.why_wrong: PERC is used only when gestalt probability is very low, and it is always positive at age 50 or over. A positive PERC leads to a D-dimer, not to treatment.

options.text: Treat her as high probability because she is over 80, and go to CTPA
options.why_wrong: Probability comes from Wells or Geneva, not from age alone. Wells 3 is 'PE unlikely', which goes to D-dimer first.

stem: An 82-year-old woman, haemodynamically stable, has pleuritic chest pain. Her two-level Wells score is 3 ('PE unlikely'). A high-sensitivity D-dimer is 650 µg/L, and the laboratory cut-off is 500 µg/L. Using the pathway shown, what is the correct interpretation?

explanation: Confirmed, stable PE goes to sPESI (1 point each: age above 80, cancer, chronic heart failure or lung disease, HR 110 or more, SBP below 100, SaO2 below 90%). He scores 1 for his heart rate. With sPESI 1 or more, the tree asks whether RV dysfunction AND a raised troponin are both present: RV/LV 1.0 or more and TAPSE below 16 mm show RV dysfunction, and the troponin is raised, so he is intermediate-high risk. Management: anticoagulate (LMWH at first), monitor in HDU/ICU for 2-3 days, involve the PE response team, and give rescue thrombolysis if he becomes unstable (ESC 2019 I B). Routine primary thrombolysis is not recommended (III B): in PEITHO it prevented decompensation but increased major bleeding and haemorrhagic stroke. In the AHA/ACC 2026 categories he is C3. Trap: reacting to 'big RV plus troponin' with thrombolysis in a normotensive patient.

options.text: High risk: give systemic thrombolysis now
options.why_wrong: High risk requires haemodynamic instability (cardiac arrest, obstructive shock or persistent hypotension). He is normotensive.

options.text: Intermediate-low risk: anticoagulate on the ward without close monitoring
options.why_wrong: With sPESI of 1 or more plus both RV dysfunction and a raised troponin he is intermediate-high, not intermediate-low.

options.text: Low risk: start a DOAC and discharge early
options.why_wrong: His sPESI is 1 (HR 110 or more), and RV dysfunction with a raised troponin also rules out low risk.

options.text: Intermediate-high risk: anticoagulate (LMWH initially) and monitor closely, with rescue reperfusion if he deteriorates; no routine thrombolysis

stem: A 67-year-old man has CTPA-confirmed PE. BP 118/74 mmHg, HR 114, SaO2 93% on air; no cancer and no chronic heart or lung disease. Echo shows an RV/LV ratio of 1.2 and TAPSE of 14 mm, and the hs-troponin is raised. What is his ESC 2019 risk class and the correct initial management?

explanation: Low gradient (Vmax below 4 m/s, MG below 40 mmHg) with AVA of 1.0 cm² or less is discordant grading, and the tree then asks for the LVEF. Below 50% means classical low-flow, low-gradient AS (ACC/AHA stage D2), assessed with low-dose dobutamine stress echo. True severe: MG 40 mmHg or more (or Vmax 4 m/s or more) with AVA still 1.0 cm² or less at higher flow, leading to AVR. Pseudo-severe: AVA rises above 1.0 cm², so treat the cardiomyopathy. No flow reserve (stroke volume rises less than 20%): the test is inconclusive, so use a CT calcium score (ESC 2021: severe likely at 2000 AU or more in men, 1200 AU or more in women). Trap: trusting a low gradient in a patient with low flow.

options.text: Low-dose dobutamine stress echocardiography (up to 20 µg/kg/min)
Measure the stroke volume index and, if it is below 35 mL/m², obtain a CT calcium score
options.why_wrong: That is the paradoxical branch for LVEF of 50% or more. With LVEF below 50% this is classical low-flow, low-gradient AS.

options.text: Call it moderate AS and repeat the echo in 1-2 years
options.why_wrong: A low gradient with AVA of 1.0 cm² or less and a low LVEF may hide true severe AS; it cannot be called moderate until flow has been increased.

options.text: Exercise treadmill test to unmask symptoms
options.why_wrong: He is already symptomatic, and exercise testing is contraindicated in symptomatic severe AS. It also does not answer the low-flow question.

stem: A 74-year-old man with exertional breathlessness has a calcified aortic valve. Echo: LVEF 30%, mean gradient 26 mmHg, peak velocity 3.3 m/s, AVA 0.8 cm²; the measurements have been rechecked. Following the pathway shown, what is the next step?

explanation: Severe AS with symptoms means AVR is indicated (ACC/AHA 2020 1 A; ESC I). The Heart Team then chooses the route by age, life expectancy, surgical risk and anatomy. ACC/AHA 2020: under 65 years (or life expectancy over 20 years) SAVR; 65-80 years SAVR or transfemoral TAVI after shared decision-making; over 80 (or life expectancy under 10 years) transfemoral TAVI (all COR 1). ESC 2025: TAVI at 70 or over with a tricuspid valve and suitable transfemoral anatomy (I A); SAVR under 70 at low surgical risk (I). SAVR is favoured by a bicuspid valve, unfavourable anatomy or the need for other cardiac surgery. Trap: quoting the older ESC 2021 cut-off of 75 years.

options.text: Both guidelines recommend surgical AVR, because her surgical risk is low
options.why_wrong: Surgical risk no longer decides on its own: ESC 2025 recommends TAVI from age 70 with a tricuspid valve and suitable transfemoral anatomy (I A).

options.text: ESC 2025 recommends surgical AVR, because TAVI is reserved for patients aged 75 or older
options.why_wrong: 75 years was the ESC 2021 cut-off. ESC 2025 lowered it to 70.

options.text: ESC 2025 recommends transfemoral TAVI (age 70 or over, tricuspid valve, suitable anatomy: I A), whereas ACC/AHA 2020 offers SAVR or transfemoral TAVI after shared decision-making for ages 65-80
Neither guideline recommends intervention until her LVEF falls below 50%
options.why_wrong: Symptoms caused by severe AS are a class I trigger for valve replacement in both guidelines, whatever the LVEF.

stem: A 72-year-old woman has symptomatic severe high-gradient aortic stenosis (Vmax 4.6 m/s) of a tricuspid valve. Her surgical risk is low, she needs no other cardiac surgery, and CT shows suitable transfemoral access. Which statement matches the guidelines?

explanation:
The SCAI staging step first asks whether there is hypoperfusion (cold or mottled skin, altered mentation, urine below 30 mL/h, lactate 2 mmol/L or more). Without it: A (at risk) or B (relative hypotension or tachycardia, perfusion intact). With it, the course decides: C (classic, hypoperfusion needing one intervention beyond fluids), D (deteriorating despite initial therapy) or E (extremis: ongoing CPR or ECMO, lactate 8 mmol/L or more, pH below 7.2). Shock is defined by hypoperfusion, so normotensive shock with a rising lactate is already stage C, and a falling BP with intact perfusion is still B. ACC 2025 guidance notes that stage B patients have the highest risk of worsening within 24 hours. Trap: staging by the BP number instead of perfusion.

**References:** PERKI 2024 §4.3.2 · ESC 2023 §7.2 · ACC/AHA 2025 §8.1, §8.2

options.text: A further fall in systolic BP to 80 mmHg with unchanged perfusion and lactate
options.why_wrong: Hypotension or tachycardia without hypoperfusion is still stage B. The stage depends on perfusion, not on BP alone.

options.text: Cool, clammy skin and oliguria with a lactate of 3 mmol/L, needing an inotrope or vasopressor
A heart rate rising to 120 bpm
options.why_wrong: Haemodynamic instability without hypoperfusion defines stage B.

options.text: Ongoing CPR with a lactate of 9 mmol/L and pH 7.1
options.why_wrong: That is stage E (extremis), not C.

stem: Twelve hours after an anterior STEMI treated with primary PCI, a 64-year-old man has SBP 86 mmHg (baseline 125), HR 108, warm peripheries, normal mentation and a urine output of 50 mL/h; lactate is 1.4 mmol/L. He is at SCAI stage B. Which new finding would move him to stage C?

explanation:
In the cause branch, MI-related shock without a mechanical complication goes to emergency angiography and culprit revascularization, whatever the time from onset (ACC/AHA 2025 COR 1, B-R; ESC 2023 I). Only the culprit vessel is treated at the index procedure: routine PCI of non-infarct arteries in shock is harmful (CULPRIT-SHOCK; ACC/AHA 2025 3: Harm, B-R; ESC 2023 III). Non-culprit lesions are staged later. If shock persists, a microaxial flow pump is reasonable in selected LV-dominant STEMI shock (2a B-R), and routine IABP or VA-ECMO gives no benefit (3: No benefit). With inferior STEMI, think of RV infarction too. Trap: 'complete revascularization' is right in stable STEMI but harmful in shock.

**References:** PERKI 2024 §4.4.1, §4.3.2 · ESC 2023 §10.1, §7.2 · ACC/AHA 2025 §8.1, §8.2

options.text: Proceeding with revascularization even though symptom onset was 20 hours ago
options.why_wrong: This is recommended. In ACS with cardiogenic shock, culprit revascularization is indicated irrespective of time from onset (ACC/AHA 2025 COR 1, B-R).

options.text: Urgent echocardiography to look for a mechanical complication and RV infarction
options.why_wrong: This is recommended. Point-of-care echo is part of the shock work-up, and inferior STEMI makes RV infarction a real possibility.

options.text: Norepinephrine as the first vasopressor if she remains hypotensive
options.why_wrong: This is recommended. Norepinephrine is a reasonable first choice (ACC 2025 guidance); dopamine is the vasopressor to avoid.

options.text: Emergency CABG if the culprit lesion cannot be treated by PCI
options.why_wrong: This is recommended. Culprit revascularization in shock is by PCI or, if PCI is not feasible or fails, CABG.

options.text: PCI of the LAD and circumflex stenoses during the same procedure as the RCA

stem: A 69-year-old woman with inferior STEMI and cardiogenic shock (SBP 78 mmHg, lactate 5 mmol/L) is taken for emergency angiography 20 hours after symptom onset. The right coronary artery is occluded, and there are severe stenoses in the LAD and circumflex. Which part of the plan is NOT recommended?

explanation: In the shockable loop, an organised rhythm at a rhythm check leads to the pulse-check node: is there a pulse or another sign of ROSC, such as an abrupt rise in ETCO2 or an arterial waveform? With a pulse, the next step is the post-ROSC 12-lead ECG, which decides emergent angiography (ST elevation) and the rest of the bundle. Without a pulse it is PEA: continue CPR and adrenaline on the non-shockable pathway and look for the H's and T's. Drug timing in the AHA sequence: adrenaline after shock 2 and every 3-5 minutes, amiodarone 300 mg after shock 3 (ERC gives both after the third shock). Trap: carrying on with the drug-and-shock routine after the rhythm has changed.

options.text: Deliver a third shock and give amiodarone 300 mg
options.why_wrong: Shocks and amiodarone are for persisting VF or pulseless VT. An organised rhythm is not shockable.

options.text: Give the next dose of adrenaline immediately
options.why_wrong: Adrenaline is repeated every 3-5 minutes only while the arrest continues, and a dose was given 2 minutes ago. First establish whether there is a pulse.

options.text: Continue CPR for another 2-minute cycle without a pulse check
options.why_wrong: An organised rhythm at a rhythm check calls for a brief pulse check (under 10 seconds), and the abrupt rise in ETCO2 points to ROSC.

options.text: Check for a pulse; if present (ROSC), start post-arrest care with a 12-lead ECG to look for ST elevation

stem: During resuscitation of a 58-year-old man in VF arrest, a second shock has been given, followed by adrenaline 1 mg, and CPR has continued for 2 minutes. At the rhythm check the monitor shows an organised narrow-complex rhythm at 90/min, and waveform capnography has just risen abruptly from 14 to 42 mmHg. Following the pathway shown, what is the next step?

explanation: The post-ROSC node asks the 12-lead ECG question first. ST elevation: emergent angiography (AHA 2025 COR 1, B-NR). No ST elevation but shock, recurrent VT/VF or ongoing ischaemia: emergency angiography is reasonable (2a). No ST elevation and stable: no emergency angiography (3: No benefit, B-R), and the ACC/AHA 2025 ACS guideline and ESC 2023 agree. Because he does not follow commands, the comatose bundle applies: temperature 32-37.5 °C (COR 1) for at least 36 hours (2a), MAP of 65 mmHg or more (COR 1), SpO2 90-98%, PaCO2 35-45 mmHg (COR 1), prompt EEG, and multimodal prognostication at least 72 hours after normothermia. Trap: sending every VF survivor to the cath lab, and prognosticating too early.

options.text: No emergency coronary angiography; temperature control at 32-37.5 °C for at least 36 hours, MAP of at least 65 mmHg, SpO2 90-98% and PaCO2 35-45 mmHg
Emergency coronary angiography, because the arrest rhythm was VF
options.why_wrong: In a comatose but stable patient without ST elevation, emergency angiography is no better than a delayed or selective strategy (AHA 2025 3: No benefit; COACT, TOMAHAWK).

options.text: Cooling to 33 °C for 12 hours, then neuroprognostication at 24 hours
options.why_wrong: Temperature control lasts at least 36 hours (2a), and prognostication is multimodal and no earlier than 72 hours after normothermia, off sedation.

options.text: 100% oxygen throughout the ICU stay to keep PaO2 above 150 mmHg
options.why_wrong: 100% oxygen is given only until SpO2 can be measured reliably; then titrate to SpO2 90-98% (PaO2 60-105 mmHg).

stem: A 61-year-old man has ROSC after 12 minutes of VF arrest. He is intubated and does not follow commands. The post-ROSC 12-lead ECG shows no ST elevation; MAP is 78 mmHg without vasopressors, and there is no recurrent arrhythmia or ongoing ischaemia. Which plan follows AHA 2025?

explanation: A stable patient goes to the Aortic Dissection Detection Risk Score: 1 point for each category present, namely high-risk conditions (Marfan or other connective-tissue disease, family history, known aortic valve or aortic disease, recent aortic manipulation, known aneurysm), high-risk pain (abrupt, severe, tearing) and high-risk examination findings (pulse or BP deficit, focal neurological deficit with pain, new AR murmur, hypotension or shock). He scores only the pain category, so ADD-RS = 1. ADD-RS 0-1 leads to D-dimer: below 500 ng/mL makes acute aortic syndrome unlikely (ADvISED), and 500 or more leads to ECG-gated CTA from neck to pelvis. ADD-RS 2-3 goes straight to CTA. ESC 2024 recommends this ADD-RS-based algorithm (I). If suspicion stays high despite a negative D-dimer, image anyway. Trap: scoring each feature instead of each category, or skipping the D-dimer step.

options.text: ECG-gated CT angiography straight away, because the pain is abrupt and severe
options.why_wrong: Direct CTA is for an ADD-RS of 2-3 (or an unstable patient). He scores in only one category, pain, so his ADD-RS is 1.

options.text: Discharge: an ADD-RS of 1 is low risk and needs no further testing
options.why_wrong: An ADD-RS of 0-1 still needs a D-dimer before acute aortic syndrome is called unlikely.

options.text: ADD-RS 1: measure D-dimer, and image with CT angiography if it is 500 ng/mL or more
Bedside transthoracic echo and immediate surgical referral
options.why_wrong: That is the unstable branch. He is haemodynamically stable.

stem: A 54-year-old man has had abrupt, severe chest pain radiating to the back for 2 hours. He has no known aortic or connective-tissue disease and no family history of aortic disease; pulses and BP are equal in both arms, there is no aortic regurgitation murmur and no neurological deficit, and BP is 150/90 mmHg. The ECG shows no ischaemia. Using the pathway shown, what is the next step?

explanation: The BP branch first asks whether the patient is hypotensive (in which case BP is never lowered and tamponade, rupture or acute AR is sought). He is hypertensive, so it checks for beta-blocker contraindications. With none, an IV beta-blocker (esmolol or labetalol) is given first to blunt dP/dt and prevent reflex tachycardia, and a vasodilator (nitroprusside, nicardipine) is added only if SBP stays high once the HR is controlled. The guidelines' targets differ: ESC 2014 aims for HR about 60 or less and SBP 100-120 mmHg; ACC/AHA 2022 aims for SBP below 120 mmHg (or the lowest tolerated) and HR 60-80. Add IV opioid analgesia. Uncomplicated type B is then managed medically with imaging surveillance, and subacute TEVAR should be considered (ESC 2024 IIa). Trap: a vasodilator before the beta-blocker, or using the general emergency rule of no more than 25% in the first hour.

options.text: IV nitroprusside first, to bring SBP quickly below 120 mmHg
options.why_wrong: A vasodilator without prior beta-blockade causes reflex tachycardia and raises aortic shear stress (dP/dt). Rate control comes first.

options.text: IV esmolol or labetalol first; targets HR about 60 or less and SBP 100-120 mmHg (ESC 2014), or HR 60-80 and SBP below 120 mmHg (ACC/AHA 2022)
IV beta-blocker first, aiming for SBP below 140 mmHg and HR below 100, as in ACS
options.why_wrong: Those are not dissection targets. Dissection needs SBP of about 120 mmHg or lower and HR of about 60 (ESC) or 60-80 (ACC/AHA).

options.text: IV diltiazem first, because beta-blockers worsen dissection
options.why_wrong: A non-dihydropyridine CCB is used only when a beta-blocker is contraindicated, and he has no contraindication.

options.text: Lower BP by no more than 25% in the first hour to protect cerebral perfusion
options.why_wrong: The 25%-in-the-first-hour rule is for hypertensive emergencies without a compelling condition. Aortic dissection is the exception that needs rapid lowering.

stem: A 60-year-old man has CT-confirmed uncomplicated type B aortic dissection. BP 186/104 mmHg, HR 102; he has no bronchospasm, no AV block and no heart failure. What should be the first IV drug, and what are the haemodynamic targets?

explanation: In the lipid tree, documented ASCVD without a recurrent event within 2 years lands in the very-high-risk category: LDL-C below 1.4 mmol/L (55 mg/dL) AND a reduction of at least 50% from baseline (ESC/EAS 2019 I A). Both halves must be met. With a baseline of 100 mg/dL, a 50% fall means 50 mg/dL or less, which is stricter than 'below 55', so his working goal is 50 mg/dL or less. When the baseline is higher (say 160 mg/dL), the 'below 55' half is the stricter one. The goal below 40 mg/dL is for a recurrent event within 2 years on maximal statin. Trap: forgetting the 'and at least 50%' half of the ESC goal when the baseline LDL-C is already low.

options.text: Below 70 mg/dL (1.8 mmol/L)
options.why_wrong: That is the goal for the high-risk category. Documented ASCVD is very high risk.

options.text: Below 55 mg/dL (1.4 mmol/L), whatever the percentage fall
options.why_wrong: This forgets the second half of the very-high-risk goal, a fall of at least 50% from baseline. From 100 mg/dL, 54 mg/dL is only a 46% fall.

options.text: Below 40 mg/dL (1.0 mmol/L)
options.why_wrong: A goal below 40 mg/dL may be considered (IIb B) only after a second vascular event within 2 years on a maximally tolerated statin.

options.text: 50 mg/dL or less: below 55 mg/dL and also at least a 50% fall from 100 mg/dL

stem: A 58-year-old man had a myocardial infarction 2 months ago and has had no further event. His untreated LDL-C before the MI was 100 mg/dL (2.6 mmol/L). Under ESC/EAS 2019 (goals unchanged in the 2025 focused update), what is his full LDL-C goal?

explanation:
She is on a maximally tolerated high-intensity statin and above goal, so the tree asks how big the gap is. From 62 to below 55 mg/dL she needs a fall of only about 11% (more if the 50% reduction from baseline is not yet met), which is a small gap, and the answer is ezetimibe (about 20-25% extra lowering; ESC/EAS 2019 I B; IMPROVE-IT). The guidelines frame this differently. ESC: very-high-risk goal below 1.4 mmol/L (55 mg/dL) and at least 50% reduction. ACC/AHA 2025 ACS: add a nonstatin if LDL-C is 70 mg/dL or more on maximal statin (COR 1, A), reasonable at 55-69 mg/dL (2a, B-R). Recheck lipids 4-8 weeks after the change (ACC/AHA 2025 COR 1, C-LD). Trap: treating 70 mg/dL as the finishing line after ACS.

**References:** PERKI 2024 §6.3.2 · ESC 2023 §13.3.2 · ACC/AHA 2025 §11.2 · Newer lipid documents: ESC/EAS 2025 focused update; ACC/AHA 2026 dyslipidemia guideline

options.text: Add ezetimibe: she is above the ESC goal of below 55 mg/dL, and ACC/AHA 2025 ACS rates adding a nonstatin at 55-69 mg/dL as reasonable (2a, B-R)
No change: an LDL-C below 70 mg/dL is at goal after an MI
options.why_wrong: Below 70 mg/dL is the old ACC/AHA 2018 add-on threshold (and the ESC goal for high-risk, not very-high-risk, patients). After ACS the ESC goal is below 55 mg/dL with at least a 50% fall.

options.text: Reduce atorvastatin to 40 mg because the LDL-C is already low
options.why_wrong: Statins are never down-titrated because LDL-C is low, and hers is still above goal.

options.text: Start a PCSK9 inhibitor, because ezetimibe cannot be combined with a high-intensity statin
options.why_wrong: Ezetimibe is the standard add-on to a maximally tolerated statin (ESC I B). A PCSK9 inhibitor is for a large gap, or when statin plus ezetimibe is not enough.

stem: Six weeks after an NSTEMI, a 63-year-old woman taking atorvastatin 80 mg daily (good adherence, no side effects) has an LDL-C of 62 mg/dL (1.6 mmol/L). What should be done?

explanation:
GLS detects impairment of longitudinal fibre function earlier than EF changes, which is why it is used to identify early cardiotoxicity and subclinical dysfunction in infiltrative and valvular disease.

Why the other options are wrong: It does not assess valve severity, coronary anatomy or pericardial structure — those require Doppler, angiography/CT and CT/MR respectively.

options.text: Valve stenosis severity
Subclinical systolic dysfunction before ejection fraction falls
Pericardial thickness
Coronary anatomy

stem: Global longitudinal strain is clinically valuable because it can detect:

explanation:
Dabigatran is approximately 80% renally cleared, the highest of the DOACs, and accumulates dangerously in severe renal impairment.

Why the other options are wrong: Warfarin is hepatically metabolised and usable in renal failure. Unfractionated heparin is the preferred parenteral agent in severe renal impairment. Argatroban is hepatically cleared and is used in renal failure.

options.text: Unfractionated heparin
Warfarin
Argatroban
Dabigatran

stem: Which anticoagulant is contraindicated in severe renal impairment because of predominant renal clearance?

explanation:
Functional TR predominates, driven by right ventricular and annular dilation — commonly from left-sided heart disease, pulmonary hypertension, or atrial fibrillation causing atrial-functional TR.

Why the other options are wrong: Primary causes such as endocarditis, rheumatic disease, Ebstein anomaly, carcinoid and device-lead-related injury are important but far less common.

options.text: Primary, from leaflet disease
Secondary (functional), from annular dilation and right ventricular remodelling
Caused by carcinoid syndrome
Congenital in origin

stem: Most cases of significant tricuspid regurgitation in adults are:

explanation:
The cough is bradykinin-mediated, a class effect of ACE inhibition. ARBs block the AT1 receptor directly without affecting bradykinin, so the cough resolves while RAAS blockade is preserved.

Why the other options are wrong: Switching within the ACE inhibitor class reproduces the same mechanism. Beta-blockers and thiazides are different drug classes and would abandon RAAS blockade rather than substitute for it.

options.text: A thiazide diuretic
An angiotensin receptor blocker
A beta-blocker
A different ACE inhibitor

stem: A patient develops a dry cough on ramipril. The most appropriate substitution is:

explanation:
Established atherosclerotic disease is a very-high-risk category requiring an LDL-C below 55 mg/dL and at least a 50% reduction from baseline. Ezetimibe is the usual next step, with a PCSK9 inhibitor added if the goal remains unmet.

Why the other options are wrong: 78 mg/dL is above target for this risk group. Fibrates lower triglycerides but do not achieve LDL goals. Niacin failed to improve outcomes when added to statin therapy in AIM-HIGH and HPS2-THRIVE.

options.text: Stop the statin and start niacin
Accept this as adequate control
Add ezetimibe, and a PCSK9 inhibitor if still above goal
Switch to a fibrate

stem: A patient on maximally tolerated atorvastatin has an LDL-C of 78 mg/dL two years after myocardial infarction. The next step is:

explanation:
'Valvular AF' — mechanical prosthetic valves or moderate-to-severe mitral stenosis — is the setting where DOACs are not recommended and warfarin remains standard.

Why the other options are wrong: Advanced age and CKD stage 3 are common DOAC indications with dose adjustment. Prior GI bleeding influences agent choice within the DOAC class rather than mandating warfarin.

options.text: Moderate-to-severe rheumatic mitral stenosis
Previous gastrointestinal bleeding
Chronic kidney disease stage 3
Age 78 with hypertension and diabetes

stem: Which patient with atrial fibrillation should receive WARFARIN rather than a DOAC?

explanation:
Rifampicin is a potent inducer of CYP3A4 and P-glycoprotein, substantially lowering DOAC exposure and risking stroke. Strong inducers (rifampicin, carbamazepine, phenytoin, St John's wort) are generally contraindicated with DOACs, and warfarin with INR monitoring is preferred.

Why the other options are wrong: Induction lowers rather than raises levels. This is a genuinely dangerous and frequently encountered combination in high tuberculosis-burden settings.

options.text: Reduced apixaban levels and thromboembolic risk
No clinically relevant interaction
Increased apixaban levels and bleeding risk
Apixaban becomes renally cleared

stem: A patient on apixaban for atrial fibrillation is started on rifampicin for tuberculosis. The consequence is:

explanation:
Viability testing distinguishes dysfunctional but living myocardium — hibernating from chronic hypoperfusion, or stunned after acute ischaemia — from scar, since only the former can recover contractile function.

Why the other options are wrong: Scarred segments will not improve regardless of revascularisation, which is precisely what the test is designed to exclude.

options.text: Hypertrophied
Hibernating or stunned and may recover function after revascularisation
Irreversibly scarred and will not recover
Normally contracting

stem: Viability assessment before revascularisation aims to identify myocardium that is:

explanation:
Uncomplicated Type B dissection is managed medically first. Intervention (usually TEVAR) is reserved for complications: malperfusion, rupture, rapid expansion, or refractory pain or hypertension.

Why the other options are wrong: Surgery is the default for Type A, not uncomplicated Type B. Thrombolysis and anticoagulation are dangerous and contraindicated in dissection.

options.text: Immediate thrombolysis
Emergency open surgical repair
Medical therapy with strict heart rate and blood pressure control
Anticoagulation

stem: An uncomplicated Stanford Type B dissection should initially be managed with:

explanation:
Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole inhibits CYP2C9, which metabolises the more potent S-enantiomer of warfarin, and also displaces it from protein binding — producing marked INR elevation and bleeding risk.

Why the other options are wrong: All antibiotics can raise INR modestly by disrupting gut flora vitamin K production, but co-trimoxazole is the standout for a direct pharmacokinetic interaction. It also causes hyperkalaemia with RAAS blockers.

options.text: Amoxicillin
Cephalexin
Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole
Nitrofurantoin

stem: Which antibiotic most significantly raises the INR in a patient on warfarin?

explanation:
Loop diuretic resistance is partly driven by distal tubular sodium reabsorption. Adding a thiazide blocks that segment, producing synergistic sequential nephron blockade.

Why the other options are wrong: An oral thiazide alone is far weaker than a loop diuretic. Fluids worsen congestion. High-dose ACE inhibition risks hypotension and does not address diuretic resistance.

options.text: Stop diuretics and give fluids
Add a thiazide for sequential nephron blockade
Start an ACE inhibitor at high dose
Switch to an oral thiazide alone

stem: A patient on high-dose IV furosemide has an inadequate diuretic response. The most rational next step is:

explanation:
Trastuzumab-related dysfunction is typically not dose-dependent and frequently recovers after interruption and cardioprotective therapy, often permitting rechallenge.

Why the other options are wrong: Anthracycline toxicity is cumulative-dose related and largely irreversible. Radiation causes progressive fibrosis affecting pericardium, valves and coronaries years later.

options.text: Radiotherapy to the mediastinum
Doxorubicin
Cyclophosphamide-induced haemorrhagic myocarditis
Trastuzumab

stem: Which cancer therapy is characteristically associated with cardiac dysfunction that is often REVERSIBLE on discontinuation?

explanation:
A minimum 36-hour washout is mandatory. Overlapping the two produces additive bradykinin accumulation and a sharply increased risk of angioedema.

Why the other options are wrong: No washout or deliberate overlap is dangerous. Seven days is unnecessarily long and leaves the patient without RAAS blockade.

options.text: Concurrent administration for 1 week
A washout of at least 7 days
A washout of at least 36 hours
No washout period

stem: Switching a patient from an ACE inhibitor to sacubitril-valsartan requires:

explanation:
The relative refractory period is the vulnerable window: a strong enough stimulus can trigger an action potential, but conduction is heterogeneous — the substrate for re-entrant VT/VF. This is the R-on-T phenomenon.

Why the other options are wrong: In the absolute refractory period NO stimulus can trigger a response, which is protective. The plateau falls within the absolute refractory period. Resting phase stimulation produces a normal beat.

options.text: Absolute refractory period
Relative refractory period
Resting phase
Plateau phase

stem: A premature ventricular beat falling on the peak of the T wave is dangerous because it lands in the:

explanation:
Type 2 MI results from supply-demand mismatch without an acute atherothrombotic plaque event — classically sepsis, tachyarrhythmia, severe anaemia or hypotension. Management targets the precipitant.

Why the other options are wrong: Type 1 requires plaque rupture/erosion with thrombus. Type 4a is PCI-related. Dismissing it as lab error misses real myocardial injury with prognostic weight.

**References:** PERKI 2024 §4.1 · ESC 2023 §12.1

options.text: A laboratory error
Type 1 myocardial infarction
Type 2 myocardial infarction
Type 4a myocardial infarction

stem: A patient with severe sepsis and a heart rate of 140 has a modestly elevated troponin without chest pain or ECG changes. The most likely explanation is:

explanation:
Peripartum cardiomyopathy has a recognised genetic contribution, and current guidance recommends genetic testing. Drug selection must account for lactation, and specialist input is needed on agents compatible with breastfeeding.

Why the other options are wrong: Blanket statements about ACE inhibitor safety ignore lactation considerations. Subsequent pregnancies carry substantial risk, particularly if EF has not normalised. Anticoagulation may be indicated given thromboembolic risk at low EF.

options.text: Future pregnancies carry no additional risk
Genetic testing is now recommended, and drug choice must account for breastfeeding status
ACE inhibitors are safe if she is breastfeeding and should be started immediately regardless
Anticoagulation is contraindicated

stem: A 32-year-old woman develops heart failure with EF 30% one month after delivery, with no other identifiable cause. Which is correct regarding management?

explanation:
Mavacamten is a cardiac myosin inhibitor targeting the underlying hypercontractility of HCM. It should be considered in patients with LVOT obstruction who remain symptomatic despite optimal medical therapy.

Why the other options are wrong: It is an entirely new drug class distinct from beta-blockers, calcium channel blockers and diuretics, and will not appear in older texts.

options.text: Blocks calcium channels
Is a diuretic
Inhibits cardiac myosin, reducing sarcomere hypercontractility
Blocks beta receptors

stem: Mavacamten is used in obstructive HCM because it:

explanation:
A pseudoaneurysm is a contained rupture whose wall is only pericardium and thrombus — it carries a high risk of frank rupture and generally requires surgical repair.

Why the other options are wrong: The TRUE aneurysm has a thinned but intact myocardial wall; it carries thrombus and arrhythmia risk but low rupture risk and is often managed medically. Reversing these is a classic error.

**References:** PERKI 2024 §3.6.3 · PNPK 2026 Bab III.C.2.b · ESC 2023 §12.2.2 · ACC/AHA 2025 §9.1

options.text: They are the same entity with different names
True aneurysm always requires urgent surgery
Pseudoaneurysm has an intact myocardial wall and low rupture risk
Pseudoaneurysm is a contained rupture walled off by pericardium, with high rupture risk

stem: Which distinguishes a left ventricular PSEUDOaneurysm from a true aneurysm, and why does it matter?

explanation:
Clopidogrel is the P2Y12 inhibitor studied alongside fibrinolysis (CLARITY-TIMI 28, COMMIT). The more potent agents were not evaluated in that context and are not recommended with lytic therapy.

Why the other options are wrong: Ticagrelor and prasugrel are preferred in the PCI setting but lack fibrinolysis evidence and raise bleeding concern. Cangrelor is an intravenous agent used periprocedurally.

**References:** PERKI 2024 §3.3 · ESC 2023 §6.6

options.text: Clopidogrel
Ticagrelor
Prasugrel
Cangrelor

stem: A patient is being given fibrinolysis for STEMI. Which P2Y12 inhibitor has the supporting evidence base in this setting?

explanation:
Rate control comes first. Vasodilating before heart rate is controlled produces reflex tachycardia, increasing aortic wall shear stress (dP/dt) and risking propagation of the dissection.

Why the other options are wrong: Nitroprusside is used, but only AFTER beta-blockade. Amlodipine is too slow for an emergency, and furosemide does not address the mechanism.

options.text: Intravenous furosemide
Intravenous sodium nitroprusside
Oral amlodipine
Intravenous esmolol or labetalol

stem: A patient with acute aortic dissection has BP 190/110 and heart rate 105. The correct FIRST agent is:

explanation:
In ventricular secondary MR the leaflets are structurally normal — the problem is ventricular geometry. Optimising GDMT can reduce ventricular dimensions and thereby the regurgitation before intervention is considered.

Why the other options are wrong: Proceeding straight to intervention skips the step that may itself improve the MR. Balloon valvuloplasty treats mitral STENOSIS, not regurgitation.

options.text: Transcatheter edge-to-edge repair before any medical therapy
Optimise guideline-directed medical therapy for heart failure
Mitral balloon valvuloplasty
Immediate mitral valve replacement

stem: A patient has severe secondary mitral regurgitation due to a dilated, poorly functioning left ventricle. The first management step is:

explanation:
NYHA class describes current functional limitation and can improve with treatment. ACC/AHA staging describes structural disease progression and does not move backward — a patient does not get 'destaged'.

Why the other options are wrong: They are deliberately different axes and are often assessed together in a single vignette. NYHA applies across HF phenotypes.

options.text: ACC/AHA stage is symptom-based
NYHA is symptom-based and reversible; ACC/AHA stage is structural and progressive
They measure the same thing on different scales
NYHA applies only to HFrEF

stem: NYHA class and ACC/AHA stage differ in that:

explanation:
Digoxin reduces HF hospitalisation but not mortality, so it is reserved for selected symptomatic patients already on optimal therapy, or for rate control when other agents are unsuitable.

Why the other options are wrong: It is not a mortality-reducing pillar. Beta-blockers are generally preferred for AF rate control. Digoxin has no meaningful preload effect.

options.text: Preferred rate control in all AF
Symptom and hospitalisation reduction in selected patients despite optimal therapy
First-line mortality-reducing therapy
Preload reduction

stem: The main role of digoxin in contemporary HFrEF management is:

explanation:
Bradycardia from rate-limiting medication, electrolyte disturbance, hypothyroidism, or acute ischaemia may resolve entirely once the cause is corrected, making permanent pacing unnecessary.

Why the other options are wrong: Age and sex are not reversible causes. Prior ablation may cause block, but it is not reversible in the same sense.

options.text: Prior ablation
Female sex
Rate-limiting drugs, hyperkalaemia, hypothyroidism and ischaemia
Advanced age

stem: Which reversible cause should be excluded before implanting a permanent pacemaker for symptomatic bradycardia?

explanation:
CAST found excess mortality when Class Ic agents were used to suppress PVCs after MI — presumed proarrhythmia from slowed conduction across scarred myocardium. Class Ic is contraindicated in structural heart disease.

Why the other options are wrong: Pulmonary fibrosis is an amiodarone toxicity. Bradycardia is not the limiting concern. The issue is proarrhythmic death, not pharmacokinetics.

options.text: It causes pulmonary fibrosis
It is renally cleared and accumulates
It increased mortality in structural heart disease in the CAST trial
It causes severe bradycardia

stem: Flecainide should be avoided in a patient with prior myocardial infarction and reduced LV function chiefly because:

explanation:
Free wall rupture causes abrupt haemopericardium and tamponade, presenting as sudden collapse with PEA and raised venous pressure — often fatal before intervention is possible.

Why the other options are wrong: Recurrent pain with ST elevation suggests reinfarction or stent thrombosis. Gradual troponin change and new AF are non-specific post-MI findings.

**References:** PERKI 2024 §3.6.3 · PNPK 2026 Bab III.C.2.b · ESC 2023 §12.2.2 · ACC/AHA 2025 §9.1

options.text: New atrial fibrillation
Sudden collapse with pulseless electrical activity and distended neck veins
Recurrent chest pain with new ST elevation
Gradual rise in troponin

stem: Which finding on day 3 post-MI would most specifically suggest free wall rupture rather than reinfarction?

explanation:
Only bisoprolol, carvedilol and metoprolol SUCCINATE (extended release) have mortality-benefit evidence in HFrEF. The distinction from tartrate is a frequently tested and clinically real difference.

Why the other options are wrong: Metoprolol tartrate is the immediate-release salt used for rate control and lacks the HFrEF trial evidence. Atenolol and propranolol have no HFrEF mortality data.

options.text: Atenolol
Propranolol
Metoprolol succinate
Metoprolol tartrate

stem: Which beta-blocker has established mortality benefit in HFrEF?

explanation:
SCORE2 and the older-persons algorithm SCORE2-OP predict 10-year risk of both fatal and non-fatal cardiovascular events, replacing the fatal-only original SCORE. SCORE2-Diabetes exists for type 2 diabetes.

Why the other options are wrong: The original SCORE underestimated total burden by counting only fatal events. Framingham and QRISK3 are not the ESC instruments.

options.text: SCORE, predicting fatal events only
QRISK3 exclusively
Framingham risk score
SCORE2 and SCORE2-OP, predicting fatal and non-fatal events

stem: The 2025 ESC/EAS focused update on dyslipidaemias recommends which risk algorithms?

explanation:
The guideline moved to a single, more intensive first-instance target of 120-129 mmHg systolic for most patients when tolerated, replacing the older stepwise approach.

Why the other options are wrong: The two-step approach of reaching under 140/90 first and only later considering under 130/80 reflects prior guidance and is now outdated in the European framework.

options.text: Under 140 mmHg
Under 150 mmHg in all adults

stem: Under the 2024 ESC hypertension guideline, the first-instance systolic BP treatment target for most treated patients is:

explanation:
Gradient is flow-dependent. With reduced EF and low stroke volume index (under 35), the ventricle cannot generate a high gradient even across a critically narrow valve, so a low gradient does not exclude severe stenosis.

Why the other options are wrong: Accepting 'moderate' based on gradient alone is the classic error that leads to under-treatment. Confirm with low-dose dobutamine stress echocardiography.

options.text: Possible classical low-flow, low-gradient severe aortic stenosis
Moderate aortic stenosis
Normal valve function
Severe aortic regurgitation

stem: An echo reports aortic valve area 0.8 cm², mean gradient 26 mmHg, LVEF 38% and stroke volume index 27 mL/m². The correct interpretation is:

explanation:
PREVENT estimates 10-year cardiovascular risk incorporating kidney and metabolic measures alongside traditional factors, and now guides who receives antihypertensive drug therapy.

Why the other options are wrong: The pooled cohort equations are what PREVENT replaces. SCORE2 and SCORE2-OP are the European algorithms. Framingham is older still.

options.text: The pooled cohort equations, unchanged
The Framingham risk score
The PREVENT calculator, integrating cardiovascular, kidney and metabolic health
SCORE2 only

stem: The 2025 ACC/AHA multisociety High Blood Pressure Guideline replaced the 2017 document. Which risk tool does it introduce to drive treatment decisions?

explanation:
Hypertrophy adds functioning myocytes and therefore voltage; infiltration adds mass WITHOUT electrical tissue. The discordance between wall thickness and low voltage is the single most characteristic clue.

Why the other options are wrong: Increased voltage with thick walls is the expected pattern in true hypertrophy. Axis deviation and tachycardia are non-specific.

options.text: Increased QRS voltage with thick walls
Left axis deviation
Low QRS voltage despite thick walls
Sinus tachycardia

stem: Which finding most strongly suggests cardiac amyloidosis rather than hypertensive LVH?

explanation:
Both present identically clinically and neither has persistent ST elevation. The biomarker is the discriminator: troponin elevation indicates myocardial necrosis, defining NSTEMI.

Why the other options are wrong: Persistent ST elevation would make it a STEMI. Rest pain and nitrate responsiveness occur in both.

**References:** PERKI 2024 §1.4 · ESC 2023 §2.1 · ACC/AHA 2025 §2.1

options.text: Pain at rest
Presence of ST elevation
Response to nitrates
Elevated cardiac troponin

stem: The feature that distinguishes NSTEMI from unstable angina is:

explanation:
Iron deficiency is defined independently of anaemia (ferritin under 100, or 100-299 with transferrin saturation under 20%). IV iron improves symptoms and quality of life and reduces HF hospitalisation risk.

Why the other options are wrong: Oral iron is poorly absorbed in the HF inflammatory state and did not improve outcomes in trials. Transfusion is not indicated without anaemia.

options.text: Intravenous ferric carboxymaltose
Oral ferrous sulphate
Blood transfusion
No treatment, as haemoglobin is normal

stem: A symptomatic HFrEF patient has ferritin 70 ng/mL and no anaemia. Guideline-supported management is:

explanation:
Tachycardia shortens diastole, which is precisely when the ventricle fills through the narrowed valve. Slowing the rate directly restores filling time and is mechanistically the key intervention.

Why the other options are wrong: Aggressive diuresis alone risks reducing cardiac output. ACE inhibitors are contraindicated in pregnancy. Delivery may be needed later but does not address the acute mechanism.

options.text: High-dose diuresis alone
Immediate caesarean section
Starting an ACE inhibitor
Rate control to lengthen diastole

stem: A pregnant woman with severe mitral stenosis develops rapid AF with pulmonary oedema. The most important immediate therapeutic lever is:

explanation:
CMR identifies patchy non-ischaemic scar, typically basal septal and subepicardial, while FDG-PET with appropriate dietary preparation identifies active inflammation that may respond to immunosuppression.

Why the other options are wrong: Echo and chest radiography lack sensitivity for patchy myocardial involvement. Angiography assesses coronaries, not infiltration.

options.text: Coronary angiography and left ventriculography
Exercise ECG and carotid ultrasound
Cardiac MRI with late gadolinium enhancement plus FDG-PET
Transthoracic echocardiography and chest radiography
