Because RBBB delays only the late (right ventricular) part of activation, the initial QRS vector is preserved, so Q waves of MI and ST elevation remain interpretable, unlike LBBB. T waves that are concordant with the R' (upright in V1 in RBBB), or new ST deviation, are what should raise concern. Study aid; verify thresholds against the current full guideline.

options.text: Anterior ischaemia (Wellens-type), so urgent angiography is needed
options.why_wrong: Wellens T waves occur with a narrow QRS after an episode of chest pain. With RBBB, T inversion in V1-V3 opposite to the R' is the expected secondary change.

options.text: Arrhythmogenic right ventricular cardiomyopathy, because T inversion beyond V1 is always pathological
options.why_wrong: T inversion in V1-V3 is a major ARVC criterion only in the absence of complete RBBB. In complete RBBB it is secondary and non-specific.

options.text: Secondary repolarisation change of right bundle branch block, discordant to the terminal R' wave, and expected in V1-V3
Acute pulmonary embolism, because RBBB with T inversion is diagnostic of PE
options.why_wrong: PE can cause new RBBB and anterior T inversion, but in an asymptomatic patient these findings are neither specific nor diagnostic.

stem: A 58-year-old asymptomatic man has the ECG shown on routine review. The house officer is worried about the T-wave inversion in V1-V3 and asks for urgent troponin. What is the best interpretation of those T waves?

explanation: ESC 2021 pacing guideline: in unexplained syncope with bifascicular block, an EP study should be considered; an HV interval of 70 ms or more, or second/third-degree His-Purkinje block during incremental atrial pacing or drug challenge, is a class I indication for pacing. If the EP study is negative, an implantable loop recorder is reasonable. Empirical pacing may be considered in selected elderly or frail patients (IIb). The PR of 220 ms reflects AV-node or His-Purkinje delay; it does not by itself prove the third fascicle is diseased. Study aid; verify thresholds against the current full guideline.

options.text: Electrophysiology study: pacing is indicated if the HV interval is 70 ms or more or infra-Hisian block is induced
Tilt-table testing, because a normal Holter makes an arrhythmic cause unlikely
options.why_wrong: Syncope without prodrome in bifascicular block suggests intermittent high-grade AV block; a single normal Holter does not exclude it. The conduction-system work-up comes first.

options.text: Reassurance, because a PR of 220 ms with bifascicular block is a benign 'trifascicular' finding
options.why_wrong: So-called trifascicular block (bifascicular block + prolonged PR) with unexplained syncope is the classic setting of paroxysmal infranodal AV block, not a benign finding.

options.text: ICD implantation for presumed ventricular tachycardia
options.why_wrong: With LVEF 60% and no structural disease an ICD is not indicated; the leading mechanism is bradyarrhythmic.

stem: A 74-year-old woman has had two episodes of sudden syncope without prodrome. Her ECG shows sinus rhythm, PR 220 ms, right bundle branch block and left anterior fascicular block. Echocardiography shows LVEF 60% and 24-hour Holter monitoring is unremarkable. What is the most appropriate next step according to ESC pacing guidance?

explanation: Sokolow-Lyon: SV1 + RV5 or RV6 above 35 mm. Cornell voltage: RaVL + SV3 above 28 mm in men or above 20 mm in women (Cornell product: Cornell voltage x QRS duration above 2440 mm.ms; ESC hypertension guidance). ECG criteria are specific but insensitive, so a negative ECG does not exclude LVH: echocardiography is the reference. Supporting findings are left atrial abnormality and a 'strain' pattern (downsloping ST depression with asymmetric T inversion in I, aVL, V5-V6). Study aid; verify thresholds against the current full guideline.

options.text: Both criteria are negative, because Cornell voltage needs more than 28 mm
options.why_wrong: 28 mm is the threshold for men. For women the Cornell voltage threshold is above 20 mm.

options.text: Both criteria are positive
options.why_wrong: Sokolow-Lyon (S in V1 + R in V5 or V6) is 14 + 18 = 32 mm, below the 35 mm threshold.

options.text: Cornell positive (23 mm; female cut-off 20 mm), Sokolow-Lyon negative (32 mm)
Sokolow-Lyon is positive and Cornell negative
options.why_wrong: This reverses the two sums: Sokolow-Lyon = SV1 + RV5 = 32 mm (negative), Cornell = RaVL + SV3 = 23 mm (positive in a woman).

stem: A 54-year-old woman with long-standing hypertension has these ECG voltages: S in V1 14 mm, R in V5 18 mm, R in aVL 10 mm, S in V3 13 mm (standard calibration). Which statement about LVH voltage criteria is correct?

explanation: The strip shows atrial fibrillation: irregularly irregular RR intervals, no P waves and a fibrillatory baseline, ventricular rate about 110/min. ESC 2024 AF uses CHA2DS2-VA (sex no longer scored): age 65-74 = 1, hypertension = 1, diabetes = 1 -> 3. OAC is recommended at a score of 2 or more (class I) and should be considered at 1 (IIa). DOACs are first choice (no mechanical valve, no moderate-severe MS). The AF-CARE pathway also asks to treat comorbidities (C), avoid stroke (A), reduce symptoms by rate/rhythm control (R) and evaluate dynamically (E). Study aid; verify thresholds against the current full guideline.

options.text: Oral anticoagulation with a DOAC (CHA2DS2-VA score 3)
Aspirin 100 mg daily, because this is his first documented episode
options.why_wrong: Aspirin is not recommended for stroke prevention in AF, and the first episode carries the same stroke risk as recurrent AF.

options.text: No antithrombotic therapy until the AF has lasted more than 48 hours
options.why_wrong: The 48-hour rule concerns peri-cardioversion anticoagulation, not long-term stroke prevention, which follows the risk score.

options.text: Warfarin in preference to a DOAC because of his diabetes
options.why_wrong: DOACs are preferred over VKAs except with a mechanical valve or moderate-to-severe mitral stenosis; diabetes is not a reason to choose warfarin.

stem: A 72-year-old man with hypertension and type 2 diabetes is found to have the rhythm shown on lead II. He is haemodynamically stable, creatinine clearance is 70 mL/min and he has no valve disease. Apart from rate control, which antithrombotic strategy is recommended?

explanation: Typical (counter-clockwise) flutter: atrial rate about 300/min (240-350), negative sawtooth F waves in II, III and aVF with no isoelectric baseline, positive F waves in V1; 2:1 AV conduction gives a ventricular rate of about 150/min. Rule of thumb: any regular narrow tachycardia at about 150/min is flutter with 2:1 block until proven otherwise; look for the second F wave hidden in the T wave or QRS. ESC 2019 SVT: CTI ablation is recommended for recurrent symptomatic typical flutter (class I), with very high acute success. Anticoagulation follows the same rules as AF. Study aid; verify thresholds against the current full guideline.

options.text: Slow-fast AV nodal reentry; ablation of the slow pathway
options.why_wrong: AVNRT has no atrial activity between QRS complexes. Here regular sawtooth flutter waves at about 300/min are visible, with only every second one conducted.

options.text: Macro-reentry around the tricuspid annulus through the cavotricuspid isthmus; catheter ablation of the isthmus
Focal atrial tachycardia from the crista terminalis; adenosine will terminate it permanently
options.why_wrong: Focal AT shows discrete P waves with an isoelectric baseline at 150-250/min. Here there is a continuous sawtooth baseline. Adenosine may terminate some focal ATs but does not 'permanently' cure them; in flutter it only transiently increases AV block, unmasking F waves without stopping the circuit.

options.text: Sinus tachycardia; treat the underlying cause
options.why_wrong: A fixed rate of exactly about 150/min with a sawtooth baseline in the inferior leads is flutter with 2:1 block until proven otherwise.

stem: A 60-year-old with recurrent palpitations has a regular narrow-complex tachycardia at 150/min. The lead II strip is shown. Which mechanism and definitive therapy are correct?

explanation: The strip is a regular narrow-complex tachycardia at about 170/min with no visible P waves (retrograde P at the J point): a re-entrant, AV-node-dependent SVT such as AVNRT. ESC 2019 SVT acute management of a stable patient: vagal manoeuvres (class I; the modified Valsalva - strain, then lie flat with legs raised - markedly increases success, REVERT trial), then IV adenosine as a rapid bolus with flush (class I); then IV verapamil/diltiazem or a beta-blocker (IIa); synchronised cardioversion if drugs fail or the patient becomes unstable (class I). Warn the patient about transient chest discomfort and flushing with adenosine; record a rhythm strip during administration. Study aid; verify thresholds against the current full guideline.

options.text: Immediate synchronised DC cardioversion under sedation
options.why_wrong: Cardioversion is first-line only for haemodynamically unstable SVT, or for stable SVT when vagal manoeuvres and drugs fail.

options.text: IV amiodarone infusion to terminate and prevent recurrence
options.why_wrong: Amiodarone is not a first-line drug for re-entrant SVT; vagal manoeuvres and adenosine terminate most AV-node-dependent tachycardias rapidly.

options.text: Vagal manoeuvre (modified Valsalva), then rapid IV adenosine
IV verapamil as the first step, before any vagal manoeuvre
options.why_wrong: Verapamil or diltiazem is a second-line option (after vagal manoeuvres and adenosine fail) and must be avoided in hypotension or HFrEF.

stem: A 28-year-old woman presents with sudden-onset palpitations. BP 112/70 mmHg, she is alert and has no chest pain. The rhythm strip is shown. What is the most appropriate first treatment?

explanation: In typical AVNRT the antegrade limb is the slow pathway and the retrograde limb the fast pathway, so atria and ventricles are activated almost together: the retrograde P is hidden in or just after the QRS (pseudo-S in II, III, aVF; pseudo-r' in V1), with RP below 70 ms. In orthodromic AVRT the RP is usually above 70 ms (P in the ST segment) because the circuit includes ventricular myocardium and the accessory pathway. Long-RP differential (RP > PR): atypical AVNRT, atrial tachycardia and PJRT. Comparing with a sinus-rhythm ECG is what proves the pseudo-r' is new. Study aid; verify thresholds against the current full guideline.

options.text: Orthodromic AVRT over a concealed accessory pathway
options.why_wrong: In orthodromic AVRT the impulse must travel through the ventricle before reaching the pathway, so the retrograde P sits in the ST segment with an RP usually above 70 ms.

options.text: Atypical (fast-slow) AVNRT
options.why_wrong: Atypical AVNRT is a long-RP tachycardia (RP longer than PR) with inverted P waves well before the next QRS, not a P buried at the J point.

options.text: Sinus tachycardia with first-degree AV block
options.why_wrong: Sinus P waves are upright in the inferior leads and precede the QRS; the pseudo-S is an inverted retrograde P wave.

options.text: Typical (slow-fast) AVNRT

stem: The lead II strip of the tachycardia is shown (a pseudo-S wave at the end of each QRS); on the full 12-lead there is also a pseudo-r' in V1. Both are absent in sinus rhythm, and the RP interval is about 50 ms. Which mechanism best fits?

explanation: Pre-excitation: short PR (below 120 ms), delta wave and a wide QRS with secondary ST-T changes. Localising rules: delta positive in V1 (RBBB-like, 'type A') = left-sided pathway; delta negative in I and aVL = lateral left ventricular wall activated first = left lateral pathway, the commonest location. Negative delta in V1 = right-sided; negative delta in II, III, aVF = posteroseptal. Knowing the location matters for ablation planning (transseptal or retrograde aortic access for left-sided pathways) and for not mislabelling the negative delta in I/aVL as a lateral infarction. Study aid; verify thresholds against the current full guideline.

options.text: Right free wall
options.why_wrong: Right-sided pathways pre-excite the right ventricle first, giving a negative delta wave in V1 (LBBB-like pattern) and a positive delta in I and aVL.

options.text: Left lateral (left free wall) atrioventricular groove
Posteroseptal region near the coronary sinus ostium
options.why_wrong: Posteroseptal pathways give negative delta waves in the inferior leads (II, III, aVF), often mimicking inferior Q waves.

options.text: Anteroseptal region near the His bundle
options.why_wrong: Anteroseptal pathways give a positive delta in I, II and aVF with a negative or isoelectric delta in V1.

stem: A 19-year-old has the resting ECG shown. In the delta waves, the initial QRS deflection is negative in leads I and aVL and positive in V1. Where is the accessory pathway most likely located?

explanation: Irregular + wide + varying QRS morphology at very high rates in a patient with WPW = pre-excited AF. A shortest pre-excited RR of 250 ms or less marks a high-risk pathway. ESC 2019 SVT: haemodynamically unstable -> synchronised cardioversion (I); stable -> IV ibutilide or procainamide (IIa) or flecainide/propafenone (IIb), cardioversion if drugs fail (I). IV amiodarone is not recommended (III) and AV-nodal blockers (verapamil, diltiazem, beta-blockers, digoxin, adenosine) must be avoided. Definitive therapy is catheter ablation of the pathway (class I after pre-excited AF). Study aid; verify thresholds against the current full guideline.

options.text: IV verapamil to slow AV-node conduction
options.why_wrong: Blocking the AV node removes the competing conduction (and its concealed conduction into the pathway), so more impulses pass the accessory pathway; ventricular fibrillation can follow.

options.text: IV adenosine to reveal the underlying rhythm
options.why_wrong: Adenosine is AV-nodal blocking and can accelerate conduction over the pathway in pre-excited AF; the rhythm is already evident (irregular, varying QRS width).

options.text: IV digoxin for ventricular rate control
options.why_wrong: Digoxin shortens the accessory pathway refractory period and blocks the AV node: contraindicated in pre-excited AF.

options.text: IV procainamide or ibutilide; cardiovert if he deteriorates

stem: The young man whose baseline ECG is shown now presents with palpitations: an irregular, very fast wide-complex tachycardia with QRS width that varies from beat to beat; the shortest RR is about 200 ms. BP 108/70 mmHg, he is alert. Which treatment is appropriate?

explanation: Wide-complex tachycardia (QRS 120 ms or more) is VT until proven otherwise, especially after MI (about 80% of WCT overall, more than 90% with structural heart disease). AV dissociation (more QRS than P waves, P waves unrelated to QRS), capture beats and fusion beats are highly specific for VT but are visible in only a minority of tracings. Other VT clues: very wide QRS (>140 ms RBBB-like, >160 ms LBBB-like), extreme ('northwest') axis, precordial concordance, initial R in aVR, and Brugada step 1-2 criteria. Study aid; verify thresholds against the current full guideline.

options.text: The rate of about 170/min
options.why_wrong: Rate does not discriminate: both VT and SVT with aberrancy commonly run at 150-200/min.

options.text: The regularity of the RR intervals
options.why_wrong: Monomorphic VT and SVT with aberrancy are both regular; regularity does not separate them.

options.text: AV dissociation (P waves unrelated to the QRS complexes)
The patient's preserved consciousness, which argues for SVT
options.why_wrong: Haemodynamic tolerance does not exclude VT; many patients in VT are conscious with a normal blood pressure. Treating 'stable means SVT' is a classic dangerous trap.

stem: A 67-year-old with a prior anterior MI has the regular wide-complex tachycardia shown at about 170/min; P waves (marked) are visible at a slower, independent rate. Which feature of this tracing most specifically establishes the diagnosis?

explanation: ESC 2022 VA: tolerated sustained monomorphic VT -> electrical cardioversion is first-line provided the anaesthetic/sedation risk is low (class I). IV procainamide should be considered in patients with known or suspected structural heart disease (IIa); IV amiodarone may be considered (IIb). After termination: ischaemia work-up, LVEF, and in post-MI scar VT, ICD and/or catheter ablation as indicated. AHA ACLS allows adenosine for a stable, regular, monomorphic wide-complex tachycardia; it may terminate SVT with aberrancy and some idiopathic (outflow-tract) VT, but scar-related VT is usually unaffected. Study aid; verify thresholds against the current full guideline.

options.text: IV verapamil, which is safe because he is haemodynamically stable
options.why_wrong: Verapamil in VT can cause profound hypotension and arrest; it is never given for an undiagnosed wide-complex tachycardia.

options.text: Unsynchronised defibrillation at maximum energy
options.why_wrong: Unsynchronised shocks are for pulseless VT, VF or polymorphic VT; a shock on the T wave of organised VT risks VF. Monomorphic VT with a pulse is cardioverted synchronised.

options.text: Synchronised DC cardioversion under sedation
IV metoprolol for rate control and observation, since stable VT is benign
options.why_wrong: Sustained VT is never 'rate-controlled'; it must be terminated, and the substrate (prior MI scar) then needs evaluation for ICD/ablation.

stem: The same patient (rhythm shown) has BP 118/72 mmHg, no chest pain and a normal mental state. Sedation can be given safely by the anaesthetist. According to ESC 2022 ventricular arrhythmia guidance, what is the recommended first-line treatment?

explanation: Brugada algorithm (1991), each 'yes' = VT: (1) absence of an RS complex in all precordial leads; (2) RS interval above 100 ms in any precordial lead; (3) AV dissociation; (4) morphology criteria for VT in both V1-V2 and V6. Only if all four are negative is SVT with aberrancy diagnosed. Sensitivity is high but specificity falls in pre-excited tachycardia, patients on class I drugs and pre-existing BBB. The Vereckei aVR algorithm is an alternative (initial R in aVR, initial r or q >40 ms, notched negative onset, vi/vt <=1 = VT). Study aid; verify thresholds against the current full guideline.

options.text: SVT with aberrancy, because RS complexes are present so step 1 is negative
options.why_wrong: A negative step 1 only means you continue to step 2; it does not prove SVT. The algorithm calls SVT only after all four steps are negative.

options.text: Indeterminate until the V1 and V6 morphology criteria (step 4) are applied
options.why_wrong: The algorithm is sequential: as soon as one step is positive, the diagnosis is VT and later steps are not needed.

options.text: VT only if the RS interval exceeds 140 ms
options.why_wrong: 140 ms is the QRS-width criterion for a RBBB-like VT. The RS (R onset to S nadir) cut-off in Brugada step 2 is 100 ms.

options.text: VT, established at step 2 (RS interval above 100 ms in a precordial lead)

stem: A regular wide-complex tachycardia is analysed with the Brugada algorithm. RS complexes are present in V3-V5. In V4 the interval from the onset of the R wave to the nadir of the S wave is 110 ms. P waves cannot be identified. What is the conclusion?

explanation: Mobitz I (Wenckebach): progressive PR prolongation until a P wave is not conducted, then reset; RR intervals shorten before the pause and the pause is less than twice the PP, producing grouped beating. With a narrow QRS the level is almost always the AV node, it worsens with vagal tone (sleep, athletes) and improves with exercise or atropine. ESC 2021: pacing is not indicated for asymptomatic Mobitz I due to vagal tone; it is considered for symptomatic Mobitz I or when EP study proves an infranodal level. Study aid; verify thresholds against the current full guideline.

options.text: Infranodal (His-Purkinje) block; permanent pacemaker
options.why_wrong: Progressive PR prolongation before the dropped beat is the signature of decremental AV-nodal conduction; infranodal block drops beats without warning (constant PR).

options.text: AV-nodal block with high vagal tone; no pacing, reassurance
Complete heart block with junctional escape; temporary pacing
options.why_wrong: Conducted beats have a PR that lengthens and then resets after the pause: P waves and QRS are related, so this is not AV dissociation.

options.text: Mobitz II; avoid exercise until an EP study
options.why_wrong: Mobitz II has a constant PR before the non-conducted P wave. This strip shows progressive PR lengthening and grouped beating, i.e. Mobitz I.

stem: A 21-year-old marathon runner is asymptomatic. This strip was captured at 03:00 on a Holter recorder; the QRS is narrow. What are the level of block and the appropriate management?

explanation: Mobitz II: constant PR in conducted beats, then sudden failure of conduction of a P wave; usually with BBB (wide QRS), because the lesion is in the His-Purkinje system. It may progress abruptly to complete heart block with a slow, unreliable ventricular escape. ESC 2021 pacing: permanent pacing is indicated (class I) in second-degree Mobitz II, high-degree and third-degree AV block irrespective of symptoms, once reversible causes (drugs, hyperkalaemia, acute ischaemia, Lyme disease) are excluded. Atropine helps nodal block; isoprenaline or pacing is used for infranodal block. Study aid; verify thresholds against the current full guideline.

options.text: The block is in the AV node, so pacing is needed only if syncope occurs
options.why_wrong: Constant PR with a sudden non-conducted P wave plus a wide QRS localises disease to the His-Purkinje system, which carries a high risk of progression to complete block.

options.text: Infranodal block: pace even if asymptomatic; atropine may worsen it
Atropine is the definitive treatment because it improves AV conduction
options.why_wrong: Atropine speeds the sinus rate and AV node but not the His-Purkinje system; the higher atrial rate can produce more infranodal block.

options.text: This is Mobitz I, because a beat is dropped
options.why_wrong: Both Mobitz types drop beats; the discriminator is the PR before the pause: progressive lengthening in Mobitz I, constant in Mobitz II.

stem: A 76-year-old woman with occasional light-headedness has the rhythm strip shown: the conducted beats have a constant PR interval and a wide QRS (bundle branch block form). Electrolytes and medications are unremarkable. Which statement is correct?

explanation: Third-degree AV block: atrial and ventricular rhythms are each regular but independent (PP constant, RR constant, PR varying randomly), with the atrial rate faster than the ventricular rate. A wide escape at 30-40/min indicates a ventricular (infranodal) escape focus, which is slow and unreliable. In unstable bradycardia (hypotension, altered mental state, shock, ischaemia, heart failure): atropine may be tried, but expect little effect in infranodal block; use adrenaline/dopamine or isoprenaline infusion and pacing (transcutaneous as a bridge to transvenous). Then exclude reversible causes and implant a permanent pacemaker (ESC 2021 class I for third-degree block). Study aid; verify thresholds against the current full guideline.

options.text: IV amiodarone to suppress the wide ventricular complexes
options.why_wrong: The wide complexes are the escape rhythm keeping her alive; suppressing them can cause asystole.

options.text: Arrange elective permanent pacemaker implantation next week, as she is not in cardiac arrest
options.why_wrong: Hypotension and reduced consciousness are signs of haemodynamic compromise; she needs immediate rate support now, and permanent pacing once stable.

options.text: Temporary pacing or a chronotropic infusion now
Synchronised DC cardioversion
options.why_wrong: Cardioversion treats tachyarrhythmias; it has no role in complete heart block and the shock cannot synchronise usefully to restore conduction.

stem: A 79-year-old is drowsy and pale with BP 80/50 mmHg. The rhythm strip shown has regular P waves at about 75/min and regular wide QRS complexes at about 38/min with no fixed relationship between them. What is the most appropriate immediate management?

explanation:
Inferior MI (usually RCA): the AV-nodal artery and vagal (Bezold-Jarisch) reflexes cause AV-nodal block - progressive (first degree -> Wenckebach -> complete), narrow junctional escape, often atropine-responsive and transient after reperfusion. Anterior MI (proximal LAD): septal necrosis damages the bundle branches - Mobitz II or complete block with a wide, slow escape, often preceded by new bifascicular block; mortality is high because it reflects infarct size. ESC 2021: permanent pacing after acute MI is decided only after a waiting period of several days, because much of the block resolves after reperfusion. Study aid; verify thresholds against the current full guideline.

**References:** PERKI 2024 §3.6.2 · ESC 2023 §12.2.5 · ACC/AHA 2025 §9.2

options.text: Patient 1: nodal block, narrow escape, often transient; patient 2: infranodal block, wide escape, worse prognosis
Both have AV-nodal block that resolves in most cases within days
options.why_wrong: Anterior MI causes block by necrosis of the septum and bundle branches (infranodal); it rarely resolves and signals a large infarct.

options.text: Patient 1 needs immediate permanent pacing, while patient 2 can be observed
options.why_wrong: This reverses the risk: inferior-MI block is usually transient (reperfuse first, temporary pacing only if unstable), whereas anterior-MI block is unstable and often needs pacing.

options.text: Both have the same mechanism: ischaemia of the sinus node
options.why_wrong: AV block concerns the AV node or the His-Purkinje system, not the sinus node. The AV-nodal artery arises from the RCA in about 80-90% (right-dominant) circulations.

stem: Two patients develop complete heart block during acute STEMI: patient 1 with an inferior STEMI, patient 2 with an extensive anterior STEMI. Which statement is correct?

explanation:
Anterior leads V1-V4 = LAD territory. ST elevation in I and aVL (high lateral, first diagonal territory) plus reciprocal depression in II, III, aVF localises the occlusion proximal to D1; elevation in V1 (and aVR) suggests a site proximal to the first septal branch. Proximal LAD STEMI puts a large myocardial mass at risk. ESC 2023: primary PCI is the reperfusion of choice when it can be delivered within 120 minutes of STEMI diagnosis; otherwise fibrinolysis within 10 minutes of diagnosis. Study aid; verify thresholds against the current full guideline.

**References:** PERKI 2024 §1.5.2.1 · PNPK 2026 Bab III.B.4.a · ESC 2023 §3.2.1 · ACC/AHA 2025 §3.1.2

options.text: Mid-to-distal occlusion of a 'wrap-around' LAD
options.why_wrong: A wrap-around LAD supplying the inferior apex gives concomitant inferior ST elevation, not inferior reciprocal depression, and spares I/aVL.

options.text: Proximal LAD occlusion (before the first diagonal branch)
Left circumflex occlusion
options.why_wrong: LCx occlusion gives lateral (I, aVL, V5-V6) and/or posterior changes (ST depression V1-V3), not ST elevation from V1.

options.text: Left main occlusion
options.why_wrong: Left main occlusion typically presents with diffuse ST depression and ST elevation in aVR (often with shock); ST elevation localised to V1-V4 with I/aVL points to the LAD.

stem: A 55-year-old smoker has had 1 hour of chest pain. In the ECG shown there is ST elevation in V1-V4 that extends to I and aVL, with reciprocal ST depression in the inferior leads. Which culprit lesion is most likely?

explanation:
Lead III faces about +120 degrees, i.e. rightward-inferior, the RCA territory; lead II faces +60 degrees. The ST vector in RCA occlusion points rightward and inferiorly, so ST elevation III > II and reciprocal depression in I and aVL (which face leftward). LCx occlusion directs the ST vector leftward: II >= III and I/aVL not depressed. Next steps in an RCA inferior STEMI: right-sided leads (V4R) for RV involvement, posterior leads if V1-V3 are depressed, and watch for AV block and vagal bradycardia/hypotension. Study aid; verify thresholds against the current full guideline.

**References:** PERKI 2024 §1.5.2.1 · PNPK 2026 Bab III.B.4.a · ESC 2023 §3.2.1 · ACC/AHA 2025 §3.1.2

options.text: Left circumflex artery
options.why_wrong: LCx occlusion favours ST elevation in II at least equal to III, with an isoelectric or elevated ST in I/aVL and sometimes lateral V5-V6 elevation.

options.text: Left anterior descending artery
options.why_wrong: An LAD occlusion produces anterior ST elevation (V1-V4); only a wrap-around LAD adds inferior elevation, and then without the III > II pattern and reciprocal I/aVL depression.

options.text: Right coronary artery
First diagonal branch
options.why_wrong: Isolated D1 occlusion gives ST elevation in I, aVL (and V2) with inferior reciprocal depression, the opposite of this tracing.

stem: A 62-year-old has inferior ST elevation, shown in the ECG: the elevation is greater in lead III than in lead II, and there is ST depression in I and aVL. Which artery is most likely occluded?

explanation:
Triad of RV infarction: hypotension, raised JVP, clear lungs (Kussmaul sign may be present) in an inferior (proximal RCA) STEMI. ST elevation in V4R is the most useful ECG marker (Fourth Universal Definition: 0.5 mm or more in V3R/V4R, 1 mm or more in men younger than 30; classic teaching uses 1 mm in V4R) but it is transient, often gone within 12 hours, so record it early. Management: early reperfusion, maintain preload (avoid nitrates, diuretics, morphine excess), cautious fluids, treat bradycardia/AV block (AV-sequential pacing if needed), inotropes if hypotension persists. Study aid; verify thresholds against the current full guideline.

**References:** PERKI 2024 §3.6 · PNPK 2026 Bab III.C.2.b · ESC 2023 §12.2 · ACC/AHA 2025 §9

options.text: Sublingual nitroglycerin to relieve the ongoing ischaemic pain
options.why_wrong: Nitrates reduce preload, on which an infarcted right ventricle depends; they can precipitate profound hypotension in RV infarction and are contraindicated with SBP below 90 mmHg.

options.text: IV furosemide to offload the raised jugular venous pressure
options.why_wrong: The raised JVP with clear lungs reflects RV failure, not LV fluid overload; diuresis drops preload and worsens hypotension.

options.text: Posterior leads V7-V9 before anything else
options.why_wrong: Posterior leads are used when V1-V3 show isolated ST depression; with hypotension, raised JVP and clear lungs in an inferior STEMI the question is RV infarction, assessed with V4R.

options.text: Record V4R; if RV infarction, avoid nitrates and give IV fluid

source: ESC 2023 §12.2; ACC/AHA 2025 §9; PERKI 2024 §3.6; PNPK 2026 Bab III.C.2.b
stem: The patient with the inferior STEMI shown becomes hypotensive (BP 84/56 mmHg) with clear lung fields and a raised JVP. The cath lab is being activated. Which immediate step is most appropriate?

explanation:
Posterior (inferobasal) MI is usually LCx or RCA occlusion. V1-V3 view the posterior wall from the front, so posterior ST elevation appears as ST depression, posterior Q waves as tall broad R waves, and posterior T inversion as upright T waves (the 'mirror test'). Fourth Universal Definition of MI and ESC 2023: ST elevation of 0.5 mm or more in V7-V9 (1 mm or more in men younger than 40) = posterior STEMI -> primary PCI pathway. Isolated ST depression of 0.5 mm or more in V1-V3 is the cue to record V7-V9. Study aid; verify thresholds against the current full guideline.

**References:** PERKI 2024 §1.5.2.1 · PNPK 2026 Bab III.B.4.a · ESC 2023 §3.2 · ACC/AHA 2025 §3.1.2

options.text: 2 mm or more, as in V2-V3
options.why_wrong: 2 mm is the V2-V3 threshold in men aged 40 or more. The posterior leads are far from the heart, so their threshold is lower.

options.text: 1 mm or more in at least two leads, as in the limb leads
options.why_wrong: 1 mm is the threshold for most standard leads and for V7-V9 only in men younger than 40.

options.text: 0.5 mm (0.05 mV) or more
No threshold applies: troponin must decide
options.why_wrong: Reperfusion is decided on the ECG and symptoms, not on troponin; waiting for troponin delays treatment of an occluded artery.

stem: A 59-year-old has ongoing chest pain. The ECG shown has ST depression in V1-V3 with tall R waves and upright T waves; there is no ST elevation in the standard leads. Posterior leads are recorded. Which ST elevation in V7-V9 confirms a posterior STEMI in this patient?

explanation:
Wellens syndrome: history of anginal pain, now pain-free; type A = biphasic T (up then down) in V2-V3, type B (about 75%) = deep symmetric T inversion; little or no ST elevation, preserved precordial R waves, no pathological Q waves; normal or mildly raised troponin. It indicates a critical proximal LAD stenosis with spontaneous reperfusion. Manage as high-risk NSTE-ACS with an early invasive strategy (ESC 2023) and avoid stress testing. If pain recurs with ST elevation, treat as STEMI. Study aid; verify thresholds against the current full guideline.

**References:** PERKI 2024 §1.5.2.1 · PNPK 2026 Bab III.B.4.a · ESC 2023 §3.2 · ACC/AHA 2025 §3.1.2

options.text: Exercise stress test to provoke ischaemia before deciding on angiography
options.why_wrong: Stress testing in Wellens syndrome can precipitate an anterior STEMI because the proximal LAD lesion is critical.

options.text: Immediate fibrinolysis
options.why_wrong: There is no ST elevation and the patient is pain-free; fibrinolysis is not indicated without STEMI criteria.

options.text: Discharge with outpatient follow-up, because the patient is pain-free and the ECG shows no ST elevation
options.why_wrong: The pain-free state is exactly when Wellens T waves are seen; the artery has reperfused but remains critically narrowed and prone to reocclusion.

options.text: Admit and arrange early coronary angiography for a probable critical proximal LAD stenosis; avoid stress testing

stem: A 52-year-old had 2 hours of chest pain last night and is now pain-free. hs-cTn is minimally elevated. The ECG taken pain-free is shown: deep symmetric T-wave inversion in V2-V3, preserved R waves, no pathological Q waves and little ST deviation. What is the best next step?

explanation:
de Winter pattern: 1-3 mm upsloping ST depression at the J point in V1-V6 that continues into tall, positive, symmetric T waves, often with 0.5-1 mm ST elevation in aVR and a normal QRS. It occurs in about 2% of acute LAD occlusions, typically proximal. It is a STEMI-equivalent ('occlusion MI') pattern: with ongoing symptoms it is managed like STEMI, with immediate reperfusion by primary PCI (ACC/AHA 2025 tells clinicians to manage 'ST-segment elevation or equivalent' on the STEMI pathway; de Winter is not named in the guideline table and is drawn from de Winter et al. 2008). Distinguish it from hyperkalaemia (narrow-based peaked T, short QT, no J-point depression) and from benign early repolarisation. Study aid; verify thresholds against the current full guideline.

**References:** PERKI 2024 §1.5.2.1 · PNPK 2026 Bab III.B.4.a · ESC 2023 §3.2 · ACC/AHA 2025 §3.1.2

options.text: Activate primary PCI as a STEMI equivalent
NSTE-ACS pathway with angiography within 24 hours
options.why_wrong: This pattern reflects an acute LAD occlusion despite the absence of ST elevation; delaying reperfusion loses myocardium.

options.text: Repeat the ECG and hs-cTn in 1 hour before deciding
options.why_wrong: Serial troponin is for possible NSTE-ACS; an occlusion pattern with ongoing pain needs immediate reperfusion, not observation.

options.text: Treat for hyperkalaemia, because the T waves are tall
options.why_wrong: The potassium is normal, and hyperacute T waves rising from upsloping J-point depression in the precordial leads with chest pain are the de Winter pattern.

stem: A 49-year-old has had 45 minutes of crushing chest pain. The ECG shown has 1-3 mm upsloping ST depression at the J point in V1-V6 continuing into tall, symmetric T waves, and slight ST elevation in aVR. Potassium is 4.2 mmol/L. What is the next step?

explanation:
Original Sgarbossa (GUSTO-1, 1996): concordant ST elevation 1 mm or more in any lead = 5; concordant ST depression 1 mm or more in V1-V3 = 3; discordant ST elevation 5 mm or more = 2. A score of 3 or more is specific (about 90%) but insensitive. Smith-modified Sgarbossa (2012) replaces the absolute 5 mm with a proportion: discordant ST elevation/S-wave depth of 0.25 or more (6/20 = 0.30 here), which improves sensitivity while keeping specificity. Both apply to ventricular paced rhythms too. ESC 2023: patients with LBBB (or pacing) and ongoing ischaemic symptoms should be managed like STEMI whatever the score; the score supports the decision, it does not replace clinical judgement. Study aid; verify thresholds against the current full guideline.

**References:** PERKI 2024 §1.5.2.1 · PNPK 2026 Bab III.B.4.a · ESC 2023 §3.2.1 · ACC/AHA 2025 §3.1.2

options.text: Original Sgarbossa score is 5, which is diagnostic of acute MI
options.why_wrong: 5 points are given only for concordant ST elevation of 1 mm or more. Discordant ST elevation of 5 mm or more scores 2.

options.text: Both criteria are negative, because discordant ST elevation is always expected in LBBB
options.why_wrong: Discordant ST elevation is expected, but excessive discordance relative to the QRS (ST/S ratio of 0.25 or more) is the Smith-modified marker of occlusion.

options.text: Original Sgarbossa score is 3, because any ST elevation above 5 mm in V1-V3 scores 3
options.why_wrong: 3 points are given for concordant ST depression of 1 mm or more in V1-V3, not for discordant ST elevation.

options.text: Sgarbossa score 2 (not diagnostic) but Smith-modified positive (ST/S 0.30)

stem: A 71-year-old with known LBBB has ongoing chest pain. In V2 the S wave is 20 mm deep with 6 mm of ST elevation (discordant). No lead shows concordant ST elevation, and there is no concordant ST depression in V1-V3. Which statement is correct?

explanation: Tall, narrow-based, peaked ('tented') T waves with a short QT are the earliest ECG sign of hyperkalaemia. Progression: PR prolongation and P-wave flattening -> QRS widening -> sine wave -> VF/asystole; the ECG correlates poorly with the exact level, so any change is an emergency. Order: (1) protect - IV calcium (gluconate or chloride), repeat if the ECG does not improve; (2) shift - insulin + glucose, nebulised salbutamol (bicarbonate if acidotic); (3) remove - binders, diuretics, dialysis; stop the culprit drugs (ACEi, MRA). Calcium does not change the serum potassium. Study aid; verify thresholds against the current full guideline.

options.text: IV calcium gluconate, to stabilise the myocardial membrane
IV insulin with glucose first; calcium is reserved for sine-wave patterns
options.why_wrong: Insulin-glucose shifts potassium into cells but takes 15-30 minutes. Any hyperkalaemic ECG change is an indication for IV calcium first.

options.text: Oral sodium polystyrene sulfonate as the first step
options.why_wrong: Binders remove potassium over hours to days; they do nothing to protect against an imminent arrhythmia.

options.text: IV furosemide alone
options.why_wrong: Loop diuretics remove potassium slowly and depend on residual renal function; they are not a first-line emergency treatment with ECG changes.

stem: A 64-year-old with chronic kidney disease on an ACE inhibitor and spironolactone has serum potassium 7.0 mmol/L and the ECG shown. What should be given first, and why?

explanation: Severe hyperkalaemia depolarises the resting membrane, inactivating fast sodium channels: conduction slows, the QRS widens and merges with the T wave into a sine wave, which precedes VF or asystole. Treatment: IV calcium immediately (the ECG should improve within minutes; repeat if not), insulin-glucose and salbutamol, sodium bicarbonate if acidotic, and definitive removal by haemodialysis in a dialysis-dependent patient. In cardiac arrest from hyperkalaemia, ALS continues with calcium and shift therapy, and dialysis during CPR can be considered. Study aid; verify thresholds against the current full guideline.

options.text: Ventricular tachycardia: give IV amiodarone, then cardiovert if needed
options.why_wrong: The broad 'sine-wave' complex is the QRS fusing with the T wave in severe hyperkalaemia. Antiarrhythmics do not treat it and can worsen conduction.

options.text: Peri-arrest hyperkalaemia: IV calcium now, shift therapy, urgent dialysis
Synchronised cardioversion is the first treatment
options.why_wrong: Cardioversion does not reverse the depolarised membrane; calcium does. Shocks can provoke asystole in severe hyperkalaemia.

options.text: Wait for the laboratory potassium result before starting any treatment
options.why_wrong: With this ECG in a dialysis patient who missed sessions, treatment must start immediately; a point-of-care or laboratory value only confirms it.

stem: A haemodialysis patient who missed two sessions arrives weak and confused, with the ECG shown. Which statement is correct?

explanation: Bazett: QTc = QT / sqrt(RR in seconds) = 440 / sqrt(0.64) = 440 / 0.8 = 550 ms. Prolonged QTc: 450 ms or more in men, 460 ms or more in women; a QTc above 500 ms, or an increase of more than 60 ms from baseline, is the usual threshold to stop or avoid QT-prolonging drugs because torsades risk rises steeply. Bazett overcorrects at fast rates (it overestimates the QTc), so Fridericia (QT / cube root of RR) is often preferred above about 90/min - but even with Fridericia this QTc stays above 500 ms. Measure QT in lead II or V5 using the tangent method; exclude U waves. Study aid; verify thresholds against the current full guideline.

options.text: 440 ms: normal, no action needed
options.why_wrong: This is the uncorrected QT; at a rate of 94/min the QT must be corrected for the shorter RR.

options.text: About 550 ms: stop the drug and correct K and Mg
About 690 ms: give IV magnesium now for torsades
options.why_wrong: 440/0.64 forgets the square root. Bazett divides QT by the square root of RR (in seconds): 440/0.8 = 550 ms. Magnesium is for torsades or a very prolonged QT with ectopy, not for a miscalculated value.

options.text: About 350 ms: short QT, so the drug can continue
options.why_wrong: This multiplies by the square root of RR instead of dividing (440 x 0.8).

stem: A 70-year-old receiving IV haloperidol for delirium has a QT interval of 440 ms at a heart rate of about 94/min (RR 0.64 s). Using Bazett's formula, what is the QTc, and what is the appropriate action?

explanation: Only the type 1 (coved) pattern is diagnostic: J-point/ST elevation of 2 mm or more in at least one right precordial lead (V1-V2, standard or 2nd-3rd intercostal space) with a coved ST segment followed by a negative T wave. Type 2 (saddle-back) is suggestive only. High-placed V1-V2 leads increase sensitivity, and a drug challenge can unmask type 1. ESC 2022: a spontaneous type 1 pattern establishes the diagnosis; an induced type 1 pattern requires supporting clinical features (arrhythmic syncope, family history). Avoid fever (treat promptly with antipyretics) and the drugs listed on brugadadrugs.org. In an asymptomatic person without family history, an induced type 1 pattern alone carries low arrhythmic risk (ESC 2022: Brugada syndrome 'may be considered', IIb); the drug test should be done in a monitored setting and only if the result would change management. Study aid; verify thresholds against the current full guideline.

options.text: High V1-V2 leads (2nd-3rd intercostal space), then consider a sodium-channel blocker challenge
Implant a prophylactic ICD now to prevent sudden death
options.why_wrong: An ICD is for patients who survived cardiac arrest or have sustained VT (class I), or with a spontaneous type 1 pattern and arrhythmic syncope (IIa); a type 2 pattern in an asymptomatic person is not an indication.

options.text: Exercise stress test to unmask a type 1 pattern at peak exercise
options.why_wrong: Brugada ST elevation is accentuated at rest, by vagal tone, fever and sodium-channel blockers; exercise testing is used for long QT and CPVT.

options.text: Start a beta-blocker to suppress ventricular arrhythmias
options.why_wrong: Beta-blockers do not prevent Brugada arrhythmias; isoproterenol (acute electrical storm) and quinidine are the drugs that do.

stem: An asymptomatic 34-year-old man has a 'saddle-back' ST elevation of 2 mm in V2 (type 2 Brugada pattern) on a screening ECG. There is no family history of sudden death. What is the most appropriate next diagnostic step?

explanation: Genotype-trigger-ECG triad: LQT1 (KCNQ1, IKs loss) - exercise, especially swimming; broad-based T waves; best response to beta-blockers. LQT2 (KCNH2/hERG, IKr loss) - auditory triggers, emotion, postpartum; low-amplitude notched T. LQT3 (SCN5A, late INa gain) - rest/sleep; long ST segment, late peaked T; mexiletine can shorten QT. ESC 2022: beta-blockers (nadolol or propranolol preferred) are recommended for LQTS patients with documented QT prolongation; avoid QT-prolonging drugs; ICD after cardiac arrest or recurrent arrhythmic syncope despite beta-blockers; left cardiac sympathetic denervation as an adjunct. Study aid; verify thresholds against the current full guideline.

options.text: LQT1 (KCNQ1, reduced IKs); a non-selective beta-blocker such as nadolol or propranolol
LQT2 (KCNH2, reduced IKr); mexiletine
options.why_wrong: LQT2 events are typically triggered by sudden auditory stimuli or emotion and in the postpartum period, with notched T waves; beta-blockers are still first-line.

options.text: LQT3 (SCN5A, gain of late sodium current); events during exercise
options.why_wrong: LQT3 events occur at rest or during sleep (bradycardia-dependent), with a long isoelectric ST segment and late T wave.

options.text: Brugada syndrome; quinidine
options.why_wrong: Brugada syndrome shows coved right precordial ST elevation, not QT prolongation, and events occur at rest or sleep, often with fever.

stem: A 16-year-old girl has had two syncopal episodes while swimming. Her resting QTc is repeatedly 490 ms with broad-based T waves; electrolytes are normal and she takes no drugs. Which genotype is most likely and what is first-line therapy?

explanation: Acute pericarditis (ESC 2015 criteria): diagnosis needs 2 of 4 - pericarditic chest pain, friction rub, new widespread ST elevation or PR depression, new or worsening effusion; the 2025 ESC myocarditis and pericarditis guidelines also count raised CRP and CMR evidence of pericardial inflammation as supporting criteria. First-line therapy is unchanged in ESC 2025 (aspirin or NSAID plus colchicine, class I). Treatment: aspirin or NSAID at high dose with gastroprotection plus colchicine (weight-adjusted, for at least 3 months) - colchicine halves recurrences; exercise restriction until resolution. Corticosteroids are second line. ECG stages (Spodick): I diffuse ST elevation + PR depression; II normalisation; III T inversion; IV normal. Study aid; verify thresholds against the current full guideline.

options.text: Primary PCI, because there is ST elevation in several territories
options.why_wrong: Diffuse concave ST elevation with PR depression, no reciprocal change outside aVR/V1, normal wall motion and normal troponin point to pericarditis, not occlusion.

options.text: Corticosteroids as first-line therapy
options.why_wrong: Corticosteroids are second-line (contraindication or failure of aspirin/NSAID and colchicine, or specific indications) because they increase recurrence.

options.text: Therapeutic anticoagulation for the effusion
options.why_wrong: Anticoagulation has no role and may cause haemopericardium.

options.text: High-dose aspirin or an NSAID (with gastroprotection) plus colchicine

stem: A 32-year-old has pleuritic chest pain that improves on sitting forward, two weeks after a viral illness. The ECG is shown; echocardiography shows a small effusion and normal wall motion, troponin is normal. What is the recommended first-line therapy?

explanation:
Pericarditis vs early repolarisation: in pericarditis the ST elevation is diffuse (limb and precordial leads), with PR depression (atrial injury current) and PR elevation/ST depression in aVR; the ST/T ratio in V6 is 0.25 or more and the ECG evolves over time. Early repolarisation: young men, athletes; ST elevation mainly in V2-V5 with tall T waves, J-point notching/slurring, ST/T ratio in V6 below 0.25, stable over time. Pericarditis vs STEMI: STEMI has territorial elevation with reciprocal depression (other than aVR), convex or straight ST segments, Q waves and regional wall-motion abnormality. Study aid; verify thresholds against the current full guideline.

**References:** PERKI 2024 §1.6 · ESC 2023 §3.5

options.text: A notched or slurred terminal QRS (J wave) in V4-V6
options.why_wrong: J-point notching or slurring is the hallmark of early repolarisation, not pericarditis.

options.text: PR depression and an ST/T ratio of 0.25 or more in V6
ST elevation that is unchanged on ECGs taken months apart
options.why_wrong: Stability over time favours early repolarisation; pericarditis evolves through stages over days to weeks.

options.text: Concave (upward-concave) ST morphology
options.why_wrong: Concavity is seen in both pericarditis and early repolarisation (and in many STEMIs), so it does not discriminate.

stem: A 26-year-old athlete with chest pain has widespread ST elevation similar to the ECG shown. Which finding most favours acute pericarditis over benign early repolarisation?

explanation: Pacemaker troubleshooting: (1) failure to capture - spike without depolarisation (lead dislodgement or fracture, rising threshold from fibrosis, hyperkalaemia, drugs); (2) failure to pace/output - no spike when one is due (oversensing, battery or lead failure); (3) undersensing - spikes despite intrinsic beats, falling inappropriately (risk of R-on-T); (4) oversensing - inappropriate inhibition and pauses. Ventricular pacing from the RV apex gives an LBBB-like QRS with a superior axis; the Sgarbossa criteria can be applied to paced rhythms. Immediate management of loss of capture with bradycardia: increase output, transcutaneous pacing, and interrogate the device. Study aid; verify thresholds against the current full guideline.

options.text: Failure to capture
Undersensing
options.why_wrong: Undersensing means the device misses native beats and fires spikes inappropriately soon after them; here the problem is spikes that do not depolarise the ventricle.

options.text: Oversensing
options.why_wrong: Oversensing (e.g. myopotentials, T waves) inhibits output, causing pauses without spikes; here spikes are present on time.

options.text: Normal function in hysteresis mode
options.why_wrong: Hysteresis delays the onset of pacing after a native beat, but a delivered spike without a following QRS is never normal.

stem: A pacemaker patient (VVI, lower rate 60/min) feels dizzy. The rhythm strip shows pacing spikes delivered on schedule (1000 ms after each preceding paced or sensed event); several spikes are not followed by a QRS complex, and the native ventricular beats that appear (about 38/min) correctly reset the pacing interval. Which pacemaker problem is present?

explanation: In PLAX the descending thoracic aorta is seen in cross-section behind the LA at the posterior atrioventricular groove. The parietal pericardium reflects between the LA and the aorta, so a pericardial effusion lies anterior to the DAo and tapers between it and the LA/LV wall, whereas a left pleural effusion lies posterior to the DAo (often with lung or atelectasis visible). Size (end-diastole, ESC 2015): small < 10 mm, moderate 10-20 mm, large > 20 mm. An isolated anterior space is more often epicardial fat; confirm with the subcostal and apical views. Study aid; verify thresholds against the current full guideline.

options.text: Fluid lies behind and lateral to the DAo and never passes in front of it
options.why_wrong: This is the pleural pattern: a left pleural effusion collects posterior to the descending aorta because the aorta lies outside the pericardial sac.

options.text: Fluid tapers in front of the DAo, between the aorta and the LA wall
Only an anterior echo-free space is seen, with no fluid behind the LV
options.why_wrong: An isolated anterior space is usually epicardial fat (granular, moves with the heart). Free-flowing pericardial fluid collects posteriorly (dependent) first.

options.text: The space is wider at end-systole than at end-diastole on M-mode
options.why_wrong: Effusion size is measured at end-diastole and the systolic-diastolic change does not tell pericardial from pleural fluid; the key landmark is the descending aorta.

source: ESC 2015 pericardial diseases; Otto, Textbook of Clinical Echocardiography; Mastering Cardiology — Echo pack; ESC 2015 pericardial guideline superseded by the ESC 2025 myocarditis and pericarditis guideline - verify
stem: A 58-year-old woman with breast cancer has dyspnoea. On the parasternal long-axis view (labelled schematic shown) an echo-free space is seen behind the LV posterior wall. Which relationship to the round structure behind the LA at the atrioventricular groove (DAo) identifies the fluid as pericardial rather than a left pleural effusion?

explanation: Normally the septal tricuspid leaflet inserts slightly apical to the anterior mitral leaflet (the normal offset is under about 8 mm/m²). Ebstein anomaly: apical displacement of the septal (and posterior/inferior) leaflet ≥ 8 mm/m² BSA, a large sail-like anterior leaflet, an atrialised portion of the RV and usually TR; associated ASD/PFO and accessory pathways (WPW). Loss of the offset (both valves at the same level) points to an AV septal defect; a reversed offset to congenitally corrected TGA. The moderator band identifies the morphological RV. Study aid; verify thresholds against the current full guideline.

options.text: Any apical offset of the septal tricuspid leaflet relative to the mitral hinge
options.why_wrong: A small apical offset of the septal tricuspid leaflet is normal (as in the figure). Its absence suggests an atrioventricular septal defect.

options.text: Mitral hinge point lying apical to the septal tricuspid leaflet hinge point
options.why_wrong: A reversed offset (left-sided AV valve more apical) suggests congenitally corrected transposition, where the left-sided valve is a tricuspid valve.

options.text: Apical displacement ≥ 8 mm/m² of the anterior leaflet with a normal septal one
options.why_wrong: In Ebstein anomaly the anterior leaflet stays attached to the annulus and is large and sail-like; it is the septal (and posterior) leaflet that is displaced apically.

options.text: Septal tricuspid leaflet displaced apically by ≥ 8 mm/m² of body surface area

source: ESC 2020 adult congenital heart disease; Otto, Textbook of Clinical Echocardiography; Mastering Cardiology — Echo pack
stem: A 22-year-old has a holosystolic murmur at the left sternal border and a large right heart. Compare the apical four-chamber schematic shown, in which the septal tricuspid leaflet hinges only slightly closer to the apex than the anterior mitral leaflet. Which finding in the patient would establish Ebstein anomaly?

explanation: PSAX at mitral level shows the six basal segments of the ASE/AHA 17-segment model, viewed from the apex: anterior (top), anterolateral and inferolateral (right of the screen), inferior (bottom), inferoseptal and anteroseptal (left, next to the RV). Typical territories: LAD = anterior and anteroseptal; RCA = inferior and inferoseptal (and the RV free wall); LCx = anterolateral and inferolateral (the inferolateral wall varies with dominance). Wall motion score: 1 normal, 2 hypokinetic, 3 akinetic, 4 dyskinetic; WMSI = sum / number of segments scored. Study aid; verify thresholds against the current full guideline.

options.text: Right coronary artery
Left anterior descending artery
options.why_wrong: The LAD supplies the anterior and anteroseptal segments (top and upper-left of this ring), not the inferior and inferoseptal ones.

options.text: Left circumflex artery
options.why_wrong: The LCx supplies the anterolateral and inferolateral segments (right side of the ring); the inferior and inferoseptal segments belong to the RCA in a right-dominant system.

options.text: Left main stem
options.why_wrong: A left main problem would involve the anterior, anteroseptal and lateral segments, not an isolated inferior and inferoseptal pair.

source: ASE/EACVI 2015 chamber quantification (17-segment model, coronary territories); Mastering Cardiology — Echo pack
stem: Two days after an inferior myocardial infarction, the parasternal short-axis view at mitral valve level (segment ring shown) shows akinesis of the basal inferior and basal inferoseptal segments; the other four basal segments thicken normally. Which artery is most likely responsible in a right-dominant circulation?

explanation: In PSAX at aortic valve level the right coronary cusp is anterior, the non-coronary cusp lies next to the interatrial septum and the left coronary cusp is on the right of the screen. A bicuspid valve has only two commissures and opens as an elliptical 'fish-mouth' orifice in systole; a raphe can mimic a third commissure in diastole. Commonest fusion: right-left coronary cusps (most cases). Look for associated aortopathy (measure root and ascending aorta) and coarctation; TOE, CT or CMR if TTE is non-diagnostic. Study aid; verify thresholds against the current full guideline.

options.text: Accept three diastolic closure lines as proof of three functioning cusps
options.why_wrong: A raphe (fused commissure) can look like a third closure line in diastole, so a diastolic frame alone can miss a bicuspid valve.

options.text: Measure the aortic annulus here and call it bicuspid if it exceeds 25 mm
options.why_wrong: Annulus size does not define valve morphology, and the annulus is measured in the zoomed PLAX (or by CT), not in this view.

options.text: Check the systolic opening for two commissures and an oval orifice
Rely on an eccentric closure line on PLAX M-mode as the deciding sign
options.why_wrong: An eccentric closure line suggests a bicuspid valve but is neither sensitive nor specific; the short-axis systolic opening is the key observation.

source: ESC/EACTS 2021 VHD; ESC 2024 aortic and peripheral arterial disease; Otto; Mastering Cardiology — Echo pack; ESC/EACTS 2025 VHD guideline published - thresholds here are the 2021 values, verify
stem: A 30-year-old has an ejection click. The diastolic parasternal short-axis frame at aortic valve level (as shown) shows three closure lines in a 'Mercedes-Benz' pattern. What is the most reliable way to exclude a bicuspid aortic valve?

explanation: The apical two-chamber view shows only the LV and LA: the anterior wall on the right of the screen and the inferior wall on the left (the LA appendage and coronary sinus help confirm the view). Apical four-chamber = inferoseptal and anterolateral walls; apical three-chamber (long-axis) = anteroseptal and inferolateral walls. Mid-to-apical anterior akinesis = LAD territory. After anterior STEMI with apical akinesis look for LV thrombus (contrast echo or CMR when the apex is poorly seen). Study aid; verify thresholds against the current full guideline.

options.text: Right coronary artery (posterior descending)
options.why_wrong: The RCA supplies the inferior wall, which is on the left of the screen in the apical two-chamber view and contracts normally here.

options.text: Left circumflex artery
options.why_wrong: The LCx territory (anterolateral and inferolateral walls) is displayed in the apical four- and three-chamber views, not in the two-chamber view.

options.text: First obtuse marginal branch
options.why_wrong: Obtuse marginal branches supply the lateral wall, which is not shown in the two-chamber view.

options.text: Left anterior descending artery

stem: Three days after a STEMI, the apical two-chamber view is recorded (schematic shown). The wall on the right of the screen is akinetic from the mid segment to the apex, while the opposite wall thickens normally. Which artery is the most likely culprit?

explanation: Modified Simpson (biplane method of discs): the LV is traced in apical 4- and 2-chamber views at end-diastole and end-systole and divided into 20 elliptical discs, V = π/4 · Σ a·b · L/20. SV = EDV - ESV = 102 - 42 = 60 mL; EF = 60/102 = 59%. ASE 2015 normal LVEF: 52-72% in men, 54-74% in women. ESC 2021 HF categories: HFrEF ≤ 40%, HFmrEF 41-49%, HFpEF ≥ 50%. Index volumes to BSA (EDVi upper limit about 74 mL/m² in men, 61 mL/m² in women). Study aid; verify thresholds against the current full guideline.

options.text: SV 60 mL; EF 59%, within the normal ASE range
SV 60 mL; EF 41%, in the mildly reduced range
options.why_wrong: 41% is ESV/EDV, the fraction of blood left behind. EF = (EDV - ESV) / EDV = 60 / 102 = 59%.

options.text: SV 144 mL; EF 59%, a hyperdynamic ventricle
options.why_wrong: Stroke volume is EDV minus ESV (60 mL), not their sum.

options.text: SV 60 mL; EF 59%, in the HF mildly reduced EF band
options.why_wrong: The ESC 2021 HF categories are reduced ≤ 40%, mildly reduced 41-49% and preserved ≥ 50%; 59% is preserved and within the ASE normal range.

stem: The biplane method of discs shown gives an end-diastolic volume of 102 mL and an end-systolic volume of 42 mL. Which statement is correct?

explanation: Apical foreshortening (the imaging plane misses the true apex) is the commonest cause of underestimated LV volumes: the apex looks thick and rounded and the long axis is short. Fix: move the transducer one interspace lower and more lateral to find the longest LV and a thin, conical apex. Trace at end-diastole (largest frame/after mitral closure) and end-systole (smallest frame) along the compacted myocardium. Use contrast when two or more contiguous segments are not seen; 3-D echo avoids geometric assumptions and foreshortening. Study aid; verify thresholds against the current full guideline.

options.text: Off-axis two-chamber view, overestimating both LV volumes
options.why_wrong: The longer of the two lengths is usually the correct one; a shorter long-axis length with a thick, rounded apex points to foreshortening of the four-chamber view.

options.text: Tracing inside the trabeculations, which overestimates the volumes
options.why_wrong: Tracing inside the trabeculations excludes cavity and underestimates the volumes; the border should be traced at the compacted myocardium, with trabeculae and papillary muscles counted as cavity.

options.text: Foreshortened four-chamber view, underestimating the LV volumes
No error: a 1.4 cm difference between the views is expected
options.why_wrong: The long-axis lengths in the two apical views should be similar (difference within about 10%); 17% is too much.

source: ASE/EACVI 2015 chamber quantification; Otto, Textbook of Clinical Echocardiography; Mastering Cardiology — Echo pack
stem: For biplane Simpson volumes, the LV long axis measures 6.8 cm in the apical four-chamber view, where the apex looks thick and rounded, and 8.2 cm in the two-chamber view. What is the most likely error and its effect?

explanation: E-point septal separation (EPSS) is the shortest distance between the anterior mitral leaflet at the E point and the septum; normal ≤ 7 mm, and larger values indicate a dilated, poorly contracting LV (low flow, large cavity). The notch between the A and C points (B-bump, A-C shoulder) indicates a raised LV end-diastolic pressure. LVEDD 70 mm is dilated (ASE 2015 upper limits about 58 mm men, 52 mm women). Pitfalls: EPSS is unreliable in mitral stenosis, severe AR (jet restricts the anterior leaflet) and regional asynergy. Study aid; verify thresholds against the current full guideline.

options.text: Normal LV: an E-point septal separation of 15 mm is within normal limits
options.why_wrong: EPSS is normally ≤ 7 mm; 15 mm means the anterior leaflet opens far from the septum because forward flow is low and the LV is dilated (LVEDD 70 mm here).

options.text: Dilated LV with reduced EF and raised LV end-diastolic pressure
Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy with systolic anterior motion of the mitral valve
options.why_wrong: HCM gives a small cavity, a thick septum and leaflet-septal contact in systole (SAM), not a 70 mm LV with a wide EPSS.

options.text: Normal LV size with an isolated mitral leaflet prolapse
options.why_wrong: Prolapse is a late-systolic posterior 'hammock' movement; the figure shows a dilated LV, a wide EPSS and a B-bump.

source: ASE/EACVI 2015 chamber quantification; Otto, Textbook of Clinical Echocardiography; Feigenbaum's Echocardiography; Mastering Cardiology — Echo pack
stem: A 55-year-old has exertional dyspnoea. The M-mode through the mitral leaflet tips from the parasternal window is shown (caliper and measured values in the figure); a notch interrupts the closure between the A and C points. Which interpretation fits best?

explanation: With normal LVEF and no myocardial disease, ASE/EACVI 2016 uses four variables: average E/e' > 14; septal e' < 7 or lateral e' < 10 cm/s; TR velocity > 2.8 m/s; LAVI > 34 mL/m². More than half abnormal = diastolic dysfunction, less than half = normal, exactly half = indeterminate. Here septal e' 10 and lateral 13 cm/s (average 11.5), average E/e' about 7, TR 2.3 m/s, LAVI 26 mL/m²: 0 of 4 abnormal = normal. The figure's E/A 1.5 and DT 200 ms fit normal relaxation. (ASE published an update in 2025; the 2016 algorithm is the one taught here.) Study aid; verify thresholds against the current full guideline.

options.text: Normal diastolic function: none of the four criteria is abnormal
Grade II pseudonormal filling, because E/A > 1 in a hypertensive patient
options.why_wrong: Pseudonormal filling has E/A 0.8-2 with reduced e', raised E/e' and a large LA; here e', E/e', TR velocity and LAVI are all normal.

options.text: Indeterminate, because E/A alone cannot separate normal from pseudonormal
options.why_wrong: E/A alone cannot, but in preserved EF the four criteria are applied; with 0 of 4 abnormal the function is normal.

options.text: Grade I dysfunction, because a DT of 200 ms is prolonged
options.why_wrong: DT 200 ms is normal (roughly 160-240 ms in adults); grade I needs E/A ≤ 0.8 with normal filling pressure.

source: ASE/EACVI 2016 diastolic function recommendations (Nagueh et al.); Mastering Cardiology — Echo pack; ASE 2025 diastolic function update published - verify
stem: A 45-year-old with treated hypertension has LVEF 62% with normal LV wall thickness and mass. The mitral inflow and septal e' values are shown. Lateral e' is 13 cm/s, TR peak velocity 2.3 m/s and LA volume index 26 mL/m². How is diastolic function classified?

explanation: For reduced LVEF (or myocardial disease with normal EF), the 2016 algorithm starts with mitral inflow: E/A ≤ 0.8 with E ≤ 50 cm/s = normal LA pressure, grade I; E/A ≥ 2 = elevated LA pressure, grade III; otherwise check average E/e' > 14, TR velocity > 2.8 m/s and LAVI > 34 mL/m² (2-3 positive = elevated, grade II; 2-3 negative = normal, grade I). The figure: E 0.45 m/s, A 0.75 m/s, E/A 0.6, DT 260 ms, IVRT 110 ms = impaired relaxation with normal LA pressure. Study aid; verify thresholds against the current full guideline.

options.text: Elevated LA pressure, because every patient with LVEF < 50% has raised filling pressure
options.why_wrong: Reduced EF does not guarantee raised filling pressure; the algorithm grades it from the inflow pattern and, if needed, three supportive criteria.

options.text: Indeterminate until the TR velocity and LA volume index are measured
options.why_wrong: The three supportive criteria are needed only when E/A is > 0.8 and < 2, or ≤ 0.8 with E > 50 cm/s.

options.text: Normal LA pressure with grade I dysfunction: E/A ≤ 0.8 and E ≤ 50 cm/s
Grade II dysfunction, because the deceleration time exceeds 200 ms
options.why_wrong: A prolonged DT (260 ms) is part of the impaired-relaxation (grade I) pattern; grade II is not defined by a long DT.

source: ASE/EACVI 2016 diastolic function recommendations (Nagueh et al.); Mastering Cardiology — Echo pack; ASE 2025 diastolic function update published - verify
stem: A 66-year-old with ischaemic cardiomyopathy (LVEF 38%) has the mitral inflow shown. What does the ASE/EACVI 2016 algorithm conclude about left atrial pressure?

explanation: Pseudonormal (grade II) filling: E/A 0.8-2 (here 1.4, E 0.85 m/s, DT 170 ms) looks normal because a raised LA pressure pushes E back up despite impaired relaxation. The clues: low e' (septal 5, lateral 6 cm/s), average E/e' > 14, TR velocity > 2.8 m/s and LAVI > 34 mL/m² (3 of 3 positive) = elevated LA pressure, grade II. Other unmaskers: Valsalva (E/A falls by ≥ 50%), pulmonary vein S/D < 1 and Ar-A duration > 30 ms. Study aid; verify thresholds against the current full guideline.

options.text: Normal LA pressure, grade I, because E/A is still below 2
options.why_wrong: E/A between 0.8 and 2 does not settle the grade; the three supportive criteria decide, and all three are abnormal here.

options.text: Grade III dysfunction, because DT is shorter than 200 ms
options.why_wrong: Grade III in the 2016 algorithm needs E/A ≥ 2; a DT of 170 ms is above the < 160 ms restrictive range and DT is not a branch point.

options.text: Normal diastolic function, because E/A lies between 0.8 and 2
options.why_wrong: A normal-looking E/A with reduced e' (5 cm/s septal) is the pseudonormal trap: raised LA pressure restores E.

options.text: Elevated LA pressure, grade II (3 of 3 criteria positive)

source: ASE/EACVI 2016 diastolic function recommendations (Nagueh et al.); Mastering Cardiology — Echo pack; ASE 2025 diastolic function update published - verify
stem: A 59-year-old with dilated cardiomyopathy (LVEF 30%) is in sinus rhythm. The mitral inflow and septal e' are shown. Lateral e' is 6 cm/s (average E/e' about 15.5), TR peak velocity 3.1 m/s and LA volume index 41 mL/m². What is the conclusion?

explanation: Restrictive filling (grade III): tall E (1.10 m/s), small A (0.40 m/s), E/A 2.8, DT 130 ms (< 160 ms), short IVRT (50 ms), very low e' (4 cm/s) and E/e' about 28. In reduced EF, E/A ≥ 2 = elevated LA pressure. A restrictive pattern that persists despite treatment or a Valsalva manoeuvre (irreversible) carries a poor prognosis; one that reverts to grade II with decongestion is a good sign. Study aid; verify thresholds against the current full guideline.

options.text: Grade II, but only once TR velocity and LA volume are known
options.why_wrong: With reduced EF an E/A ≥ 2 directly indicates elevated LA pressure (grade III); the supportive criteria are not needed.

options.text: Grade III with elevated LA pressure, decided on E/A alone
Normal 'supernormal' filling of a young, fit heart
options.why_wrong: E/A > 2 can be normal in the young, but then e' is brisk; here e' is 4 cm/s and LVEF 25%.

options.text: Grade I, because E/A is above 0.8
options.why_wrong: Grade I is E/A ≤ 0.8 (with E ≤ 50 cm/s); an E/A of 2.8 with DT 130 ms is the restrictive end of the spectrum.

stem: A 72-year-old is admitted with decompensated heart failure (LVEF 25%). The mitral inflow and septal e' are shown. How is diastolic function graded?

explanation: In the reduced-EF limb, E/A > 0.8 and < 2 leads to three criteria: average E/e' > 14, TR velocity > 2.8 m/s, LAVI > 34 mL/m². Two or three positive = elevated LA pressure (grade II); two or three negative = normal (grade I). If only two can be measured and they disagree (here E/e' negative, LAVI positive), LA pressure and grade are indeterminate. Helpers: pulmonary vein S/D < 1 in reduced EF supports raised LA pressure; consider other data (BNP, clinical picture) or invasive measurement. Study aid; verify thresholds against the current full guideline.

options.text: Normal LA pressure, grade I, because average E/e' is below 14
options.why_wrong: One negative criterion is not enough when the other available criterion (LAVI 38 mL/m²) is positive.

options.text: Elevated LA pressure, grade II, because LAVI exceeds 34 mL/m²
options.why_wrong: A large LA alone does not prove raised current pressure; with only two criteria available they must agree.

options.text: Indeterminate: the two available criteria disagree
Grade III, because E/A is above 0.8 in a patient with reduced EF
options.why_wrong: Grade III needs E/A ≥ 2; 1.2 sends you to the three supportive criteria.

stem: A 70-year-old has LVEF 40%. Mitral E 0.70 m/s, A 0.60 m/s (E/A 1.2), average E/e' 11 and LA volume index 38 mL/m²; the TR jet is too faint to measure. Following the algorithm shown, what is the conclusion?

explanation: Normal-EF algorithm (no myocardial disease): average E/e' > 14 (here 13, negative); septal e' < 7 or lateral e' < 10 cm/s (positive); TR velocity > 2.8 m/s (3.0, positive); LAVI > 34 mL/m² (36, positive) = 3 of 4 abnormal (> 50%) = diastolic dysfunction. Then grade it with the second algorithm (mitral inflow and LA pressure criteria). In HFpEF work-up, ESC 2021 also weighs natriuretic peptides and, when unclear, diastolic stress echo or invasive haemodynamics. Study aid; verify thresholds against the current full guideline.

options.text: Diastolic dysfunction: three of the four criteria are abnormal
Indeterminate, because exactly half of the criteria are abnormal
options.why_wrong: Septal and lateral e' together form one criterion (septal < 7 or lateral < 10 cm/s); counting them separately distorts the tally. The count is 3 of 4.

options.text: Normal, because an average E/e' below 14 overrides the other findings
options.why_wrong: No single variable overrides the others in the preserved-EF algorithm; the majority rule applies.

options.text: Not assessable until E/A is measured, which sets the grade first
options.why_wrong: E/A is the first step of the reduced-EF/myocardial-disease algorithm; in normal EF the four criteria come first, then the grading algorithm.

stem: A 68-year-old woman with exertional dyspnoea has LVEF 60% and no regional wall motion abnormality. Septal e' 6 cm/s, lateral e' 8 cm/s, average E/e' 13, TR peak velocity 3.0 m/s and LA volume index 36 mL/m². What does ASE/EACVI 2016 conclude?

explanation: DVI (velocity ratio) = V(LVOT) / V(AV) = 1.0 / 4.6 = 0.22, or the same ratio of VTIs. It avoids squaring the LVOT diameter, the main error in the continuity equation. ASE/EACVI 2017 and ESC 2021: severe AS = Vmax ≥ 4.0 m/s, mean gradient ≥ 40 mmHg, AVA < 1.0 cm² (indexed < 0.6 cm²/m²), DVI < 0.25. The figure is concordant: Vmax 4.6 m/s, mean 50 mmHg. With an LVOT velocity < 1.5 m/s the simplified Bernoulli equation (4V²) is adequate. Study aid; verify thresholds against the current full guideline.

options.text: 0.05: the velocity ratio squared, indicating critical stenosis
options.why_wrong: DVI is the plain ratio V(LVOT)/V(AV), not its square; 1.0/4.6 = 0.22.

options.text: 0.22: within the 0.25-0.50 band, so moderate stenosis
options.why_wrong: The arithmetic is right but the cut-off is misplaced: < 0.25 is severe; 0.25-0.50 is moderate.

options.text: 4.6: the AV-to-LVOT ratio above 4, so severe stenosis
options.why_wrong: The ratio is inverted; DVI = LVOT velocity (or VTI) / aortic jet velocity (or VTI).

options.text: 0.22: below 0.25, consistent with severe stenosis

stem: A 76-year-old has exertional syncope. CW Doppler through the aortic valve is shown; the inner, denser envelope is the LVOT signal, which peaks at 1.0 m/s (confirmed with PW in the LVOT). What is the dimensionless velocity index (DVI) and what does it mean?

explanation: Doppler measures the maximal pressure drop at the vena contracta. Downstream, part of the kinetic energy reconverts to pressure (pressure recovery), most when the aorta is small (< 3.0 cm), so the catheter gradient measured further along is lower. The energy loss index, EOA·Aa/(Aa - EOA) indexed to BSA, corrects for this (< 0.6 cm²/m² suggests severe AS). Peak-to-peak gradient compares non-simultaneous peaks and is always lower than the Doppler peak instantaneous gradient (85 mmHg here); compare mean with mean. Study aid; verify thresholds against the current full guideline.

options.text: Doppler angle error, which has overestimated the true jet velocity
options.why_wrong: Misalignment can only underestimate velocity (cos θ ≤ 1); it never makes Doppler read higher than the truth.

options.text: Pressure recovery, and peak-to-peak is not peak instantaneous
The CW envelope is an MR jet, which always gives the higher velocity
options.why_wrong: An MR jet starts at mitral closure and lasts through isovolumic relaxation; the figure's envelope is confined to ejection with an LVOT signal inside it.

options.text: Simplified Bernoulli overestimates whenever LVOT velocity is under 1 m/s
options.why_wrong: Ignoring the proximal velocity is valid when it is < 1-1.5 m/s; it causes overestimation only when LVOT velocity is high.
