stem: A 64-year-old woman with a small aorta (sinotubular junction 2.4 cm) has the aortic CW Doppler shown. At catheterisation the peak-to-peak gradient is 45 mmHg and the mean gradient 38 mmHg. What best explains the discrepancy?

explanation: Continuity equation: AVA = LVOT area × VTI(LVOT) / VTI(AV) = π × (2.0/2)² × 20 / 100 = 3.14 × 0.2 = 0.63 cm². Indexed AVA = 0.63 / 1.7 = 0.37 cm²/m². Severe AS: AVA < 1.0 cm², indexed < 0.6 cm²/m² (indexing matters in small patients). The LVOT diameter is squared, so a 1 mm error in a 20 mm LVOT changes the AVA by about 10%. Use the velocity ratio (DVI) as a diameter-free cross-check. Study aid; verify thresholds against the current full guideline.

options.text: 0.80 cm² and 0.47 cm²/m²: severe stenosis
options.why_wrong: This uses D² instead of π(D/2)² for the LVOT area (4 cm² instead of 3.14 cm²).

options.text: 2.51 cm² and 1.48 cm²/m²: no significant stenosis
options.why_wrong: This uses the diameter as the radius (π × 2²); the LVOT radius is 1.0 cm.

options.text: 0.63 cm² and 0.37 cm²/m²: severe stenosis
0.63 cm² and 1.07 cm²/m²: moderate stenosis
options.why_wrong: Indexing divides by BSA (0.63 / 1.7 = 0.37), it does not multiply.

source: ASE/EACVI 2017 aortic stenosis update (Baumgartner et al.); ESC/EACTS 2021 valvular heart disease; ACC/AHA 2020 valvular heart disease; Mastering Cardiology — Echo pack; ESC/EACTS 2025 VHD guideline published - thresholds here are the 2021 values, verify
stem: In a 70-year-old (BSA 1.7 m²): LVOT diameter 2.0 cm (mid-systole, zoomed PLAX), LVOT VTI 20 cm and aortic CW VTI 100 cm. Which aortic valve area and indexed area are correct?

explanation: Classical low-flow, low-gradient AS: AVA < 1.0 cm², mean gradient < 40 mmHg, LVEF < 50% and SVi ≤ 35 mL/m². Low-dose dobutamine echo: true severe AS if the mean gradient reaches ≥ 40 mmHg (ACC/AHA: Vmax ≥ 4 m/s) with AVA staying ≤ 1.0 cm²; pseudo-severe if AVA rises > 1.0 cm² with a low gradient; no flow reserve if SV rises < 20% (then CT calcium score helps). ESC 2021 and ACC/AHA 2020 recommend intervention for symptomatic true severe low-flow AS. Paradoxical low-flow AS (LVEF ≥ 50%) is confirmed with CT calcium scoring. Study aid; verify thresholds against the current full guideline.

options.text: True severe AS with flow reserve: intervention is indicated
Pseudo-severe AS: the AVA is small only because flow is low
options.why_wrong: Pseudo-severe AS shows an AVA that opens to > 1.0 cm² with a mean gradient that stays < 40 mmHg as flow rises; here the gradient reaches 45 mmHg with AVA 0.9 cm².

options.text: No contractile reserve: proceed to CT calcium scoring
options.why_wrong: Contractile reserve is an SV increase ≥ 20%; a 30% rise shows reserve, and the test is conclusive.

options.text: Moderate AS, because the resting mean gradient is below 40 mmHg
options.why_wrong: In low-flow states the gradient underestimates severity; the resting gradient cannot grade AS when SVi ≤ 35 mL/m².

stem: A 74-year-old has dyspnoea and LVEF 30%. At rest: AVA 0.8 cm², mean gradient 28 mmHg, Vmax 3.2 m/s, SVi 28 mL/m². Low-dose dobutamine (up to 20 µg/kg/min): stroke volume rises by 30%, mean gradient 45 mmHg, AVA 0.9 cm². What is the interpretation?

explanation: AR severity (ASE 2017; ESC 2021): severe = vena contracta > 0.6 cm, jet width ≥ 65% of LVOT, PHT < 200 ms (here 170 ms), holodiastolic flow reversal in the descending aorta (end-diastolic velocity > 20 cm/s; in the abdominal aorta it is very specific), EROA ≥ 0.30 cm², RVol ≥ 60 mL, RF ≥ 50% and LV dilatation in chronic AR. Mild: VC < 0.3 cm, PHT > 500 ms. PHT is load-dependent, so combine several parameters. In bicuspid disease also measure the aortic root and ascending aorta. Study aid; verify thresholds against the current full guideline.

options.text: Vena contracta width of 0.4 cm on colour Doppler imaging
options.why_wrong: A vena contracta of 0.3-0.6 cm is intermediate (moderate); severe AR needs > 0.6 cm.

options.text: Holodiastolic reversal in the descending aorta (EDV > 20 cm/s)
Colour jet width equal to 30% of the LVOT diameter

explanation: The AR pressure half-time reflects how fast aortic and LV diastolic pressures equalise. It depends on the orifice but also on LV compliance and filling pressure (a stiff or overfilled LV raises LV pressure quickly and shortens the PHT), on aortic compliance and on systemic vascular resistance (vasodilators shorten it). Acute severe AR gives a very short PHT with premature mitral closure. Interpret PHT with load-independent measures (vena contracta, PISA, RVol). explanation: MVA = 220 / PHT (220 / 220 ms = 1.0 cm² here). The PHT shortens, and the area is overestimated, when LV diastolic pressure rises fast: significant AR, a stiff LV (LVH, elderly) and immediately (24-72 h) after balloon commissurotomy (abrupt LA compliance change); an ASD decompresses the LA and also shortens it. Then use planimetry (PSAX, leaflet tips, 3-D best), the continuity equation or PISA. explanation: TAPSE = systolic excursion of the lateral tricuspid annulus towards the apex (M-mode from A4C); here 14 mm. ASE 2015 abnormal RV function: TAPSE < 17 mm, tissue Doppler S' < 9.5 cm/s, FAC < 35%, RV free-wall strain magnitude < 20%. stem: A 58-year-old with acute pulmonary embolism has BP 118/72 mmHg and a raised troponin. The M-mode of the lateral tricuspid annulus is shown. Which interpretation is correct?

explanation: Dynamic LVOT obstruction (SAM-septal contact) gives a late-peaking, concave 'dagger' CW envelope because the obstruction worsens as the ventricle empties. LVOT obstruction = peak gradient ≥ 30 mmHg; ≥ 50 mmHg is the usual threshold for septal reduction therapy (myectomy or alcohol septal ablation) in patients with NYHA III-IV symptoms despite maximal medical therapy (ESC 2023). Cardiac myosin inhibitors (mavacamten) are an alternative or add-on. If the resting gradient is < 50 mmHg in symptomatic patients, provoke it (Valsalva, standing, exercise echo). stem: A 42-year-old has NYHA III dyspnoea despite a maximally tolerated beta-blocker. The septum is 21 mm thick with systolic anterior motion of the mitral valve. Apical CW Doppler at rest is shown. Which statement is correct?

explanation: Constriction: the myocardium relaxes normally, so e' is preserved (septal ≥ 9 cm/s in the Mayo criteria); the tethered lateral annulus moves less than the septum, so septal e' exceeds lateral e' (annulus reversus). Other signs: respiratory septal shift (septal bounce), mitral E inspiratory fall > 25%, hepatic vein expiratory diastolic reversal, plethoric IVC, thick pericardium. explanation: The figure shows exaggerated ventricular interdependence: mitral E falls on inspiration (here by about a third; > 25-30% is abnormal) while tricuspid inflow rises (> 40-60%). Tamponade signs: RA systolic collapse lasting > 1/3 of the cycle, RV early diastolic collapse, plethoric IVC (sensitive, not specific), swinging heart. Right-heart collapse may be absent when right-heart pressures are high (PH, RVH) or the effusion is loculated (post-operative); pulsus paradoxus and respiratory inflow variation may be absent with severe AR, a large ASD, severe LV dysfunction with high LVEDP or positive-pressure ventilation. explanation: Mitral regurgitation begins at mitral closure (during isovolumic contraction, before the aortic valve opens) and continues through isovolumic relaxation, so its envelope is longer than the LVOT signal and rounder. Its velocity reflects LV-LA pressure: LV systolic pressure ≈ systolic BP + LVOT gradient, so MR is always faster. Taking the MR jet as the LVOT signal overestimates the obstruction (a classic error). Use colour to separate the jets, PW mapping to localise the obstruction, and timing against the ECG. Study aid; verify thresholds against the current full guideline.

stem: In a patient with HCM and systolic anterior motion, two systolic CW envelopes are recorded from the apex as the beam is angled: one peaks at 4.2 m/s, the other at 6.0 m/s. Which feature identifies the 6.0 m/s signal as mitral regurgitation rather than LVOT obstruction?

explanation: Aliasing occurs when the Doppler shift exceeds the Nyquist limit (PRF/2). Maximum velocity v = c · PRF / (4 f0 cos θ), so it rises with a higher PRF (shallower sample volume) and a lower transmitted frequency. The mitral sample must stay at the leaflet tips, so at a fixed depth the first step is the maximum velocity scale. Practical fixes: move the baseline, use high-PRF mode, a lower-frequency probe, or switch to CW (no aliasing, but no range resolution). PW localises (range-gated) but aliases; CW measures high velocities but samples along the whole beam. Study aid; verify thresholds against the current full guideline.

options.why_wrong: The wall filter removes low-velocity signals near the baseline; it does not change the Nyquist limit.

stem: Pulsed-wave Doppler of mitral inflow is recorded at 16 cm depth in a patient with severe MR; the E wave wraps around and appears below the baseline. Which change most directly raises the maximum velocity that PW can display?

explanation: Doppler shift Δf = 2 f0 V cos θ / c, so the recorded velocity = true V × cos θ. At 30°, cos θ = 0.87: true V = 4.0 / 0.87 ≈ 4.6 m/s. Gradient 4V²: 64 mmHg recorded versus about 85 mmHg true (≈ 25% underestimated). Below 20° the velocity error is ≤ 6%. In AS, interrogate from the apex, right parasternal, suprasternal and subcostal windows (with the non-imaging pencil probe) and report the highest velocity. Study aid; verify thresholds against the current full guideline.

stem: The CW beam meets an aortic stenosis jet at an angle of 30°. The recorded peak velocity is 4.0 m/s. What are the true velocity and the effect on the peak gradient?

explanation: In severe TR, RV blood regurgitates into the right atrium during systole, so the systolic x descent is filled in and replaced by a large cv (s) wave, followed by a steep y descent when the tricuspid valve opens. A pulsatile liver and a pansystolic murmur louder on inspiration (Carvallo sign) complete the picture.

options.text: A giant a wave on every beat with a normal x descent
options.why_wrong: Giant a waves reflect resistance to RV filling (tricuspid stenosis, pulmonary hypertension, RVH); TR changes the systolic part of the trace.

options.text: Loss of the a wave with a preserved x descent
options.why_wrong: An absent a wave means no organised atrial contraction (atrial fibrillation); it is not the signature of TR.

options.text: The systolic x descent is replaced by a large cv (systolic) wave, followed by a steep y descent
A blunted or absent y descent
options.why_wrong: In severe TR the y descent is steep, because the overfilled RA empties rapidly; an absent y descent is the pattern of tamponade.

stem: A 68-year-old man has severe functional tricuspid regurgitation secondary to pulmonary hypertension. Compared with the normal jugular venous waveform shown, which change is expected in his neck?

explanation: Irregular cannon a waves mean AV dissociation: atria and ventricles beat independently, and on the beats where the atrium happens to contract during ventricular systole it pushes against a closed tricuspid valve. With a slow regular pulse and syncope this points to complete heart block; with a broad-complex tachycardia it favours VT. Giant a waves, by contrast, occur on every beat.

options.text: The right atrium contracting against a closed tricuspid valve on beats where atrial and ventricular systole coincide
The right atrium contracting against a stenotic tricuspid valve on every beat
options.why_wrong: Resistance to RV filling (tricuspid stenosis, stiff RV) gives giant a waves on every beat, not intermittent ones.

options.text: Regurgitation of right ventricular blood into the right atrium during systole
options.why_wrong: That is the cv wave of tricuspid regurgitation, which is present on every beat and replaces the x descent.

options.text: Rapid early diastolic filling that is stopped abruptly by a rigid pericardium
options.why_wrong: That mechanism produces the steep y descent of constrictive pericarditis, not intermittent large waves.

stem: A 74-year-old man presents with syncope. His pulse is regular at 36/min. In the neck, very large venous pulsations appear on some beats but not on others, at irregular intervals. What produces these waves?

explanation: In tamponade the fluid-filled pericardium fixes the total volume of the heart. Blood can enter the RA only when blood leaves the heart, which happens in ventricular systole, so the systolic x descent is kept; when the tricuspid valve opens there is no space for rapid ventricular filling, so the y descent disappears. Contrast constriction, where early filling is rapid and then stops abruptly (steep y, Kussmaul sign).

options.text: Tricuspid valve obstruction slows emptying of the right atrium
options.why_wrong: Obstructed RA emptying (tricuspid stenosis, RA myxoma) gives a slow, shallow y descent, and there is no valve obstruction here.

options.text: Total cardiac volume is fixed by the pericardial fluid, so there is no room for rapid early diastolic filling when the tricuspid valve opens
Loss of organised atrial contraction
options.why_wrong: Absent atrial contraction removes the a wave (atrial fibrillation); it does not abolish the y descent.

options.text: The right heart cannot accept the inspiratory increase in venous return, so the JVP rises with inspiration
options.why_wrong: That is Kussmaul sign, which belongs to constrictive pericarditis and is uncommon in tamponade; it does not explain the absent y descent.

stem: A 58-year-old woman with a large malignant pericardial effusion is hypotensive, with a raised JVP and pulsus paradoxus. The x descent is preserved but the y descent is absent (see the patterns shown). What explains the loss of the y descent?

explanation: Blood returns to the heart because mean systemic filling pressure (about 7 mmHg) exceeds right atrial pressure. RA pressure is the back-pressure: when it rises the gradient narrows and venous return falls. Volume, venoconstriction and the muscle and respiratory pumps all increase venous return.

options.text: Sympathetic venoconstriction of the splanchnic venous reservoir
options.why_wrong: Venoconstriction moves blood out of the reservoir and raises mean systemic filling pressure, so venous return increases.

options.text: A rise in right atrial pressure
The fall in intrathoracic pressure during inspiration
options.why_wrong: Inspiration lowers RA pressure (the respiratory pump), which widens the driving gradient and increases venous return.

options.text: Rhythmic contraction of the leg muscles during walking
options.why_wrong: The skeletal-muscle pump squeezes blood toward the heart and increases venous return.

options.text: Rapid infusion of 1 L of crystalloid
options.why_wrong: Extra volume raises mean systemic filling pressure and increases venous return.

stem: In Guyton's model, venous return = (mean systemic filling pressure − right atrial pressure) / resistance to venous return. With everything else held constant, which change REDUCES venous return to the right atrium?

explanation: Normally inspiration delays P2 (more RV filling, more compliant pulmonary bed). In an ASD the atria act as one chamber: the extra inspiratory venous return is shared between both sides, and the left-to-right shunt falls as right-sided filling rises, so RV stroke volume and the timing of P2 barely change through the respiratory cycle. The result is a wide AND fixed split.

options.text: Right bundle branch block delays P2 by a constant amount
options.why_wrong: RBBB delays P2 and widens the split, but the split still varies with respiration; it is wide, not fixed.

options.text: Pulmonary valve stenosis fixes the duration of RV ejection
options.why_wrong: Pulmonary stenosis delays P2 and gives a wide split that still varies with breathing.

options.text: The left ventricle empties in two directions, so A2 comes early
options.why_wrong: An early A2 explains the wide split of MR and VSD, which still widens on inspiration; it does not fix the split.

options.text: The shared atria spread the inspiratory rise in venous return across both sides, and the left-to-right shunt falls as right-sided filling rises, so RV volume and P2 timing hardly change

stem: A 30-year-old woman with a secundum atrial septal defect has wide splitting of S2 that does not change between inspiration and expiration (see the splitting patterns shown). What best explains why the split is FIXED?

explanation: The mitral valve opens when falling LV pressure drops below LA pressure. A high LA pressure (tight stenosis) means this crossover comes very soon after aortic closure, so the A2-OS interval is short. A shorter A2-OS interval therefore means a higher LA pressure and more severe MS (Braunwald's Heart Disease).

options.text: Patient B has the tighter stenosis, because a narrower valve takes longer to open
options.why_wrong: The relationship is the reverse: the higher the LA pressure, the sooner LV pressure falls below it after A2 and the earlier the valve snaps open.

options.text: Patient A has the higher left atrial pressure and the tighter stenosis
The A2-opening snap interval reflects LV systolic function and says nothing about severity
options.why_wrong: The interval is set by the LA-LV pressure crossover in early diastole and is a classic bedside marker of MS severity.

options.text: Patient A is more likely to have a third heart sound
options.why_wrong: An S3 is not heard in significant mitral stenosis, because inflow across the narrow valve is too slow to be checked abruptly.

stem: Two patients have rheumatic mitral stenosis and are in sinus rhythm. The interval between A2 and the opening snap is 60 ms in patient A and 110 ms in patient B (see the sound timing shown). Which interpretation is correct?

explanation: In hypertrophic obstructive cardiomyopathy anything that makes the LV smaller (less preload, less afterload, more contractility) narrows the outflow tract and worsens the dynamic obstruction, so the murmur gets louder on standing and Valsalva and softer on squatting. Aortic stenosis behaves the opposite way, which is the classic discriminator.

options.text: Less preload increases flow across a stenotic bicuspid aortic valve
options.why_wrong: Reduced preload lowers flow across a fixed stenosis, so an aortic stenosis murmur becomes softer on standing and Valsalva.

options.text: Standing raises afterload and so increases regurgitant flow across the mitral valve
options.why_wrong: Standing and Valsalva act mainly by reducing preload; an MR murmur becomes softer, not louder, with these manoeuvres.

options.text: More venous return to the right heart augments a pulmonary flow murmur
options.why_wrong: Standing and the Valsalva strain reduce venous return; right-sided murmurs increase with inspiration, not with these manoeuvres.

options.text: Less preload makes the LV cavity smaller, bringing the septum and the anterior mitral leaflet together and worsening outflow obstruction

stem: A 19-year-old athlete has an ejection systolic murmur at the left sternal edge. It becomes louder when he stands up from squatting and during the strain phase of the Valsalva manoeuvre. What is the mechanism of this change?

explanation: Murmur shape follows the pressure gradient driving the flow. In AR the gradient between aorta and LV is largest at the moment of aortic valve closure and narrows as the aorta runs off and the LV fills, so the murmur starts at S2 and fades (decrescendo). Best heard with the diaphragm, patient leaning forward in expiration.

options.text: Regurgitant flow begins only after isovolumic relaxation and peaks in mid-diastole
options.why_wrong: That describes a mid-diastolic murmur such as the rumble of mitral stenosis; AR starts immediately at A2.

options.text: The aorta-to-LV pressure gradient is greatest just after aortic valve closure and falls as the LV fills through diastole
The leak is driven by atrial contraction, so it peaks just before S1
options.why_wrong: Late diastolic (presystolic) accentuation belongs to mitral stenosis in sinus rhythm, not to AR.

options.text: Aortic pressure rises through diastole, so the regurgitant flow increases steadily
options.why_wrong: Aortic pressure falls during diastole while LV pressure rises, so the driving gradient shrinks.

stem: Using the murmur shapes shown, why is the murmur of chronic aortic regurgitation an early diastolic DECRESCENDO?

explanation: An equiphasic lead is perpendicular to the mean QRS vector. The two directions perpendicular to aVL (−30°) are +60° and −120°. Lead II (+60°) is upright, so the vector points toward +60°: a normal axis.

options.why_wrong: −30° is the axis of aVL itself; a vector parallel to aVL would make the QRS maximally positive in aVL, not equiphasic.
−120° is also perpendicular to aVL, but a vector pointing there would make lead II (+60°) strongly negative.
At +90° the vector is 120° away from aVL, so the QRS in aVL would be clearly negative, not equiphasic.
At +120° the vector is 150° away from aVL, so aVL would be negative; +120° is the axis of lead III.

stem: On a 12-lead ECG the QRS complex is equiphasic in lead aVL and upright in lead II. Using the hexaxial reference shown, what is the approximate frontal-plane QRS axis?

explanation: Bazett: QTc = QT / √RR, with RR in seconds. √0.64 = 0.8, so QTc = 0.40 / 0.8 = 0.50 s = 500 ms, above the 450 ms (men) and 460 ms (women) limits. Remember that Bazett over-corrects at fast heart rates, so the QT should be rechecked at a slower rate or with another formula.

options.text: 400 ms: normal, no correction is needed at this rate
options.why_wrong: The QT must be corrected for rate whenever the RR interval is not 1 s; at about 94/min the uncorrected QT underestimates the QTc.

options.text: 320 ms: short
options.why_wrong: This multiplies the QT by √RR (400 × 0.8) instead of dividing by it.

options.text: 625 ms: prolonged
options.why_wrong: This divides by the RR interval itself (0.40 / 0.64) instead of by its square root.

options.text: 500 ms: prolonged

stem: A patient's ECG shows a QT interval of 400 ms with an RR interval of 640 ms (heart rate about 94/min). Using Bazett's formula and the reference values shown, what is the QTc?

explanation: A repolarisation wave is the reverse dipole of depolarisation, so on its own it would write a deflection opposite to the QRS. But ventricular repolarisation travels the other way, from epicardium to endocardium, because epicardial action potentials are shorter. The two reversals cancel, so the normal T wave is concordant with the QRS in most leads.

options.text: Repolarisation spreads in the same direction as depolarisation and produces the same dipole
options.why_wrong: The repolarisation dipole is reversed (positive behind, negative ahead); if it also travelled the same way as depolarisation the T wave would be inverted.

options.text: The T wave is produced by atrial repolarisation, which follows ventricular depolarisation
options.why_wrong: Atrial repolarisation is small and hidden in the PR segment and QRS; the T wave is ventricular repolarisation.

options.text: Ventricular repolarisation runs from epicardium to endocardium, opposite to depolarisation, because epicardial action potentials are shorter
No current flows during the plateau, so the T wave simply continues the direction of the ST segment
options.why_wrong: The ST segment is isoelectric because all cells are at the plateau; that says nothing about the direction of the T wave.

stem: Why is the normal T wave upright in the leads where the QRS complex is upright?

explanation: The septum is the first part of the ventricles to depolarise, from the left bundle, so its vector points from left to right. That vector moves away from I, aVL, V5 and V6 (small septal q waves) and toward V1 (small r wave). Loss of these septal q waves is one feature of LBBB.

options.text: An old lateral myocardial infarction
options.why_wrong: Small, narrow 'septal' q waves in the lateral leads are normal; they are not the wide, deep Q waves of infarction.

options.text: Depolarisation of the right ventricular free wall, which is activated first
options.why_wrong: The septum is activated first; the free walls follow, and the thicker LV dominates the main vector.

options.text: Normal septal depolarisation, which spreads from left to right because the septum is activated from the left bundle
Atrial repolarisation recorded just before the QRS
options.why_wrong: Atrial repolarisation is tiny and buried in the PR segment and QRS; it does not make q waves in lateral leads.

stem: A healthy 25-year-old has small, narrow q waves in leads I, aVL, V5 and V6 and a small r wave in V1. What do these deflections represent?

explanation: Re-entry persists only while the wavelength (CV × ERP) is shorter than the path length, leaving an excitable gap of recovered tissue ahead of the wavefront. Class III drugs prolong the action potential and the ERP, lengthening the wavelength until the returning impulse meets refractory tissue and the circuit is extinguished.

options.text: Lengthening the effective refractory period so the wavelength (conduction velocity × ERP) becomes longer than the circuit and the excitable gap closes
Shortening the effective refractory period so the circulating impulse is blocked sooner
options.why_wrong: Shorter refractoriness shortens the wavelength and widens the excitable gap, which favours re-entry.

options.text: Flattening the slope of phase 4 depolarisation in pacemaker cells
options.why_wrong: That targets automaticity (for example beta-blockers or ivabradine), not the re-entry circuit.

options.text: Slowing conduction velocity in the slow limb of the circuit
options.why_wrong: Slowing conduction shortens the wavelength and tends to favour re-entry unless it produces block; it is not the class III mechanism.

stem: A class III antiarrhythmic drug (an IKr blocker) terminates and prevents a re-entrant tachycardia mainly by which mechanism?

explanation: Torsades arises from early afterdepolarisations during phase 2-3 of a prolonged action potential (IKr block by sotalol, aggravated by hypokalaemia and bradycardia). EADs are bradycardia- and pause-dependent because the APD is longest at slow rates. Raising the rate (isoprenaline or pacing) shortens the APD, while magnesium, potassium repletion and stopping the drug remove the other drivers.

options.text: A faster rate reduces SR Ca2+ overload and abolishes delayed afterdepolarisations
options.why_wrong: Delayed afterdepolarisations are tachycardia-dependent (faster rates load more Ca2+); torsades is driven by early afterdepolarisations.

options.text: Overdrive pacing interrupts a fixed re-entry circuit around myocardial scar
options.why_wrong: Torsades de pointes is triggered by EADs in a long-QT setting, not by scar-related re-entry.

options.text: A faster rate prolongs refractoriness and lengthens the QT interval
options.why_wrong: Faster rates shorten the action potential duration and the QT; that shortening is what suppresses EADs.

options.text: A faster rate shortens the action potential, leaving less time for L-type Ca2+ channels to reactivate and generate early afterdepolarisations

stem: A 70-year-old woman taking sotalol has a potassium of 2.9 mmol/L, a heart rate of 45/min and a long QTc. After a pause she develops polymorphic VT with a twisting QRS axis. After IV magnesium, temporary pacing at 90-100/min is started. Using the triggered-activity diagram shown, why does a faster heart rate help?

explanation: Digoxin blocks the Na+/K+-ATPase, so intracellular Na+ rises and the Na+/Ca2+ exchanger removes less Ca2+. The SR becomes Ca2+-overloaded and releases Ca2+ spontaneously after repolarisation; the exchanger then brings in 3 Na+ for each Ca2+ extruded, a net inward current that produces delayed afterdepolarisations. Bidirectional VT points to DADs (digoxin toxicity or CPVT); treat with digoxin-specific antibody fragments and correct K+.

options.text: Early afterdepolarisations from a prolonged action potential during bradycardia
options.why_wrong: EADs are pause-dependent and cause torsades in long QT; digoxin toxicity causes Ca2+-overload DADs.

options.text: Re-entry around an anatomical obstacle such as the tricuspid annulus
options.why_wrong: Macro-re-entry round the tricuspid annulus is typical atrial flutter; bidirectional VT is a triggered rhythm.

options.text: Delayed afterdepolarisations from SR Ca2+ overload, with a transient inward current through the Na+/Ca2+ exchanger
Enhanced normal automaticity of the sinus node through a larger funny current
options.why_wrong: Enhanced sinus automaticity gives sinus tachycardia; it does not produce bidirectional VT.

stem: An 80-year-old taking digoxin has nausea, yellow-tinged vision and bidirectional ventricular tachycardia. What is the cellular mechanism of the arrhythmia?

explanation: Automatic rhythms show gradual warm-up and cool-down, cannot be started or stopped by programmed premature beats, and are not terminated by DC cardioversion (the focus simply fires again). Re-entry starts and stops abruptly and is terminated by cardioversion. Automatic tachycardias respond to slowing the rate and treating the cause.

options.text: It is a macro-re-entrant tachycardia that needs a higher-energy shock
options.why_wrong: Re-entry is reliably terminated by cardioversion; warm-up and immediate recurrence point to an automatic focus.

options.text: It is triggered by early afterdepolarisations, which are pause-dependent
options.why_wrong: EAD-triggered activity occurs with a long QT and causes torsades; it does not explain a warming-up atrial focus.

options.text: The tachycardia is automatic: the shock depolarises the focus but does not remove the abnormal pacemaker, so it fires again
It is AV nodal re-entry, best treated by repeated cardioversion
options.why_wrong: AVNRT starts and stops abruptly and is terminated by adenosine or vagal manoeuvres; repeated shocks are not the answer for an automatic rhythm.

stem: A patient with a focal atrial tachycardia has a rate that 'warms up' over several beats at onset. DC cardioversion restores sinus rhythm, but the tachycardia returns within seconds every time. What is the best explanation?

explanation: Digoxin blocks the Na+/K+-ATPase. The higher intracellular Na+ reduces the gradient that drives the Na+/Ca2+ exchanger (3 Na+ in for 1 Ca2+ out), so less Ca2+ leaves the cell, the SR loads more Ca2+ and each beat releases more. The same Ca2+ loading explains delayed-afterdepolarisation arrhythmias in toxicity.

options.text: Phosphorylation of L-type Ca2+ channels by protein kinase A
options.why_wrong: PKA-mediated phosphorylation is the beta-agonist (cAMP) pathway, as with dobutamine; digoxin does not raise cAMP.

options.text: Sensitisation of troponin C to Ca2+
options.why_wrong: Calcium sensitisation is the mechanism of levosimendan, which works without raising intracellular Ca2+.

options.text: Inhibition of phosphodiesterase 3 with a rise in cAMP
options.why_wrong: PDE3 inhibition is the mechanism of milrinone.

options.text: Inhibition of the Na+/K+-ATPase raises intracellular Na+, so the Na+/Ca2+ exchanger extrudes less Ca2+ and more Ca2+ is stored in the SR

stem: What is the mechanism of the positive inotropic effect of digoxin?

explanation: In cardiac muscle a small influx of Ca2+ through L-type (dihydropyridine-receptor) channels during the plateau opens the SR ryanodine receptors (RyR2): calcium-induced calcium release. Less trigger Ca2+ means less release and weaker contraction. In skeletal muscle the DHPR opens RyR1 mechanically, so contraction does not depend on Ca2+ entry.

options.text: Cardiac contraction needs a trigger of Ca2+ entry through L-type channels to open RyR2 (calcium-induced calcium release), whereas in skeletal muscle the DHPR is mechanically linked to RyR1
Most of the Ca2+ for cardiac contraction comes from the extracellular fluid, so blocking entry removes most of the activator Ca2+
options.why_wrong: Most systolic Ca2+ comes from the SR; the extracellular Ca2+ is a small but essential trigger for its release.

options.text: Verapamil directly blocks the ryanodine receptors of the cardiac SR
options.why_wrong: Verapamil blocks the sarcolemmal L-type channel; it reduces SR release indirectly by shrinking the trigger.

options.text: Verapamil inhibits SERCA2a, so the SR cannot reload between beats
options.why_wrong: SERCA2a is not the target of calcium channel blockers; inhibiting it would mainly slow relaxation.

stem: A patient with heart failure deteriorates after a high dose of verapamil is started. Why are non-dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers negatively inotropic in cardiac muscle, although they do not weaken skeletal muscle?

explanation: A hypertrophied ventricle relaxes slowly (impaired lusitropy) and is passively stiff. Tachycardia shortens diastole, so relaxation may not finish before the next beat, and AF removes the atrial contribution to filling. The ventricle can then only fill at a much higher pressure, which is transmitted to the pulmonary capillaries. This is why HFpEF, LVH and HCM decompensate with fast AF.

options.text: Tachycardia sharply reduces LV contractility, because the normal force-frequency relation is negative
options.why_wrong: In the normal heart the force-frequency relation is positive; the problem here is filling, not contractility.

options.text: Shortened diastole and loss of the atrial kick in a slowly relaxing, stiff ventricle, so a much higher filling pressure is needed to fill it
Loss of atrial contraction lowers left atrial pressure, so pulmonary capillary pressure falls
options.why_wrong: Losing the atrial kick in a stiff ventricle raises the LA pressure needed to fill it, which raises pulmonary capillary pressure.

options.text: Atrial fibrillation increases passive LV compliance, so the ventricle over-distends
options.why_wrong: AF does not make the ventricle more compliant; in LVH passive stiffness is increased.

stem: A 74-year-old woman with hypertensive LVH and a normal ejection fraction develops atrial fibrillation at 150/min and acute pulmonary oedema. What is the main mechanism of her decompensation?

explanation: Dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers dilate the precapillary arterioles more than the venules, so more arterial pressure is transmitted into the capillary and Pc rises, increasing filtration. Because the patient is not volume-overloaded, increasing the diuretic is the wrong response; adding an ACE inhibitor or ARB (which also dilates the venous side) reduces the oedema.

options.text: Renal sodium retention expands total body volume, so the diuretic dose should be increased
options.why_wrong: Dihydropyridine oedema is not fluid overload (the JVP is normal) and diuretics help little; adding an ACE inhibitor or ARB lessens it.

options.text: Reduced plasma oncotic pressure from suppressed hepatic albumin synthesis
options.why_wrong: Amlodipine does not lower albumin; low πc is the mechanism of nephrotic syndrome, cirrhosis and malnutrition.

options.text: Precapillary arteriolar dilatation without matching venular dilatation raises capillary hydrostatic pressure (Pc)
Increased capillary permeability from a drug-induced inflammatory reaction
options.why_wrong: Permeability oedema is seen in sepsis, burns, anaphylaxis and ARDS, not as the usual amlodipine side effect.

stem: A 62-year-old man develops bilateral ankle oedema 3 weeks after starting amlodipine. His JVP is normal. Using the capillary Starling forces shown, what is the mechanism?

explanation: The lymphatics are the main safety valve against oedema. In chronically raised left atrial pressure, pulmonary lymph flow increases greatly, so patients tolerate wedge pressures that flood the lungs of a patient with an acute rise (acute MI, acute severe MR). On a chest X-ray, interstitial oedema appears at roughly 18-25 mmHg and alveolar oedema above about 25 mmHg in the acute setting.

options.text: Chronic left atrial hypertension raises plasma oncotic pressure enough to balance the high capillary pressure
options.why_wrong: Mitral stenosis does not raise plasma oncotic pressure; the adaptation is in lymphatic removal.

options.text: Lymphatic drainage of the lung has increased greatly in the chronic patient and removes the extra filtrate
Acute papillary muscle rupture causes oedema mainly by increasing capillary permeability
options.why_wrong: Acute severe MR floods the lungs through a sudden rise in hydrostatic pressure, not through a permeability leak.

options.text: In chronic mitral stenosis the extra filtrate is reabsorbed at the venular end of the pulmonary capillaries
options.why_wrong: In the revised Starling view there is little sustained venular reabsorption; the lymphatics return most of the filtrate.

stem: A 55-year-old with long-standing severe mitral stenosis has a PCWP of 25 mmHg and clear lung fields. A patient with acute papillary muscle rupture and the same PCWP has alveolar pulmonary oedema. What best explains the difference?

explanation: Lymphatic filariasis (Wuchereria bancrofti, Brugia malayi) obstructs lymphatic drainage. Filtered fluid and protein accumulate in the interstitium, and the protein-rich fluid makes chronic lymphoedema typically non-pitting. A normal JVP and normal albumin point away from cardiac and oncotic causes.

options.text: Lymphatic obstruction, so filtered fluid and protein are not removed from the interstitium
Raised capillary hydrostatic pressure from right heart failure
options.why_wrong: Cardiac oedema is bilateral, pitting and comes with a raised JVP; the JVP here is normal.

options.text: Reduced plasma oncotic pressure
options.why_wrong: The serum albumin is normal, and hypoalbuminaemic oedema is pitting and generalised.

options.text: Increased capillary permeability from sepsis
options.why_wrong: Permeability oedema is acute and part of a systemic illness, not a chronic one-leg swelling.

stem: A 40-year-old farmer from a lymphatic filariasis-endemic district has chronic, non-pitting swelling of the left leg with thickened skin. His JVP and serum albumin are normal. Which mechanism best explains the oedema?

explanation: Angiotensin-converting enzyme is the same enzyme as kininase II, which breaks down bradykinin. ACE inhibitors therefore raise bradykinin, which causes dry cough and angioedema. ARBs act at the AT1 receptor without raising bradykinin, so switching to an ARB is the usual answer.

options.text: ACE is also kininase II, so inhibiting it allows bradykinin (and substance P) to accumulate
Blockade of AT1 receptors in the airway
options.why_wrong: AT1 blockade is the ARB mechanism, and ARBs cause much less cough because they do not raise bradykinin.

options.text: A rise in aldosterone that causes airway mucosal oedema
options.why_wrong: ACE inhibitors lower angiotensin II and aldosterone, not raise them.

options.text: Neprilysin inhibition that raises natriuretic peptides
options.why_wrong: Neprilysin inhibition is the action of sacubitril, not of an ACE inhibitor.

stem: A 60-year-old man develops a persistent dry cough 3 weeks after starting enalapril. What is the mechanism?

explanation: Natriuretic peptides are removed by the clearance receptor and degraded by neprilysin. Sacubitril inhibits neprilysin, so BNP levels rise on treatment even when wall stress falls. NT-proBNP, the inactive fragment released with BNP, is not a neprilysin substrate, so it remains a valid marker on an ARNI.

options.text: The rising BNP proves worsening heart failure, so the diuretic dose should be increased
options.why_wrong: On an ARNI a higher BNP can reflect reduced degradation rather than more wall stress; the clinical picture is improving.

options.text: Neprilysin inhibition slows the breakdown of BNP; NT-proBNP, which is not a neprilysin substrate, should be used to follow him
Valsartan directly stimulates BNP secretion from ventricular myocytes
options.why_wrong: BNP is released by ventricular wall stress; the rise on ARNI comes from inhibited breakdown by neprilysin.

options.text: BNP rises because the ARNI blocks the clearance receptor NPR-C
options.why_wrong: Sacubitril inhibits neprilysin; it does not act on the NPR-C clearance receptor.

stem: A man with HFrEF started sacubitril/valsartan 3 months ago. He feels better and is less congested, yet his BNP is higher than before treatment. What is the best interpretation?

explanation: Angiotensin II constricts the efferent more than the afferent arteriole, which keeps glomerular pressure and GFR up when renal perfusion is low. With bilateral renal artery stenosis (or stenosis to a single kidney), GFR depends on that efferent tone, so an ACE inhibitor or ARB can precipitate acute kidney injury.

options.text: Accumulated bradykinin constricts the afferent arteriole
options.why_wrong: Bradykinin is a vasodilator; the mechanism is loss of efferent angiotensin II tone.

options.text: This is the expected haemodynamic rise and needs no action
options.why_wrong: An early rise of up to about 30% is expected; a doubling of creatinine is not, and points to renovascular dependence on Ang II.

options.text: Glomerular filtration depended on angiotensin II constriction of the efferent arteriole; removing it lowered glomerular pressure (suspect bilateral renal artery stenosis)
Aldosterone escape causes sodium retention and renal congestion
options.why_wrong: Aldosterone escape is a gradual rise in aldosterone during long-term therapy; it does not cause an acute fall in GFR.

stem: A 66-year-old hypertensive smoker with an abdominal bruit starts ramipril. One week later his creatinine has risen from 1.1 to 2.4 mg/dL. What is the mechanism?

explanation: Renin release has three triggers: low renal perfusion pressure, low NaCl delivery sensed by the macula densa, and beta-1 sympathetic stimulation. Loop diuretics block NKCC2 in the macula densa cells themselves, so the macula densa 'sees' low NaCl and renin rises. Angiotensin II, natriuretic peptides, high distal NaCl and beta-blockers suppress it.

options.text: Bisoprolol
options.why_wrong: Beta-1 blockade of the juxtaglomerular cells reduces renin release.

options.text: Increased NaCl delivery to the macula densa
options.why_wrong: High distal NaCl suppresses renin; low NaCl at the macula densa stimulates it.

options.text: An infusion of atrial natriuretic peptide
options.why_wrong: Natriuretic peptides inhibit renin, aldosterone and sympathetic tone.

options.text: Furosemide
A rise in renal perfusion pressure
options.why_wrong: High renal perfusion pressure suppresses renin; low pressure stimulates it.

stem: Which of the following INCREASES renin release from the juxtaglomerular cells?

explanation: Dynamic exercise (running, cycling) is a volume load: heart rate and cardiac output rise greatly, SVR falls and diastolic pressure barely changes. Static exercise (lifting, handgrip) is a pressure load: systolic and diastolic pressure and mean arterial pressure rise markedly with only a modest rise in heart rate and output. That afterload rise is why handgrip increases MR, VSD and AR murmurs.

options.text: A fall in systemic vascular resistance with an unchanged diastolic pressure: a volume load
options.why_wrong: That is the dynamic-exercise pattern; in static exercise contracting muscle compresses its own vessels, so SVR stays the same or rises.

options.text: A four-fold rise in cardiac output driven by a large rise in stroke volume
options.why_wrong: Static exercise raises cardiac output only modestly, and stroke volume changes little.

options.text: A fall in systolic pressure from vasodilatation in the working muscle
options.why_wrong: Blood pressure rises during isometric exercise; a fall in systolic pressure during exercise is a high-risk sign.

options.text: A marked rise in both systolic and diastolic pressure with little change in stroke volume: a pressure load

stem: Compared with the responses to dynamic exercise shown, what does sustained isometric handgrip produce?

explanation: By Fick, VO2 = HR × SV × (a-vO2 difference). Training expands plasma volume and enlarges a compliant LV, raising maximal stroke volume, and adds capillaries and mitochondria, widening O2 extraction. Maximal heart rate is not trainable; it falls with age.

options.text: A higher maximal stroke volume, together with a wider maximal arteriovenous O2 difference
A higher maximal heart rate
options.why_wrong: Maximal heart rate is set by age and does not rise with training.

options.text: Better lung diffusing capacity, because VO2max in healthy people is limited by the lungs
options.why_wrong: In healthy people VO2max is limited mainly by maximal cardiac output, not by the lungs.

options.text: A higher resting heart rate, which raises cardiac output at rest
options.why_wrong: Training lowers the resting and submaximal heart rate (more vagal tone, larger stroke volume).

stem: After 6 months of endurance training, a healthy 30-year-old's VO2max has increased. What accounts for most of this increase?

explanation: Cardiac output = 180 × 0.1 L = 18 L/min. The a-vO2 difference = 20 − 5 = 15 mL/dL = 150 mL/L. VO2 = 18 L/min × 150 mL/L = 2,700 mL/min. Compared with rest (about 250 mL/min) this comes from about four-fold more cardiac output and three-fold more extraction.

options.text: About 270 mL/min
options.why_wrong: This treats the a-vO2 difference of 15 mL/dL as if it were 15 mL/L; 15 mL/dL is 150 mL/L.

options.text: About 27,000 mL/min
options.why_wrong: This converts litres to decilitres with a factor of 100 instead of 10.

options.text: About 3,600 mL/min
options.why_wrong: This uses the arterial O2 content (20 mL/dL) instead of the arteriovenous difference.

options.text: About 2,700 mL/min

stem: At peak exercise a subject has a heart rate of 180/min, a stroke volume of 100 mL, an arterial O2 content of 20 mL/dL and a mixed venous O2 content of 5 mL/dL. Using the Fick relation shown, what is the oxygen uptake?

explanation: Heart-rate recovery is the fall in heart rate in the first minute after exercise, driven by vagal reactivation. A fall of 12 beats/min or less with an upright cool-down (18 or less if the patient lies down at once) is abnormal and independently predicts mortality. Here the fall is only 8/min.

options.text: Abnormal heart-rate recovery, reflecting slow vagal reactivation; an adverse prognostic marker
A normal response: heart rate is expected to stay near its peak for several minutes
options.why_wrong: Heart rate normally falls quickly after exercise; a fall of 12/min or less in the first minute (upright) is abnormal.

options.text: Chronotropic incompetence
options.why_wrong: Chronotropic incompetence is failure to reach 85% of the age-predicted maximum; 160/min is above that for a 55-year-old.

options.text: Excess vagal tone, as seen in endurance athletes
options.why_wrong: High vagal tone speeds heart-rate recovery; a slow fall means delayed vagal reactivation.

stem: A 55-year-old completes a symptom-limited treadmill test with an upright cool-down. His peak heart rate is 160/min, and 1 minute after stopping it is 152/min. What is the best interpretation?

explanation: This is persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn. PVR stays at or above systemic pressure, so blood shunts right-to-left across the foramen ovale and the ductus arteriosus. With a ductal shunt, pre-ductal (right hand) saturation is higher than post-ductal (foot) saturation. Treatment includes oxygen, optimal ventilation, support of systemic pressure and inhaled nitric oxide, with ECMO when refractory.

options.text: Pulmonary vascular resistance has failed to fall, so desaturated blood shunts right-to-left across the ductus arteriosus to the descending aorta
Transposition of the great arteries with pulmonary hypertension
options.why_wrong: The heart is structurally normal; transposition with pulmonary hypertension or arch obstruction gives reverse differential cyanosis (foot pinker than hand).

options.text: A left-to-right ductal shunt as pulmonary resistance falls
options.why_wrong: A left-to-right shunt sends oxygenated blood into the lungs and does not cause cyanosis.

options.text: Premature closure of the foramen ovale in utero
options.why_wrong: Pre-ductal and post-ductal saturations differ because of a shunt at ductal level, not because of foramen ovale closure.

stem: A term baby born after meconium aspiration is cyanosed. Right-hand SpO2 is 95% and foot SpO2 is 80%; echocardiography shows a structurally normal heart. Using the neonatal transition shown, what is the mechanism?

explanation: Oxygenated umbilical venous blood bypasses the liver through the ductus venosus and enters the IVC. In the right atrium the Eustachian valve and the crista dividens stream it across the foramen ovale to the LA, LV and ascending aorta, so the coronary arteries and brain receive the best-oxygenated blood. Desaturated SVC blood goes to the RV and mostly crosses the ductus arteriosus.

options.text: The tricuspid valve, which channels IVC blood into the right ventricle
options.why_wrong: The desaturated SVC stream is the one that passes mainly through the tricuspid valve into the RV.

options.text: The ductus arteriosus, which draws blood from the right atrium
options.why_wrong: The ductus arteriosus connects the pulmonary trunk to the descending aorta; it plays no part in atrial streaming.

options.text: The septum primum flap pressed against the septum secundum
options.why_wrong: The flap closing against the septum secundum is what shuts the foramen ovale after birth, when LA pressure exceeds RA pressure.

options.text: The Eustachian valve and the edge of the atrial septum (crista dividens)

stem: In the fetal circulation shown, what directs the well-oxygenated blood arriving through the ductus venosus and IVC across the foramen ovale into the left atrium?

explanation: In duct-dependent systemic circulation (hypoplastic left heart, critical coarctation, interrupted arch, critical AS) the body is perfused from the pulmonary artery through the ductus. Functional ductal closure in the first days causes shock. Prostaglandin E1 (alprostadil) reopens and maintains the duct; apnoea, fever, flushing and hypotension are its recognised side effects.

options.text: IV indomethacin to close the ductus arteriosus
options.why_wrong: Closing the duct would remove systemic blood flow, which depends on the duct in HLHS; COX inhibitors are for a significant PDA in preterm infants.

options.text: A prostaglandin E1 infusion to reopen the ductus arteriosus, with readiness to ventilate because it can cause apnoea
High-flow oxygen to reopen the ductus arteriosus
options.why_wrong: A rise in PaO2 constricts the ductus; oxygen does not reopen it.

options.text: Inhaled nitric oxide to lower pulmonary vascular resistance
options.why_wrong: Inhaled NO treats persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn; it does not reopen the duct on which systemic flow depends.

stem: A 2-day-old baby with hypoplastic left heart syndrome becomes pale, mottled and acidotic with weak pulses. What is the immediate treatment?

explanation: LVOT area = 0.785 × 2.0² = 3.14 cm². Stroke volume = 3.14 × 18 = 56.5 mL. AVA = 56.5 / 90 = 0.63 cm², in the severe range (≤ 1.0 cm²). The dimensionless index 18 / 90 = 0.20 (< 0.25) agrees. Because D is squared, a 10% error in the LVOT diameter gives about a 20% error in the AVA.

options.text: About 0.31 cm²
options.why_wrong: This uses 0.785 × D (1.57 cm²) as the LVOT area; the diameter must be squared.

options.text: About 2.51 cm²
options.why_wrong: This uses π × D² as the LVOT area; the area is π × (D/2)², that is 0.785 × D².

options.text: About 0.63 cm²
About 0.20 cm²
options.why_wrong: 0.20 is the dimensionless index (VTI ratio 18 / 90), which has no units; it is not the valve area.

stem: In a patient with aortic stenosis, the LVOT diameter is 2.0 cm, the LVOT VTI is 18 cm and the aortic valve VTI is 90 cm. Using the continuity equation shown, what is the aortic valve area?

explanation: Simplified Bernoulli: ΔP = 4v² = 4 × 3.5² = 4 × 12.25 = 49 mmHg. The proximal (LVOT) velocity of 0.8 m/s is low enough to ignore; it should be included when it is about 1.5 m/s or more. A peak velocity of 3.0-3.9 m/s is in the moderate range.

options.text: 49 mmHg
14 mmHg
options.why_wrong: This multiplies the velocity by 4 without squaring it.

options.text: 196 mmHg
options.why_wrong: This squares 4v (14²) instead of multiplying 4 by v².

options.text: 12 mmHg
options.why_wrong: This squares the velocity but leaves out the factor of 4.

stem: Continuous-wave Doppler in a patient with aortic stenosis shows a peak aortic jet velocity of 3.5 m/s; the LVOT velocity is 0.8 m/s. What is the peak instantaneous gradient by the simplified Bernoulli equation?

explanation: This is classical low-flow, low-gradient AS (LVEF < 50%, SVi < 35 mL/m²). Dobutamine raises flow: in true severe AS the mean gradient reaches ≥ 40 mmHg (Vmax ≥ 4 m/s) while the AVA stays ≤ 1.0 cm²; in pseudo-severe AS the AVA rises above 1.0 cm². If stroke volume rises by less than 20% (no flow reserve), the CT calcium score is used.

options.text: A CT aortic valve calcium score as the first test
options.why_wrong: CT calcium scoring is the first confirmatory test in paradoxical low-flow AS with preserved EF; in classical low-flow AS it is used when dobutamine shows no flow reserve.

options.text: Classify the stenosis as moderate because the mean gradient is below 40 mmHg
options.why_wrong: At low flow the gradient underestimates severity; the gradient rises with the square of flow.

options.text: Low-dose dobutamine stress echocardiography
Calculate the valve area at rest with the Gorlin formula at cardiac catheterisation
options.why_wrong: The Gorlin formula is least reliable at low flow and does not test whether the valve area changes as flow rises.

stem: A 72-year-old man has an LVEF of 30%, an aortic valve area of 0.8 cm², a mean gradient of 25 mmHg and a stroke volume index of 28 mL/m². Measurements have been checked. Using the gradient-flow relation shown, what is the next step to grade the stenosis?

explanation: A tighter mitral valve holds up the LA-LV gradient for longer, so the pressure half-time lengthens. MVA ≈ 220 / PHT = 220 / 275 = 0.8 cm², which is severe (≤ 1.5 cm²). The estimate is unreliable straight after balloon mitral commissurotomy, with significant AR, or when LA or LV compliance is abnormal.

options.text: About 1.25 cm²
options.why_wrong: This divides the PHT by 220 instead of dividing 220 by the PHT.

options.text: About 0.8 cm²
About 2.75 cm²
options.why_wrong: The empirical constant is 220, not 100; MVA ≈ 220 / PHT.

options.text: The pressure half-time cannot estimate the mitral valve area; it is used only to grade aortic regurgitation
options.why_wrong: PHT is used in both lesions: it lengthens with tighter mitral stenosis and shortens with more severe AR.

stem: In a patient with rheumatic mitral stenosis, the pressure half-time of the transmitral Doppler signal is 275 ms. What is the estimated mitral valve area?

explanation: The tracing is pulsus parvus et tardus: small amplitude (parvus), slow upstroke with a late peak (tardus) and an anacrotic shoulder on the upstroke, with a narrow pulse pressure. It reflects a fixed obstruction that prolongs LV ejection. Bedside markers of severe AS: late-peaking murmur, soft or absent A2 (calcified, immobile leaflets), paradoxical splitting, sustained (heaving) apex and an S4. Loudness of the murmur is NOT a reliable severity marker (it falls when flow falls). Pitfall: in the elderly, stiff arteries can mask the slow upstroke at the carotid. Study aid; verify thresholds against the current full guideline.

options.text: Severe aortic stenosis; a soft or absent A2 supports severity
Obstructive HCM; the murmur gets louder on Valsalva strain
options.why_wrong: HCM gives a brisk early upstroke (the LV ejects freely before the outflow obstruction develops) and a spike-and-dome contour, not a slow, low-amplitude rise.

options.text: Severe aortic regurgitation; a wide pulse pressure is expected
options.why_wrong: AR gives a rapid upstroke, a high peak and a wide pulse pressure. This tracing rises slowly to a late, low peak with a narrow pulse pressure (105/80 mmHg).

options.text: Cardiac tamponade; systolic pressure falls on inspiration
options.why_wrong: Tamponade changes beat-to-beat amplitude with respiration (pulsus paradoxus); the contour of each beat stays normal. Here every beat has the same slow, delayed rise.

stem: A 76-year-old man has had two episodes of exertional syncope. The arterial pressure tracing shown was recorded. Which lesion and accompanying finding best fit this pulse?

explanation: Pulsus bisferiens: two systolic peaks (percussion wave, then tidal wave) separated by a mid-systolic dip, best felt at the carotid or brachial artery. Causes: severe AR, or mixed aortic valve disease with dominant AR; a bifid pulse is also felt in obstructive HCM (spike and dome, with a normal pulse pressure). Dicrotic pulse: the second peak is diastolic (exaggerated dicrotic wave after the notch) and occurs with a very low stroke volume, usually in a young, compliant arterial tree (dilated cardiomyopathy, sepsis, after valve surgery). Rule: both peaks before the notch = bisferiens; one before and one after = dicrotic. Study aid; verify thresholds against the current full guideline.

options.text: Isolated severe calcific aortic stenosis
options.why_wrong: Severe AS produces a slow-rising, small pulse (parvus et tardus); a bisferiens pulse is lost when stenosis dominates.

options.text: Dicrotic pulse of a low-output cardiomyopathy
options.why_wrong: In a dicrotic pulse the second peak falls in diastole, after the dicrotic notch, and the pulse pressure is low. Here both peaks are systolic, before the notch, with a pulse pressure of 90 mmHg.

options.text: Severe AR, alone or with milder AS
Pulsus alternans of severe LV systolic failure
options.why_wrong: Alternans is a beat-to-beat variation in peak pressure (strong beat, weak beat), not two peaks inside one beat.

stem: A 45-year-old has a wide pulse pressure. The arterial tracing shown has two peaks within each beat. Which lesion is classically responsible?

explanation: Pulsus alternans: regular rhythm with alternating strong and weak beats (here systolic 125 vs 108 mmHg). It marks severe LV systolic dysfunction (beat-to-beat changes in preload and contractility of a failing ventricle) and carries a poor prognosis; it may appear after a premature beat or with tachycardia. Bedside detection: deflate the cuff slowly; at first only alternate Korotkoff sounds are heard, then, a few mmHg lower, all beats (the rate of sounds doubles). Do not confuse with pulsus bigeminus (irregular), electrical alternans (ECG QRS amplitude, tamponade) or pulsus paradoxus (respiratory). Study aid; verify thresholds against the current full guideline.

options.text: Large pericardial effusion with tamponade
options.why_wrong: Tamponade is linked to pulsus paradoxus (respiratory variation) and to electrical alternans on the ECG; mechanical alternation of every other beat with a regular rhythm points to a failing LV.

options.text: Severe LV systolic dysfunction
Ventricular bigeminy
options.why_wrong: Bigeminy alternates a normal beat with a premature beat, so the rhythm is irregular (short-long coupling). Here the ECG is regular and the beats are evenly spaced.

options.text: Severe aortic regurgitation
options.why_wrong: AR gives a collapsing or bisferiens pulse with a wide pulse pressure; it does not cause strong and weak beats to alternate.

stem: A 62-year-old with breathlessness has the arterial tracing shown; the rhythm on the ECG reference is regular. What is the most likely significance of this finding?

explanation: The tracing is the spike-and-dome (jerky) pulse of obstructive HCM: a brisk early upstroke while the LV ejects freely, a mid-systolic fall as systolic anterior motion of the mitral valve obstructs the LVOT, then a smaller late dome. The obstruction is dynamic: anything that makes the LV smaller (less preload: Valsalva strain, standing; less afterload: amyl nitrite, nitrates) or more contractile increases the gradient and the murmur; anything that makes it larger (squatting, passive leg raise, handgrip) decreases them. Post-extrasystolic beat: the murmur gets louder but the aortic pulse pressure falls (Brockenbrough-Braunwald-Morrow sign). Study aid; verify thresholds against the current full guideline.

options.text: Louder on squatting; softer on Valsalva strain
options.why_wrong: Squatting raises preload and afterload and Valsalva strain lowers preload: this is the response of fixed outflow obstruction (AS), the opposite of a dynamic LVOT obstruction.

options.text: Louder with handgrip; unchanged on standing
options.why_wrong: Handgrip raises afterload, which widens the LVOT and softens the HCM murmur; handgrip makes MR, VSD and AR murmurs louder.

options.text: Louder after amyl nitrite; softer on standing
options.why_wrong: Amyl nitrite (vasodilation, reflex tachycardia, lower afterload) does make the HCM murmur louder, but standing lowers preload and also makes it louder, not softer.

options.text: Louder on standing; softer with handgrip

stem: A 22-year-old footballer has a systolic murmur at the left lower sternal border. The arterial tracing shown was recorded. Which bedside response would you expect from the murmur?

explanation: JVP: measure the vertical height of the top of the internal jugular pulsation above the sternal angle (angle of Louis), with the head turned slightly away and the trunk at whatever angle shows the top (often 30-45 degrees). Add about 5 cm (sternal angle to mid RA) to estimate RA pressure in cm H2O; divide by 1.36 for mmHg. A height above 3 cm (RA pressure above about 8 cm H2O) is raised. Pitfalls: the +5 cm constant varies between patients and positions; use the internal (not external) jugular; a very high JVP can be missed with the patient lying flat (the top is above the jaw), so sit the patient up. CT studies (Seth et al., 2002) place the sternal angle about 8-10 cm above the mid RA at 30-60 degrees, so the +5 cm convention underestimates RA pressure; for decisions use the height above the sternal angle (raised if more than 3 cm). Study aid; verify thresholds against the current full guideline.

options.text: About 11 cm H2O (about 8 mmHg): raised
About 6 cm H2O: within the normal range
options.why_wrong: The sternal angle lies roughly 5 cm above the mid right atrium, so this distance must be added to the measured height.

options.text: About 11 mmHg: raised
options.why_wrong: The JVP gives a column of blood in cm H2O, not mmHg. 1 mmHg = 1.36 cm H2O, so 11 cm H2O is about 8 mmHg.

options.text: About 1 cm H2O: low
options.why_wrong: The sternal-angle constant is added to the measured height, not subtracted from it.

stem: A patient lies at 45 degrees. The top of the internal jugular pulsation is 6 cm vertically above the sternal angle. Using the conventional bedside constant, what is the best estimate of right atrial pressure?

explanation: Cannon a waves occur when the right atrium contracts against a closed tricuspid valve. Intermittent (irregular) cannon waves = AV dissociation: complete heart block, VT with AV dissociation, accelerated junctional or ventricular rhythms; the ECG shows P waves at their own rate with a variable relation to QRS. In complete heart block the first heart sound also varies in intensity (variable PR). Regular cannon waves on every beat = atrial activation during each ventricular systole (junctional rhythm, AVNRT, VT with 1:1 retrograde conduction, VVI pacing with retrograde conduction: pacemaker syndrome). Giant but non-cannon a waves on every beat = a stiff right ventricle or tricuspid stenosis. Study aid; verify thresholds against the current full guideline.

options.text: A retrograde P wave buried at the end of every QRS
options.why_wrong: Retrograde atrial activation in every beat (junctional rhythm, AVNRT, VT with 1:1 VA conduction) makes cannon waves regular, on every beat. Here they are intermittent.

options.text: Atrial fibrillation with a slow ventricular response
options.why_wrong: In AF there is no organised atrial contraction, so a waves (cannon or normal) are absent.

options.text: Independent P waves with no fixed PR interval
Sinus rhythm with first-degree AV block
options.why_wrong: A long PR moves the a wave earlier and away from the c wave; it does not cause intermittent cannon waves (an extremely long PR could at most give regular ones).

stem: A 79-year-old with dizziness has a pulse of 40/min. The jugular tracing shown has an irregular pattern of very large a waves on some beats only. Which ECG finding is expected?

explanation: Severe tricuspid regurgitation: the x descent disappears and is replaced by a large systolic cv (or s) wave as blood regurgitates into the RA, followed by a steep y descent when the tricuspid valve opens. Associated signs: holosystolic murmur at the lower left sternal border that increases on inspiration (Carvallo sign), systolic pulsation of the liver, earlobe movement with each beat, RV heave and signs of the cause (pulmonary hypertension, RV dilatation, lead-related TR). Pitfall: with a very large, free regurgitation the murmur may be soft or absent and Carvallo may fail when the RV cannot increase its output; the giant cv wave is then the best bedside clue. Study aid; verify thresholds against the current full guideline.

options.text: An early diastolic murmur at Erb's point, louder sitting forward in expiration
options.why_wrong: That is aortic regurgitation; it does not raise the JVP or produce a systolic cv wave.

options.text: A lower sternal border holosystolic murmur, louder on inspiration
A pericardial knock with a rise of the mean JVP on inspiration
options.why_wrong: Constriction gives prominent x and y descents (M or W pattern): its x descent is preserved, not replaced by a large systolic wave as in this tracing.

options.text: Presystolic liver pulsation with a slow y descent
options.why_wrong: Presystolic hepatic pulsation, giant a waves and a slow y descent are features of tricuspid stenosis. This tracing has a steep y descent after a large systolic wave.

stem: A 58-year-old with a raised JVP has the jugular tracing shown. Which accompanying finding best confirms the underlying lesion?

explanation: Kussmaul sign: the JVP rises (or fails to fall) on inspiration. Normally inspiration lowers intrathoracic pressure, increases venous return and the JVP falls. Causes: constrictive pericarditis (classic), restrictive cardiomyopathy, RV infarction, severe right heart failure, massive PE, tricuspid stenosis. In tamponade the intrapericardial pressure falls with inspiration and is transmitted to the heart, so right-sided filling still increases: Kussmaul sign is typically absent, while pulsus paradoxus is the rule. Effusive-constrictive pericarditis can show both. Exam rule: pulsus paradoxus favours tamponade; Kussmaul sign and a pericardial knock favour constriction. Study aid; verify thresholds against the current full guideline.

options.text: Constrictive pericarditis
options.why_wrong: Constriction is the classic cause: the rigid pericardium stops the right heart from accepting the inspiratory increase in venous return.

options.text: Right ventricular infarction
options.why_wrong: RV infarction is a recognised cause: the non-compliant, ischaemic RV cannot accommodate the inspiratory increase in return.

options.text: Restrictive cardiomyopathy
options.why_wrong: Restrictive cardiomyopathy produces the sign by the same mechanism (stiff ventricle that cannot fill more on inspiration).

options.text: Cardiac tamponade

stem: The jugular tracing shown (inspiration shaded) demonstrates the mean venous pressure rising on inspiration. In which condition is this sign classically absent?

explanation: The tracing shows a raised JVP with a prominent x descent and a steep, deep y descent followed by a quick rise and plateau (M or W pattern). The steep y descent (Friedreich sign) reflects unimpeded, very rapid early diastolic filling that stops abruptly when the rigid pericardium is reached. The same abrupt halt produces the pericardial knock: an early diastolic sound (about 90-120 ms after A2), earlier and higher pitched than an S3, best at the left sternal border or apex. Other signs: Kussmaul sign, ascites out of proportion to oedema, hepatomegaly; pulsus paradoxus is less common than in tamponade. Tuberculosis is a leading cause of constriction in endemic areas. Study aid; verify thresholds against the current full guideline.

options.text: An opening snap followed by a low-pitched diastolic rumble
options.why_wrong: An opening snap marks a stenotic mitral valve opening; it is followed by a rumble and gives a loud S1. Constriction has no diastolic murmur.

options.text: A sharp early diastolic sound, earlier than an S3
A late diastolic sound just before S1
options.why_wrong: That is an S4 (atrial contraction into a stiff ventricle). In constriction atrial filling contributes little, and an S4 is not a feature.

options.text: A soft, early systolic sound just after S1
options.why_wrong: An ejection sound comes from a doming semilunar valve or dilated great artery, unrelated to pericardial disease.

stem: A 50-year-old treated for tuberculous pericarditis two years ago has ascites and the jugular tracing shown. Which auscultatory finding is most likely?

explanation: In tamponade the pericardial pressure compresses all chambers throughout diastole; the total cardiac volume is fixed, so blood can enter the heart only when blood leaves it (during ventricular ejection). The x descent (systole) is preserved and the y descent (early diastolic emptying of the RA) is blunted or absent. In constriction the heart fills very rapidly in early diastole until the rigid shell stops it: steep y descent, knock, Kussmaul sign. Bedside comparison: tamponade = Beck triad (hypotension, raised JVP, quiet heart sounds), pulsus paradoxus common, no Kussmaul, no knock; constriction = steep y, Kussmaul, knock, pulsus paradoxus uncommon. Study aid; verify thresholds against the current full guideline.

options.text: Absent y descent, pulsus paradoxus, no Kussmaul sign
Steep y descent with a rise of the JVP on inspiration
options.why_wrong: A steep y descent and Kussmaul sign are the hallmarks of constriction, not of tamponade; this tracing has no y descent.

options.text: Raised JVP with sinus tachycardia and hypotension
options.why_wrong: Both tamponade and decompensated constriction can raise the JVP and cause tachycardia and hypotension; these features do not discriminate.

options.text: Pericardial knock with ascites and hepatomegaly
options.why_wrong: A knock and ascites out of proportion to oedema are features of chronic constriction.

stem: A man is hypotensive after a stab wound to the chest. His jugular tracing is shown. Which combination of bedside findings best separates his condition from constrictive pericarditis?

explanation: Pulsus paradoxus = an inspiratory fall in systolic pressure of more than 10 mmHg (here about 21 mmHg). Mechanism in tamponade: inspiration increases RV filling; in a fixed pericardial space the septum shifts left, LV filling and stroke volume fall (ventricular interdependence), plus pooling of blood in the lungs. Measure with a cuff: the gap between the first Korotkoff sound heard in expiration only and the pressure where all beats are heard. It may be ABSENT in tamponade with ASD (shunt equalises filling), significant AR, LV dysfunction with very high LVEDP, RV hypertrophy or pulmonary hypertension, positive-pressure ventilation, or loculated effusion. Other causes of the sign: severe asthma/COPD, massive PE, tension pneumothorax, constriction (minority), hypovolaemic shock. Study aid; verify thresholds against the current full guideline.

options.text: Severe acute asthma
options.why_wrong: Asthma itself causes pulsus paradoxus (large negative intrathoracic pressure swings); it would accentuate the sign, not abolish it.

options.text: Sinus tachycardia
options.why_wrong: Tachycardia is part of tamponade and does not prevent the inspiratory fall in systolic pressure.

options.text: Spontaneous breathing
options.why_wrong: Pulsus paradoxus depends on spontaneous breathing; it is positive-pressure ventilation that removes or reverses it.

options.text: Atrial septal defect

stem: The arterial tracing shown (inspiration shaded) is from a dyspnoeic patient with a large pericardial effusion. Which coexisting condition can abolish this sign despite haemodynamic tamponade?

explanation: Apex beat = the lowest and most lateral point where the cardiac impulse is felt. Normal: 5th intercostal space at or inside the midclavicular line, less than 2.5 cm across (about one intercostal space), brief (first part of systole). Volume overload (chronic AR, MR, VSD, PDA, high-output states): eccentric hypertrophy, displaced downward and outward, diffuse, hyperdynamic. Pressure overload (AS, hypertension, HCM): sustained, heaving, little displacement. Tapping apex: MS (palpable S1). Double impulse: HCM (palpable S4) or a dyskinetic aneurysm. Pitfalls: chest deformity, obesity, COPD or a large effusion make the apex impalpable; the left lateral position exaggerates displacement. Study aid; verify thresholds against the current full guideline.

options.text: Severe aortic stenosis with preserved LV function
options.why_wrong: Pressure overload (AS, hypertension) gives concentric hypertrophy: a sustained, heaving apex that is usually not displaced until the LV dilates.

options.text: Isolated severe mitral stenosis
options.why_wrong: The LV is underfilled in MS; the apex is not displaced and feels tapping (a palpable loud S1).

options.text: Chronic severe aortic regurgitation
Obstructive hypertrophic cardiomyopathy
options.why_wrong: HCM gives a forceful, sustained apex that may be double or triple (palpable atrial kick plus a bifid systolic impulse), not a displaced diffuse one.

stem: A 52-year-old has an apex beat in the 6th intercostal space, anterior axillary line; it is diffuse, brief and hyperdynamic. Which lesion best fits this impulse?

explanation: A left parasternal lift usually means an enlarged or pressure-loaded RV (pulmonary hypertension, PS, ASD), and it is synchronous with the apex. In severe MR the regurgitant volume expands the LA during systole; the LA lies posteriorly and pushes the heart forward, producing a parasternal lift that peaks late in systole, after the apical impulse. Timing against the apex (or the carotid) separates the two. Palpation also gives: thrills (murmur of grade 4 or more), palpable P2 (pulmonary hypertension), tapping apex (MS), sustained apex (pressure overload). Study aid; verify thresholds against the current full guideline.

options.text: Late systolic expansion of a large left atrium
RV pressure overload from pulmonary hypertension
options.why_wrong: An RV heave from pressure overload is sustained and starts with the apical impulse. Echo here excludes pulmonary hypertension, and the lift peaks late in systole.

options.text: A dyskinetic anterior LV aneurysm
options.why_wrong: An aneurysm gives an ectopic impulse above and medial to the apex in the setting of a prior infarct; it is not explained by severe MR.

options.text: A palpable P2 transmitted to the lower sternal border
options.why_wrong: A palpable P2 is a brief tap in the 2nd left intercostal space at end-systole, not a lift at the lower sternum.

stem: A 64-year-old with severe primary mitral regurgitation and normal pulmonary pressures on echo has a left parasternal lift that peaks clearly later than the apical impulse. What is the best explanation?

explanation: Pulmonary hypertension in MS: RV pressure overload gives a left parasternal heave (sustained, synchronous with the apex), and a loud P2 that may be palpable in the 2nd left intercostal space; later, functional TR (giant cv wave), a Graham Steell murmur (PR) and right heart failure. Findings of the MS itself: tapping apex (palpable S1), loud S1, opening snap, mid-diastolic rumble with presystolic accentuation in sinus rhythm, malar flush. A soft S1 and absent opening snap suggest calcified, immobile leaflets. Study aid; verify thresholds against the current full guideline.

options.text: A tapping apex beat
options.why_wrong: A tapping apex is the palpable loud S1 of mobile stenotic leaflets; it is present with or without pulmonary hypertension.

options.text: A left parasternal heave with a palpable P2
A diastolic thrill at the apex
options.why_wrong: An apical diastolic thrill reflects a loud rumble; it says nothing specific about pulmonary pressure.

options.text: An apex displaced to the anterior axillary line
options.why_wrong: Isolated MS does not displace the apex (the LV is underfilled); displacement suggests coexisting MR or AR or another cause of LV dilatation.

stem: In a 35-year-old with rheumatic mitral stenosis, which palpation finding best indicates that pulmonary hypertension has developed?

explanation: Wide, fixed splitting of S2 (here about 60 ms in both phases) is the hallmark of an ASD with a significant left-to-right shunt: the volume-loaded RV ejects longer and the high-capacitance pulmonary bed delays P2. The split does not change because inspiration increases systemic venous return to the RA while the left-to-right shunt falls by the same amount (the two atria behave as one chamber). Other findings: pulmonary flow (ejection) murmur at the upper left sternal border, tricuspid flow rumble at the lower left sternal border with a large shunt, RV heave; ECG rSR' in V1 (and right axis in secundum, left axis in primum). Study aid; verify thresholds against the current full guideline.

options.text: Isolated right bundle branch block
options.why_wrong: RBBB delays P2 and widens the split, but the split still widens further on inspiration (it is not fixed).

options.text: Valvar pulmonary stenosis
options.why_wrong: PS widens the split with a soft, delayed P2, but the split still varies with respiration, and the ejection murmur is louder and often preceded by a click.

options.text: Left bundle branch block
options.why_wrong: LBBB delays A2 and gives paradoxical (reversed) splitting, which narrows on inspiration.

options.text: Secundum atrial septal defect

stem: A 30-year-old woman has a soft systolic murmur in the 2nd left intercostal space. The phonocardiogram shown was recorded in expiration and inspiration. Which condition is most likely?

explanation: Paradoxical (reversed) splitting: A2 is delayed beyond P2, so the order is P2-A2; the split is widest on expiration and narrows or disappears on inspiration (P2 moves later towards A2). Causes = anything that delays LV activation or prolongs LV ejection: LBBB, RV pacing (the LV is activated last), pre-excitation via a right-sided accessory pathway, severe AS, obstructive HCM, severe hypertension, acute ischaemia, large PDA. Opposite (wide splitting with normal order): RBBB, PS, LV pre-excitation, early A2 in severe MR or VSD, and wide fixed splitting in ASD. Study aid; verify thresholds against the current full guideline.

options.text: Complete right bundle branch block
options.why_wrong: RBBB delays RV activation and P2, giving wide splitting that still increases on inspiration.

options.text: Ostium secundum atrial septal defect
