options.why_wrong: ASD gives wide, fixed splitting with P2 after A2 in both phases.

options.text: Right ventricular apical pacing
Severe valvar pulmonary stenosis
options.why_wrong: PS prolongs RV ejection and delays P2: wide splitting in the normal order (A2 then P2).

stem: The phonocardiogram shown (expiration and inspiration, with an ECG reference) was recorded from a 70-year-old. Which of the following could produce this pattern?

explanation: S3: a low-pitched early diastolic sound about 120-180 ms after A2, at the end of rapid ventricular filling, best with the bell lightly applied at the apex in the left lateral position (LV S3) or at the lower left sternal border, louder on inspiration (RV S3). Physiological in children, young adults (under about 40) and pregnancy; pathological in older adults with HF (high filling pressure, dilated LV, prognostic) or volume overload (MR, AR, VSD, PDA). Opening snap: high-pitched, sharp, earlier (about 40-120 ms after A2), best heard between the apex and the lower left sternal border with the diaphragm, often transmitted widely to the base, followed by a rumble, with a loud S1. Pericardial knock: about 90-120 ms, higher pitched than S3. Study aid; verify thresholds against the current full guideline.

options.text: It is low pitched, about 150 ms after S2, best with the bell at the apex
It is high pitched and best heard with the diaphragm at the left sternal border
options.why_wrong: That describes an opening snap (or a knock): sharp, high-frequency, earlier after A2. The extra sound here is a low-frequency sound well into early diastole.

options.text: It falls just before S1, after the P wave of the ECG
options.why_wrong: A sound just before S1 after the P wave is an S4 (atrial contraction). This one follows S2 in early diastole.

options.text: It is followed by a rumble with presystolic accentuation
options.why_wrong: A rumble with presystolic accentuation after the sound would make it an opening snap of MS; the tracing shows no diastolic murmur.

stem: A 66-year-old with ischaemic cardiomyopathy has the apical phonocardiogram shown, with an extra sound after S2. Which feature shows that it is this sound and not an opening snap?

explanation: S4: a low-pitched sound in late diastole (presystolic), just after the P wave, generated when a forceful atrial contraction fills a stiff, non-compliant ventricle. Causes: LVH (hypertension, AS, HCM), acute ischaemia or infarction, acute MR (normal-sized LA contracting vigorously), and on the right, RVH or pulmonary hypertension. It needs an effective atrial contraction, so it is never heard in atrial fibrillation. It may be palpable as a presystolic apical impulse (double apex in HCM). Pitfall: S4-S1 versus split S1 versus ejection click: the S4 is lower pitched, best with the bell, and fades with firm pressure of the bell. Study aid; verify thresholds against the current full guideline.

options.text: A man with an acute inferior myocardial infarction
options.why_wrong: Acute ischaemia stiffens the LV and an S4 is very common in acute MI in sinus rhythm.

options.text: A woman with long-standing hypertensive heart disease
options.why_wrong: Concentric hypertrophy reduces LV compliance; a vigorous atrial contraction into it produces an S4.

options.text: A man with severe aortic stenosis in sinus rhythm
options.why_wrong: Severe AS with LV hypertrophy commonly has an S4 (palpable atrial kick), and in sinus rhythm it is expected.

options.text: A man with permanent AF and LV hypertrophy

stem: The phonocardiogram shown has an extra sound in late diastole, just after the P wave and before S1. In which patient would this sound be impossible?

explanation: An aortic ejection sound (click) occurs shortly after S1, at the abrupt end of opening of a mobile, doming valve (bicuspid valve, or a dilated aortic root). It is high pitched, heard at the apex and the base, and its timing is fixed, unaffected by respiration or manoeuvres. A preserved A2 and a mid-systolic peak here indicate mild to moderate stenosis; the click disappears when the valve calcifies (severe calcific AS). Pulmonary ejection click: valvar PS, softer on inspiration (the only right-sided sound that does so). Mid-systolic click of MVP: later in systole, moves earlier with standing or Valsalva (smaller LV) and later with squatting. Bicuspid valve: look for coarctation (radio-femoral delay). Study aid; verify thresholds against the current full guideline.

options.text: It moves earlier in systole on standing
options.why_wrong: Moving earlier with standing (smaller LV) is the behaviour of the mid-systolic click of mitral valve prolapse.

options.text: Its timing does not change with posture
It becomes softer on inspiration
options.why_wrong: Softening on inspiration is the behaviour of the pulmonary ejection click (valvar PS); an aortic ejection sound does not vary with respiration.

options.text: It becomes louder as the valve calcifies
options.why_wrong: The ejection sound of a mobile bicuspid valve fades and disappears as the leaflets calcify and stiffen.

stem: A 24-year-old has the phonocardiogram shown, with an early sound just after S1 followed by an ejection murmur. How does this early sound differ from the click of mitral valve prolapse?

explanation: Bedside severity markers in AS: a late-peaking murmur (the peak moves later as the gradient rises), soft or absent A2 (immobile leaflets) or a single S2, paradoxical splitting, pulsus parvus et tardus, a sustained apex and an S4; LV failure and AF are late signs. A thrill and loudness depend on flow and body habitus and are unreliable. Radiation to the carotids is typical but not a grading sign; the Gallavardin phenomenon (musical apical component) can mimic MR. Severity is confirmed by echo (Vmax, mean gradient, AVA). Study aid; verify thresholds against the current full guideline.

options.text: The harsh quality and loudness of the murmur
options.why_wrong: Loudness reflects flow as well as gradient; a severe stenosis with low flow (LV dysfunction, low-flow AS) can have a soft murmur. Loudness is not a reliable severity marker.

options.text: The absence of an ejection click
options.why_wrong: Absence of a click shows the valve is immobile (calcified), which fits severe calcific AS but is not by itself a grading sign; many mild degenerative valves also have no click.

options.text: The late peak and the soft second sound
Its crescendo-decrescendo (diamond) shape
options.why_wrong: Every ejection murmur through a semilunar valve, mild or severe, is crescendo-decrescendo; the position of the peak, not the shape, tracks severity.

stem: An 81-year-old with angina has the basal phonocardiogram shown. Which feature of this recording best indicates that the stenosis is severe?

explanation: The tracing shows a soft S1 and a high-pitched holosystolic plateau murmur through A2: chronic MR. Radiation follows the jet: a flail or prolapsing posterior leaflet directs the jet anteriorly against the atrial septum near the aortic root, so the murmur radiates to the base and neck and can be confused with AS; an anterior leaflet lesion directs the jet posteriorly, to the axilla, back and even the spine. Severity clues: an S3 or early diastolic flow rumble (large regurgitant volume), displaced hyperdynamic apex, wide split S2 (early A2). Acute severe MR may give a short, early, decrescendo murmur. Study aid; verify thresholds against the current full guideline.

options.text: To the axilla and the back, as in all mitral regurgitation
options.why_wrong: Axillary radiation is typical of posteriorly directed jets (anterior leaflet prolapse or flail, posterior leaflet restriction in ischaemic MR) and of central functional jets; a posterior leaflet flail sends the jet anteriorly and medially.

options.text: Along the left sternal border to the lower sternum only
options.why_wrong: Radiation to the lower left sternal border is typical of a VSD or TR, not of a flail posterior mitral leaflet.

options.text: It does not radiate because the jet is eccentric
options.why_wrong: Eccentric jets radiate, and in a predictable direction: opposite the prolapsing leaflet.

options.text: Towards the base and the neck, mimicking aortic stenosis

stem: A 59-year-old has the apical phonocardiogram shown. Echo reveals a flail posterior mitral leaflet. Where is this murmur most likely to radiate?

explanation: The figure shows a loud, harsh holosystolic murmur, maximal at the lower left sternal border: a restrictive VSD with a large pressure difference between LV and RV. Loudness is inversely related to defect size (a small restrictive defect is loudest). When pulmonary vascular resistance rises to systemic levels (Eisenmenger syndrome), the gradient and the left-to-right shunt fall, so the murmur shortens and softens or disappears, P2 becomes loud and single, and right-to-left shunting causes cyanosis and clubbing. A Graham Steell murmur (PR) and a pulmonary ejection click may appear. Bedside rule: softer murmur + louder P2 = pulmonary hypertension, not improvement. Study aid; verify thresholds against the current full guideline.

options.text: Shunt reversal from high pulmonary resistance
Spontaneous closure of the defect
options.why_wrong: Spontaneous closure (common in small muscular and perimembranous defects) removes the murmur but does not cause a loud P2 or cyanosis.

options.text: Aortic cusp prolapse into the defect causing AR
options.why_wrong: Cusp prolapse (outlet or perimembranous defects) adds an early diastolic murmur; it does not cause cyanosis or soften the systolic murmur.

options.text: A double-chambered right ventricle
options.why_wrong: Muscle bands obstructing the RV outflow add or increase a systolic ejection murmur; they do not explain a soft murmur with a loud P2.

stem: A 19-year-old with a known ventricular septal defect had the phonocardiogram shown in childhood. Now the murmur has become much softer, P2 is loud and he has central cyanosis. What is the best interpretation?

explanation: A continuous murmur runs through S2 into diastole without interruption, because flow continues from a high-pressure to a low-pressure bed throughout the cycle. PDA: machinery murmur peaking at or around S2, maximal in the left infraclavicular area (1st-2nd left intercostal space), with wide pulse pressure and bounding pulses in a large duct. Other continuous murmurs: ruptured sinus of Valsalva aneurysm, coronary arteriovenous fistula, aortopulmonary window, surgical shunts, arteriovenous fistulas, mammary souffle (pregnancy), venous hum (abolished by lying flat or jugular compression). With Eisenmenger physiology the diastolic part disappears and the murmur may vanish (differential cyanosis). Study aid; verify thresholds against the current full guideline.

options.text: Ventricular septal defect with aortic regurgitation
options.why_wrong: VSD with AR gives a to-and-fro murmur: holosystolic then early diastolic with a gap at S2. A continuous murmur envelops S2 without a break.

options.text: Patent ductus arteriosus
Cervical venous hum
options.why_wrong: A venous hum is louder in diastole, maximal above the right clavicle, and disappears with the patient supine or with light pressure on the jugular vein.

options.text: Mixed aortic stenosis and regurgitation
options.why_wrong: Combined AS and AR is a to-and-fro murmur (ejection then early diastolic), with a gap at S2.

stem: A 4-year-old has the murmur shown, maximal below the left clavicle, with bounding pulses. What is the most likely cause?

explanation: The tracing shows a loud S1, an opening snap shortly after A2 and a low-pitched rumble that fades in mid-diastole and rises again before S1 (presystolic accentuation): organic mitral stenosis. The Austin Flint murmur (severe AR) is a mid-diastolic or presystolic apical rumble caused by the AR jet impinging on the anterior mitral leaflet and premature mitral closure as LV diastolic pressure rises; it has NO opening snap, S1 is normal or soft, and it softens with amyl nitrite (less AR), whereas the MS rumble gets louder. Severity of MS: a short A2-opening snap interval and a long rumble, not loudness. Study aid; verify thresholds against the current full guideline.

options.text: Austin Flint murmur, because the rumble shows presystolic accentuation
options.why_wrong: The Austin Flint murmur can also have presystolic accentuation in sinus rhythm, so this does not discriminate; a loud S1 and an opening snap do.

options.text: Austin Flint murmur, because rumbles in AR are always functional
options.why_wrong: Rheumatic disease commonly affects both valves; an apical rumble in AR must be examined for features of organic MS.

options.text: Coexisting organic mitral stenosis: loud S1 and an opening snap
Increased flow across a normal mitral valve from a large VSD
options.why_wrong: A flow rumble is short, mid-diastolic and without an opening snap; nothing suggests a VSD here.

stem: A 40-year-old with chronic severe aortic regurgitation also has an apical diastolic rumble. The apical phonocardiogram shown was recorded. Which interpretation is best?

explanation: Algorithm path: timing (systolic) -> shape (late systolic, often after a click) -> click and response to posture (standing or Valsalva make the LV smaller, so the leaflets prolapse earlier: click earlier, murmur longer; squatting and handgrip move the click later and shorten the murmur) -> mitral valve prolapse. Systolic branch in brief: ejection (AS, PS, HCM, flow, ASD) vs holosystolic (MR, TR, VSD) vs late (MVP, papillary muscle dysfunction). Diastolic branch: early decrescendo (AR, PR) vs mid-diastolic rumble (MS, TS, flow, Austin Flint) vs continuous (PDA and mimics). Study aid; verify thresholds against the current full guideline.

options.text: Mitral valve prolapse
Obstructive hypertrophic cardiomyopathy
options.why_wrong: HCM gives an ejection (crescendo-decrescendo) murmur at the left lower sternal border without a click; it does get louder on standing, but it is not a late systolic murmur after a click.

options.text: Aortic stenosis, bicuspid valve
options.why_wrong: A bicuspid valve gives an early ejection sound right after S1 with fixed timing and an ejection murmur; neither moves with standing.

options.text: Chronic mitral regurgitation from annular dilatation
options.why_wrong: Functional MR from a dilated annulus is holosystolic, starting with S1, and has no click.

stem: Using the murmur identification algorithm shown: a late systolic murmur at the apex is preceded by a mid-systolic click; on standing both start earlier and the murmur lengthens. Which lesion is reached?

explanation: The murmur becomes louder during Valsalva strain: the behaviour of dynamic LVOT obstruction (obstructive HCM). In the strain phase venous return falls and the LV gets smaller, so systolic anterior motion of the mitral valve obstructs earlier and harder. Most other murmurs (AS, MR, VSD, AR, right-sided) become softer during strain. Same direction as Valsalva: standing from squatting, amyl nitrite, nitrates, post-extrasystolic beat. Opposite: squatting, passive leg raise, handgrip, phenylephrine, beta-blockade. Only HCM and MVP murmurs get louder or longer with Valsalva and standing. Study aid; verify thresholds against the current full guideline.

options.text: Squatting from standing
options.why_wrong: Squatting raises venous return and afterload, enlarging the LV and widening the outflow tract: the HCM murmur becomes softer.

options.text: Passive leg raising
options.why_wrong: Leg raising increases preload and LV size, which softens a dynamic outflow murmur.

options.text: Sustained isometric handgrip
options.why_wrong: Handgrip raises afterload and LV volume, reducing the outflow gradient; it softens the HCM murmur (and makes MR, VSD and AR louder).

options.text: Standing up from a squat

stem: The phonocardiogram shown compares the systolic murmur of a 30-year-old at rest and during Valsalva strain. Which other manoeuvre changes this murmur in the same direction?

explanation: Afterload manoeuvres separate regurgitant or shunt murmurs from outflow murmurs. Raising afterload (handgrip, transient arterial occlusion, phenylephrine) increases backward flow: MR, VSD and AR get louder; AS and HCM get softer. Lowering afterload (amyl nitrite) does the opposite: MR, VSD, AR softer; AS, HCM louder (and the MS rumble louder through tachycardia and higher flow). The Austin Flint rumble softens with amyl nitrite, the organic MS rumble gets louder. Study aid; verify thresholds against the current full guideline.

options.text: Obstructive hypertrophic cardiomyopathy
options.why_wrong: The HCM murmur behaves in the opposite way: softer with handgrip (more afterload, bigger LV) and louder with amyl nitrite (less afterload).

options.text: Ventricular septal defect
Valvar aortic stenosis
options.why_wrong: A fixed outflow obstruction murmur softens with handgrip (less gradient as afterload rises) and is louder after amyl nitrite (more flow).

options.text: Tricuspid regurgitation
options.why_wrong: TR is identified by an increase on inspiration (Carvallo) and a cv wave; as a right-sided murmur it tends to get louder, not softer, after amyl nitrite as venous return rises.

stem: A young man has a harsh systolic murmur at the left lower sternal border. It becomes louder with sustained handgrip and softer after inhaled amyl nitrite. Which lesion is most likely?

explanation: Inspiration increases venous return to the right heart, so right-sided murmurs and sounds (TR, PR, TS, RV S3/S4) get louder (Carvallo sign for TR). The exception is the pulmonary ejection click: in valvar PS, the inspiratory rise in RA contraction partly opens (domes) the pulmonary valve before RV systole, so the abrupt systolic opening movement and the click are smaller. The aortic ejection click does not vary with respiration. Pitfall: with severe RV failure the RV cannot raise its output and Carvallo sign may be absent. Study aid; verify thresholds against the current full guideline.

options.text: The holosystolic murmur of tricuspid regurgitation
options.why_wrong: TR increases on inspiration (Carvallo sign) as more blood returns to the RV.

options.text: The early diastolic murmur of pulmonary regurgitation
options.why_wrong: The Graham Steell murmur of PR is right sided and increases with inspiration.

options.text: The ejection click of valvar pulmonary stenosis
A right ventricular S3
options.why_wrong: A right-sided S3 or S4 increases on inspiration, which helps to localise it to the RV.

stem: Most right-sided auscultatory events become louder on inspiration. Which event characteristically becomes softer on inspiration?

explanation: Gallavardin phenomenon: in calcific AS the high-frequency components of the ejection murmur radiate to the apex and sound musical, mimicking MR, while the harsh, noisy part stays at the base. Cycle-length test: after a long RR interval (AF) or after a premature beat, LV filling and contractility increase, so the ejection murmur of AS (and HCM) becomes louder; the MR murmur changes little, because the extra volume is ejected forward while regurgitant flow stays similar. Other clues for an aortic origin: ejection shape ending before A2, slow-rising pulse; MR is holosystolic through A2. Study aid; verify thresholds against the current full guideline.

options.text: Its intensity rises after long RR intervals
It radiates towards the left axilla
options.why_wrong: Axillary radiation is typical of MR, so this would favour a mitral origin, not an aortic one.

options.text: It is high pitched and musical
options.why_wrong: Both the apical component of AS and some MR (for example a flail chord) can be musical; quality does not separate them.

options.text: It is louder with the patient sitting forward
options.why_wrong: Sitting forward in expiration brings out aortic regurgitation and pericardial rubs; it is not used to separate AS from MR.

stem: An 82-year-old in atrial fibrillation has a harsh ejection murmur at the base and a musical, high-pitched systolic murmur at the apex. Which observation best shows that the apical murmur arises from the aortic valve rather than the mitral valve?

explanation: Proportional pulse pressure = (systolic - diastolic) / systolic = (96 - 80) / 96 = about 17%. In chronic HF a value below 25% predicted a cardiac index below 2.2 L/min/m2 (Stevenson and Perloff, 1989). Bedside haemodynamic profiles: congestion (orthopnoea, raised JVP, abdominojugular reflux, S3, oedema, ascites) = wet; hypoperfusion (narrow proportional pulse pressure, cool extremities, drowsiness, hypotension with ACE inhibitor, low sodium, worsening renal function) = cold. This patient is at least cold; warm-dry, warm-wet, cold-wet and cold-dry profiles guide diuretic, vasodilator and inotropic therapy. Study aid; verify thresholds against the current full guideline.

options.text: Normal cardiac output, because the systolic pressure is above 90 mmHg
options.why_wrong: Systolic pressure can be maintained by vasoconstriction while output is low; the pulse pressure relative to systolic is the better bedside index.

options.text: A low cardiac index (about 17%, under the 25% threshold)
High filling pressures, because the pulse pressure is narrow
options.why_wrong: A narrow proportional pulse pressure tracks stroke volume and cardiac index, not filling pressure; congestion is judged by JVP, orthopnoea, S3 and oedema.

options.text: Significant aortic regurgitation, because the diastolic pressure is high
options.why_wrong: AR widens the pulse pressure and lowers the diastolic pressure; this patient has the opposite pattern.

stem: A man with chronic heart failure has cool, clammy extremities and a blood pressure of 96/80 mmHg. What does his proportional pulse pressure suggest?

explanation: Acute severe AR (endocarditis, dissection, trauma): the non-dilated LV receives a large regurgitant volume, LV diastolic pressure rises steeply and may exceed LA pressure in late diastole, closing the mitral valve early (soft or absent S1; seen as premature mitral closure on echo). The diastolic murmur is short and soft because the aortic-LV gradient disappears early; the pulse pressure is not wide and peripheral signs are absent; tachycardia and pulmonary oedema dominate. This is a surgical emergency (urgent valve surgery). Chronic severe AR is the opposite: long murmur, wide pulse pressure, collapsing pulse, displaced apex. Study aid; verify thresholds against the current full guideline.

options.text: Mild aortic regurgitation, because the murmur is short and soft
options.why_wrong: In acute severe AR the LV diastolic pressure rises rapidly and equalises with aortic pressure, so the murmur is short and soft despite a large regurgitation.

options.text: Improvement of the aortic lesion with antibiotic treatment
options.why_wrong: Pulmonary oedema with a soft S1 indicates haemodynamic deterioration, not improvement.

options.text: Chronic severe aortic regurgitation with LV decompensation
options.why_wrong: Chronic severe AR has a dilated, compliant LV, a long murmur and a wide pulse pressure with peripheral signs; the course here is acute.

options.text: Acute severe aortic regurgitation with early mitral closure

stem: A 38-year-old with Staphylococcus aureus endocarditis develops pulmonary oedema within 48 hours. The early diastolic murmur is short and soft, S1 is soft and the pulse pressure is normal. What is the best interpretation?

explanation: Collapsing (water-hammer, Corrigan) pulse: a very rapid upstroke to a high peak, then rapid collapse with no dicrotic notch and a wide pulse pressure (170/45 mmHg here). Mechanism: a large stroke volume ejected into the aorta, then rapid diastolic run-off back into the LV (AR) or into a low-resistance bed (PDA, AV fistula, ruptured sinus of Valsalva). Hyperdynamic states (anaemia, thyrotoxicosis, pregnancy, fever, beriberi, Paget disease) widen the pulse pressure too. Test: feel the radial artery with the palm while raising the patient's arm. In acute severe AR the pulse pressure is NOT wide. Study aid; verify thresholds against the current full guideline.

options.text: Calcific aortic stenosis or a fixed subaortic membrane
options.why_wrong: Fixed outflow obstruction gives a slow-rising, low-volume pulse with a narrow pulse pressure, the opposite of this tracing.

options.text: Cardiac tamponade or severe acute asthma
options.why_wrong: These cause pulsus paradoxus, a respiratory fall in systolic pressure; each beat keeps a normal contour.

options.text: AR, PDA, AV fistula or a hyperdynamic circulation
Obstructive HCM with a dynamic outflow gradient
options.why_wrong: HCM gives a brisk upstroke with a spike and dome; the pulse pressure is not wide and there is no early diastolic collapse.

stem: A 30-year-old has the arterial tracing shown at the radial artery, with a pulse that rises and falls abruptly when the arm is raised. Which group of conditions can produce it?

explanation: The figure shows a high-pitched early diastolic decrescendo murmur starting at A2: aortic regurgitation. Hill sign: popliteal (cuff) systolic pressure exceeding brachial by more than 20 mmHg; commonly quoted, poorly validated grading: 20-40 mild, 40-60 moderate, above 60 mmHg severe AR. Here 200 - 130 = 70 mmHg. Mechanism: exaggerated amplification of the large, rapid stroke-volume wave in the lower limb arteries. Caveat: intra-arterial studies suggest the cuff difference partly reflects measurement artefact, so echo is the arbiter. Other peripheral signs of severe chronic AR: Corrigan (carotid), de Musset (head bobbing), Quincke (nail-bed capillary pulsation), Traube (pistol-shot femorals), Duroziez (femoral to-and-fro bruit on compression), Muller (uvula). Study aid; verify thresholds against the current full guideline.

options.text: Positive Hill sign, suggesting severe aortic regurgitation
Normal leg-arm gradient from pulse wave amplification
options.why_wrong: Leg systolic pressure is normally only slightly higher than arm systolic pressure (about 10-20 mmHg); a 70 mmHg difference is abnormal.

options.text: Coarctation of the aorta, because the pressures differ
options.why_wrong: Coarctation produces the reverse: arm pressure higher than leg pressure, with weak, delayed femoral pulses.

options.text: Mild aortic regurgitation, as Hill sign is graded above 100 mmHg
options.why_wrong: Hill sign is a popliteal-brachial systolic difference of more than 20 mmHg; more than 60 mmHg is the figure usually quoted for severe AR (poorly validated). No grading uses 100 mmHg.

stem: A 33-year-old has the diastolic murmur shown. Systolic pressure is 200 mmHg in the popliteal artery and 130 mmHg in the brachial artery. How should this difference be read?

explanation: Auscultation areas: A = aortic (2nd right intercostal space, right sternal border), P = pulmonary (2nd left), E = Erb's point (3rd left), T = tricuspid (lower left sternal border), M = mitral (apex). The AR murmur is usually loudest along the left sternal border at Erb's point when the leaflets are diseased; when it is louder along the RIGHT sternal border, the aortic root is dilated and displaced to the right (Marfan syndrome, annuloaortic ectasia, dissection, syphilitic aortitis). Listen with the diaphragm, patient sitting forward, breath held in expiration. Marfan features (tall stature, arachnodactyly) prompt imaging of the whole aorta. Study aid; verify thresholds against the current full guideline.

options.text: Pulmonary regurgitation from pulmonary hypertension
options.why_wrong: The Graham Steell murmur of PR is loudest at the upper left sternal border (P and E areas) and increases with inspiration; area A is right sided.

options.text: Aortic root dilatation, not leaflet disease
Primary aortic valve disease such as a bicuspid valve
options.why_wrong: Valvular AR is usually loudest along the left sternal border (Erb's point); right sternal border predominance points to the aortic root.

options.text: Mitral stenosis with a Graham Steell murmur
options.why_wrong: MS gives an apical rumble (area M); a Graham Steell murmur comes from the pulmonary valve and is loudest at the left upper sternal border (areas P/E).

stem: On the auscultation map shown, a 28-year-old tall man with long fingers has an early diastolic decrescendo murmur louder at area A than at area E. What does this distribution suggest?

explanation: Isovolumetric contraction begins when the mitral valve closes (producing S1) and ends when the aortic valve opens. With both valves shut, pressure climbs steeply while volume stays constant (Guyton & Hall).

options.text: Both the mitral and aortic valves are closed and ventricular volume is constant
The aortic valve is open while ventricular volume falls
options.why_wrong: An open aortic valve means ejection has already begun — a later phase, not isovolumetric contraction.

options.text: The mitral valve is open while ventricular pressure falls
options.why_wrong: An open mitral valve with falling pressure describes diastolic filling, not isovolumetric contraction.

options.text: Ventricular volume rises steeply while pressure is unchanged
options.why_wrong: Volume cannot rise when both valves are shut; 'isovolumetric' means the volume is fixed.

stem: During isovolumetric contraction of the left ventricle, which statement is correct?

explanation: S1 marks closure of the atrioventricular (mitral then tricuspid) valves as the ventricles begin to contract — the start of isovolumetric contraction (Braunwald's Heart Disease).

options.text: Closure of the mitral and tricuspid valves at the onset of ventricular systole
Closure of the aortic and pulmonary valves
options.why_wrong: Semilunar-valve closure produces S2, not S1.

options.text: Opening of the aortic valve at the start of ejection
options.why_wrong: Valve opening is normally silent; S1 is produced by AV-valve closure.

options.text: Rapid passive filling of the ventricle in early diastole
options.why_wrong: A sound from early rapid filling is S3, not S1.

stem: The first heart sound (S1) is produced by which event?

explanation: The dicrotic notch is the small upward deflection produced when the aortic valve snaps shut and blood briefly rebounds against it; it coincides with S2 and the beginning of isovolumetric relaxation.

options.text: Closure of the aortic valve, marking the start of isovolumetric relaxation
Opening of the aortic valve at the onset of ejection
options.why_wrong: Aortic valve opening starts ejection; the notch is a brief pressure rebound after valve closure.

options.text: Mitral valve opening at the start of ventricular filling
options.why_wrong: Mitral opening is a left-atrial/ventricular event and does not create the aortic incisura.

options.text: Peak left ventricular systolic pressure
options.why_wrong: Peak systolic pressure occurs during ejection, before the valve closes.

stem: The dicrotic notch (incisura) on the aortic pressure tracing corresponds to:

explanation: S4 is a late-diastolic sound from atrial contraction ('atrial kick') against a stiff ventricle (e.g. LVH, ischaemia, HFpEF). Because it needs atrial contraction, S4 disappears in atrial fibrillation.

options.text: Atrial contraction forcing blood into a stiff, non-compliant ventricle
Rapid early diastolic filling of a dilated, volume-overloaded ventricle
options.why_wrong: That mechanism produces S3, not S4.

options.text: Turbulent flow across a stenotic aortic valve
options.why_wrong: Turbulence across a valve produces a murmur, not an S4 gallop.

options.text: Closure of the pulmonary valve during inspiration
options.why_wrong: Delayed pulmonary closure causes physiological splitting of S2, not an S4.

stem: A fourth heart sound (S4) is best explained by:

explanation: The 'a' wave requires organised atrial contraction. In atrial fibrillation there is no coordinated atrial systole, so the 'a' wave is lost. (Complete heart block gives cannon a waves; AF gives none.)

options.text: Atrial fibrillation
Complete (third-degree) heart block
options.why_wrong: In complete heart block the atria still contract, intermittently against a closed tricuspid valve, producing intermittent giant 'cannon' a waves rather than absent a waves.

options.text: First-degree AV block
options.why_wrong: First-degree block merely delays conduction; atrial contraction and the a wave persist.

options.text: Sinus tachycardia
options.why_wrong: Sinus tachycardia preserves organised atrial contraction, so the a wave is present.

stem: The 'a' wave of the jugular venous pulse is caused by right atrial contraction. In which rhythm is the 'a' wave absent?

explanation: Stroke volume = EDV - ESV, which is the horizontal width of the PV loop. The enclosed area is stroke work and the ESPVR slope (Ees) indexes contractility (Braunwald's Heart Disease).

options.text: The width of the loop (end-diastolic volume minus end-systolic volume)
The height of the loop (peak systolic minus diastolic pressure)
options.why_wrong: The vertical dimension reflects pressures generated, not the volume ejected.

options.text: The area enclosed by the loop
options.why_wrong: The enclosed area represents stroke work, not stroke volume.

options.text: The slope of the end-systolic pressure-volume relationship
options.why_wrong: That slope (Ees) indexes contractility, not stroke volume.

stem: On the left ventricular pressure-volume loop, the stroke volume is represented by:

explanation: Ees, the slope of the end-systolic pressure-volume relationship, is the classic relatively load-independent measure of contractility. Ejection fraction, SV and CO all vary with loading conditions.

options.text: The slope of the end-systolic pressure-volume relationship (Ees)
Ejection fraction
options.why_wrong: Ejection fraction is sensitive to preload and especially afterload, so it is load-dependent.

options.text: Stroke volume
options.why_wrong: Stroke volume changes with preload and afterload independent of contractility.

options.text: Cardiac output
options.why_wrong: Cardiac output depends on heart rate and loading conditions, not contractility alone.

stem: Which parameter is the most load-independent index of myocardial contractility?

explanation: Afterload is the load the ventricle must overcome to eject. Raising it (at fixed preload and contractility) shifts the aortic-valve-closure point up and to the right: the ventricle cannot eject as far, so ESV rises and SV falls (the beat-to-beat effect, before compensatory Frank-Starling on the next beat).

options.text: Increase end-systolic volume and decrease stroke volume
Decrease end-systolic volume and increase stroke volume
options.why_wrong: Higher afterload opposes ejection, so the ventricle ejects less and retains more blood.

options.text: Leave stroke volume unchanged because contractility is fixed
options.why_wrong: Even at fixed contractility, raising afterload reduces ejection (the loop ends at a higher ESV).

options.text: Increase stroke volume via the Frank-Starling mechanism
options.why_wrong: Frank-Starling responds to preload (fibre length), not to an isolated afterload rise.

stem: At constant preload and contractility, an acute rise in afterload will:

explanation: Wall stress sigma = (P x r) / (2h). A dilated ventricle (large r) has high wall stress and oxygen demand; concentric hypertrophy (increased h) normalises wall stress. This underlies the afterload burden in hypertension and aortic stenosis.

options.text: Ventricular pressure and chamber radius, and inversely proportional to wall thickness
Wall thickness, and inversely proportional to chamber radius
options.why_wrong: The relationship is reversed: thicker walls LOWER wall stress, and larger radius RAISES it.

options.text: Heart rate and contractility only
options.why_wrong: Laplace relates stress to pressure, radius and thickness, not directly to heart rate.

options.text: Blood viscosity and vessel length (Poiseuille's law)
options.why_wrong: Those are determinants of resistance to flow, not of ventricular wall stress.

stem: According to the law of Laplace, left ventricular wall stress is directly proportional to:

explanation: Preload is the degree of myocyte stretch at end-diastole, best represented by end-diastolic volume (clinically approximated by LVEDP or PCWP). It sets the operating point on the Frank-Starling curve.

options.text: Left ventricular end-diastolic volume
Mean arterial pressure
options.why_wrong: MAP reflects the downstream pressure load (an afterload correlate), not preload.

options.text: Systemic vascular resistance
options.why_wrong: SVR is a determinant of afterload, not a measure of preload.

options.text: Ejection fraction
options.why_wrong: Ejection fraction reflects ventricular emptying, not the end-diastolic filling volume.

stem: Which best estimates left ventricular preload?

explanation: MAP ~ DBP + 1/3(SBP - DBP) because the heart spends roughly two-thirds of each resting cycle in diastole. At fast heart rates diastole shortens and MAP moves closer to the arithmetic mean.

options.text: Diastolic pressure plus one-third of the pulse pressure
The simple average of systolic and diastolic pressure
options.why_wrong: Diastole occupies about two-thirds of the cardiac cycle at rest, so a plain average overestimates MAP.

options.text: Systolic pressure minus one-third of the pulse pressure
options.why_wrong: This formula is upside down; MAP lies closer to the diastolic value, not the systolic value.

options.text: Pulse pressure multiplied by heart rate
options.why_wrong: That product has no physiological meaning as MAP.

stem: Mean arterial pressure (MAP) is most accurately approximated at a normal resting heart rate by:

explanation: CO = HR x SV. Stroke volume itself is governed by preload, afterload and contractility (Guyton & Hall).

options.text: Heart rate and stroke volume
Stroke volume and systemic vascular resistance
options.why_wrong: SV x SVR is not cardiac output; MAP ~ CO x SVR relates pressure to flow and resistance.

options.text: Heart rate and ejection fraction
options.why_wrong: Ejection fraction is a ratio (SV/EDV); CO needs an absolute volume per beat (SV).

options.text: Mean arterial pressure and heart rate
options.why_wrong: Pressure times rate is the rate-pressure product (an oxygen-demand index), not cardiac output.

stem: Cardiac output is the product of:

explanation: Frank-Starling: within physiological limits, greater preload stretches sarcomeres toward their optimal overlap (~2.2 micrometres) and raises myofilament calcium sensitivity, so a greater end-diastolic volume produces a stronger contraction and larger stroke volume.

options.text: Increasing end-diastolic fibre length increases the force of the next contraction and stroke volume
Increasing heart rate increases contractility (the staircase phenomenon)
options.why_wrong: Rate-dependent potentiation (Bowditch/Treppe) is a separate mechanism from Frank-Starling.

options.text: Sympathetic stimulation raises contractility independently of fibre length
options.why_wrong: That is beta-adrenergic (homeometric) regulation, not the length-dependent Frank-Starling effect.

options.text: Rising afterload reduces stroke volume on the same beat
options.why_wrong: That is the afterload effect, not the preload-driven Frank-Starling relationship.

stem: The Frank-Starling mechanism describes how:

explanation: CO = VO2 / (CaO2 - CvO2). The A-V difference is 5 mL/dL = 50 mL/L. CO = 250 / 50 = 5 L/min (a normal resting value).

options.text: 5 L/min
0.5 L/min
options.why_wrong: This is off by a factor of ten — the arteriovenous difference must be converted from mL/dL to mL/L (5 mL/dL = 50 mL/L).

options.text: 50 L/min
options.why_wrong: This ignores the unit conversion and inverts the scale; such an output is physiologically impossible.

options.text: 2.5 L/min
options.why_wrong: Halving the true value suggests using 10 mL/dL rather than the correct 5 mL/dL A-V difference.

stem: Using the Fick principle, a patient has an oxygen consumption of 250 mL/min, arterial O2 content 20 mL/dL and mixed venous O2 content 15 mL/dL. The cardiac output is approximately:

explanation: Reduced contractility in HFrEF shifts the Frank-Starling curve down and to the right: the ventricle needs a much higher filling pressure to generate a modest stroke volume, which is why congestion develops.

options.text: Shifted downward and flattened, so a given preload generates a smaller stroke volume
Shifted upward and leftward, generating more stroke volume at any preload
options.why_wrong: An upward-left shift indicates increased contractility (e.g. catecholamines), the opposite of failure.

options.text: Unchanged, with heart failure due solely to valve disease
options.why_wrong: Reduced contractility in systolic HF depresses the curve regardless of valve status.

options.text: Steeper, so small preload changes cause large stroke-volume swings
options.why_wrong: The failing ventricle is less preload-responsive, giving a flatter not steeper curve.

stem: In systolic heart failure, the Frank-Starling curve is characteristically:

explanation: EF = SV/EDV = (EDV - ESV)/EDV, normally about 55-70%. It is a load-dependent measure of ventricular emptying, widely used to classify heart failure (HFrEF vs HFpEF) per ESC guidance.

options.text: Stroke volume divided by end-diastolic volume
Stroke volume divided by end-systolic volume
options.why_wrong: The denominator is end-diastolic (total filling) volume, not end-systolic volume.

options.text: End-diastolic volume minus end-systolic volume
options.why_wrong: That difference is the stroke volume itself, not the ejection fraction (a ratio).

options.text: Cardiac output divided by heart rate
options.why_wrong: CO/HR gives stroke volume, not ejection fraction.

stem: Left ventricular ejection fraction is defined as:

explanation: Phase 0 of fast-response cells (atrial, ventricular, His-Purkinje) is the steep depolarisation from the rapid inward Na+ current. Class I antiarrhythmics block this channel.

options.text: A fast inward sodium current through voltage-gated Na+ channels
An inward L-type calcium current
options.why_wrong: The L-type Ca2+ current drives the slow upstroke of nodal cells and the plateau of fast cells, not the rapid phase-0 upstroke here.

options.text: An outward potassium current
options.why_wrong: Outward K+ currents repolarise the cell (phases 1 and 3); they do not depolarise it.

options.text: The funny (If) pacemaker current
options.why_wrong: If drives spontaneous phase-4 depolarisation in pacemaker cells, not phase 0 of working myocardium.

stem: In a ventricular (fast-response) action potential, the rapid upstroke of phase 0 is produced by:

explanation: During phase 2, inward Ca2+ (L-type) current nearly balances outward K+ current, holding the membrane near 0 mV. This plateau triggers calcium-induced calcium release and gives the long refractory period.

options.text: Inward L-type calcium current balanced by outward potassium current
A sustained inward sodium current with no potassium efflux
options.why_wrong: Phase-0 Na+ channels inactivate quickly; the plateau is a Ca2+/K+ balance, not sustained Na+.

options.text: Pure outward potassium current driving repolarisation
options.why_wrong: Unopposed K+ efflux produces phase 3 (repolarisation), not the plateau.

options.text: Electrogenic activity of the Na+/K+-ATPase only
options.why_wrong: The pump contributes to the resting potential but does not create the plateau.

stem: The plateau (phase 2) of the ventricular action potential is maintained mainly by:

explanation: The SA node has an unstable diastolic potential because of the funny current (If) plus T-type Ca2+ influx and declining K+ efflux. If is the target of ivabradine, which slows heart rate without affecting contractility.

options.text: The funny current (If), an inward Na+ current activated on hyperpolarisation
A large inward fast Na+ current as in ventricular cells
options.why_wrong: SA nodal cells have few functional fast Na+ channels; their pacemaker drift is the If current.

options.text: Inward rectifier K+ (IK1) maintaining a stable resting potential
options.why_wrong: Strong IK1 would prevent spontaneous drift; nodal cells have little IK1, allowing pacemaking.

options.text: Chloride influx through CFTR channels
options.why_wrong: Chloride currents are not the principal pacemaker mechanism of the SA node.

stem: Spontaneous phase-4 depolarisation of the sinoatrial node is driven predominantly by:

explanation: AV-nodal conduction is slow (upstroke driven by L-type Ca2+ current), producing the PR-interval delay that lets the atria finish filling the ventricles before ventricular systole. The His-Purkinje system is the fastest-conducting tissue.

options.text: The atrioventricular (AV) node
The His-Purkinje system
options.why_wrong: The His-Purkinje network has the FASTEST conduction, rapidly activating the ventricles.

options.text: Atrial myocardium
options.why_wrong: Atrial muscle conducts faster than the AV node; it is not the rate-limiting delay.

options.text: The sinoatrial node
options.why_wrong: The SA node is the pacemaker; the deliberate conduction delay occurs at the AV node.

stem: Which component of the conduction system has the SLOWEST conduction velocity, creating the physiological delay between atrial and ventricular contraction?

explanation: The pacemaker hierarchy descends in rate: SA node 60-100, AV junction 40-60, ventricular/His-Purkinje 20-40 per minute. The fastest pacemaker (SA) sets the rhythm and overdrive-suppresses the slower ones.

options.text: SA node 60-100/min, AV junction 40-60/min, His-Purkinje 20-40/min
SA node 20-40/min, AV junction 40-60/min, His-Purkinje 60-100/min
options.why_wrong: The hierarchy is reversed: the most proximal tissue (SA node) has the fastest intrinsic rate.

options.text: SA node 100-140/min, AV junction 80-100/min, His-Purkinje 60-80/min
options.why_wrong: These rates are all too high; they describe tachycardias, not intrinsic escape rates.

options.text: All three fire at about 60-100/min
options.why_wrong: Each subsidiary pacemaker is progressively slower than the one above it, which is why the SA node normally dominates.

stem: The intrinsic (escape) pacemaker rates of the conduction system are approximately:

explanation: The long plateau keeps fast Na+ channels inactivated, so the cell cannot generate another upstroke until it repolarises and the channels recover. This effective refractory period prevents tetany and limits re-entry.

options.text: Its fast sodium channels are inactivated, producing the effective refractory period
Its resting membrane potential is maximally negative
options.why_wrong: During the plateau the membrane is near 0 mV, not maximally negative; refractoriness is due to Na+ channel inactivation.

options.text: Acetylcholine has opened potassium channels
options.why_wrong: Refractoriness is intrinsic to channel kinetics, not dependent on vagal input.

options.text: The Na+/K+-ATPase is temporarily switched off
options.why_wrong: The pump is not the basis of the refractory period; inactivated Na+ channels are.

stem: Why can a ventricular myocyte not be re-excited during the plateau of its action potential?

explanation: Contraction of the LV squeezes the vessels running through its wall (especially the subendocardium), so most LV coronary flow happens in diastole. Tachycardia shortens diastole and is a key cause of subendocardial ischaemia (the right ventricle, under lower pressure, is perfused in both phases).

options.text: Diastole, when the compressive force on intramural vessels is lowest
Systole, when aortic pressure is highest
options.why_wrong: Although aortic pressure peaks in systole, LV contraction compresses the intramural coronary vessels, so LV perfusion is throttled during systole.

options.text: Equally throughout the cardiac cycle
options.why_wrong: LV coronary flow is strongly phasic because of systolic compression; it is not uniform.

options.text: The isovolumetric contraction phase only
options.why_wrong: That brief phase is when compression begins to impede flow, not when most perfusion occurs.

stem: Blood flow to the left ventricular myocardium occurs predominantly during:

explanation: The subendocardium faces the highest wall stress and the greatest systolic compression, and it is perfused last, so it is the most vulnerable layer. Subendocardial ischaemia produces ST depression; transmural ischaemia produces ST elevation.

options.text: The subendocardium
The subepicardium
options.why_wrong: The subepicardium has the most favourable perfusion; the subendocardium is the first to suffer.

options.text: The mid-myocardium uniformly
options.why_wrong: Ischaemic vulnerability is greatest at the subendocardium, not uniform across the wall.

options.text: The epicardial fat pad
options.why_wrong: Epicardial fat is not myocardium and is not the relevant ischaemic territory.

stem: Which region of the ventricular wall is most vulnerable to ischaemia?

explanation: Coronary perfusion pressure = aortic diastolic pressure - LVEDP. A high LVEDP (failing or stiff ventricle) or a low aortic diastolic pressure (e.g. aortic regurgitation, hypotension) narrows this gradient and worsens subendocardial ischaemia.

options.text: Aortic diastolic pressure minus left ventricular end-diastolic pressure
Aortic systolic pressure minus right atrial pressure
options.why_wrong: LV subendocardial perfusion occurs in diastole, so diastolic (not systolic) aortic pressure is the driving head, and LVEDP (not RAP) is the back-pressure.

options.text: Mean arterial pressure minus central venous pressure
options.why_wrong: This generic formula ignores the phasic, diastole-dependent nature of LV coronary perfusion.

options.text: Pulmonary capillary wedge pressure minus LVEDP
options.why_wrong: Neither term represents the aortic driving pressure for coronary flow.

stem: Effective subendocardial coronary perfusion pressure for the left ventricle is best represented by:

explanation: Myocardial oxygen demand rises with heart rate, contractility and wall stress (afterload/preload). The rate-pressure product (HR x systolic BP) is a convenient clinical surrogate. Supply depends on coronary flow and arterial oxygen content.

options.text: Heart rate, contractility and ventricular wall stress
Coronary artery diameter, haemoglobin and arterial O2 saturation
options.why_wrong: Those govern oxygen SUPPLY, not demand.

options.text: Preload, blood viscosity and plasma oncotic pressure
options.why_wrong: These are not the recognised determinants of myocardial oxygen consumption.

options.text: Respiratory rate, tidal volume and PaO2
options.why_wrong: Ventilatory parameters set systemic oxygenation, not myocardial oxygen demand.

stem: Which combination lists the principal determinants of myocardial oxygen DEMAND?

explanation: The heart extracts most of the oxygen it is offered even at rest, so increased demand is met almost entirely by increasing flow. Local metabolites (adenosine, CO2, H+, low PO2) relax coronary resistance vessels; this metabolic autoregulation is the basis of coronary flow reserve.

options.text: Local metabolic vasodilation (e.g. adenosine, lowered PO2) of the coronary microvasculature
A large increase in myocardial oxygen extraction
options.why_wrong: Myocardial oxygen extraction is already near-maximal at rest, so extra demand must be met by more flow, not more extraction.

options.text: Sympathetic alpha-1 mediated coronary vasoconstriction
options.why_wrong: Vasoconstriction would reduce, not increase, coronary flow; metabolic vasodilation dominates.

options.text: A fall in aortic diastolic pressure increasing the perfusion gradient
options.why_wrong: A lower diastolic pressure would reduce the perfusion gradient, not augment flow.

stem: During exercise, the several-fold increase in coronary blood flow needed to match demand is achieved mainly by:

explanation: The resting rate (~70) is slower than the SA node's intrinsic rate (~100-110) because of constant vagal tone. Atropine blocks M2 receptors and removes this brake, so the rate climbs toward the intrinsic rate.

options.text: Blocks M2 muscarinic receptors, removing resting vagal (parasympathetic) tone
Directly stimulates beta-1 receptors on the SA node
options.why_wrong: Atropine is a muscarinic antagonist, not a beta-agonist; it unmasks the intrinsic rate rather than stimulating the node.

options.text: Increases circulating noradrenaline release
options.why_wrong: Atropine does not augment sympathetic transmitter release; it blocks the vagal brake.

options.text: Blocks the funny current to speed phase-4 depolarisation
options.why_wrong: Blocking If (as ivabradine does) would SLOW the heart, the opposite of atropine's effect.

stem: A healthy adult with a resting heart rate of 72/min is given intravenous atropine and the rate rises to about 105/min. This occurs because atropine:

explanation: Lusitropy is the rate of myocardial relaxation. Beta-1 -> Gs -> cAMP -> PKA phosphorylates phospholamban, relieving its inhibition of SERCA2a, so calcium is pumped back into the sarcoplasmic reticulum faster and the ventricle relaxes sooner — important for filling when heart rate is high.

options.text: PKA phosphorylation of phospholamban, speeding SERCA-mediated calcium reuptake into the SR
Slower calcium reuptake prolonging the plateau
options.why_wrong: Slower reuptake would impair relaxation (negative lusitropy), the opposite of the beta-1 effect.

options.text: Opening of M2-gated potassium channels in the ventricle
options.why_wrong: That is a vagal (parasympathetic) action and has little effect on ventricular relaxation.

options.text: Increased myofilament calcium sensitivity from fibre stretch
options.why_wrong: That describes length-dependent activation (Frank-Starling), not catecholamine-driven lusitropy.

stem: Positive lusitropy produced by sympathetic (beta-1) stimulation of the heart results from:

explanation: Right vagus -> SA node (rate); left vagus -> AV node (conduction). Parasympathetic fibres richly supply the nodes and atria but only sparsely the ventricles, so the vagus has a large effect on rate/conduction and little direct effect on ventricular force.

options.text: The right vagus mainly supplies the SA node (rate) and the left vagus mainly the AV node (conduction)
The vagus densely innervates the ventricular myocardium and strongly reduces contractility
options.why_wrong: Vagal supply to the ventricles is sparse; the major vagal effects are on rate and AV conduction.

options.text: The left vagus chiefly controls heart rate at the SA node
options.why_wrong: It is the RIGHT vagus that predominantly controls SA-nodal rate.

options.text: Vagal fibres release noradrenaline onto beta-1 receptors
options.why_wrong: Vagal (parasympathetic) fibres release acetylcholine onto M2 receptors, not noradrenaline.

stem: Regarding vagal innervation of the heart, which statement is correct?

explanation: Digoxin's rate-slowing effect in AF is largely indirect and vagotonic: enhanced parasympathetic tone prolongs AV-nodal refractoriness. (Its positive inotropy is a separate action via Na+/K+-ATPase inhibition.) Because the effect is vagal, it is overridden by the high sympathetic drive of exertion.

options.text: Increasing vagal (parasympathetic) tone, which slows AV-nodal conduction
Blocking beta-1 adrenergic receptors at the AV node
options.why_wrong: Digoxin is not a beta-blocker; its rate-control action is a vagotonic (cholinergic) effect.

options.text: Directly blocking L-type calcium channels like verapamil
options.why_wrong: Calcium-channel blockade is the mechanism of non-dihydropyridines, not digoxin.

options.text: Inhibiting the funny current in the SA node
options.why_wrong: If inhibition is ivabradine's mechanism and does not explain AV-nodal rate control in AF.

stem: Digoxin slows the ventricular rate in atrial fibrillation primarily by:

explanation: Beta-1 -> Gs -> adenylyl cyclase -> cAMP -> PKA, which phosphorylates L-type Ca2+ channels, phospholamban and If channels to raise rate, contractility, conduction and relaxation. Beta-blockers interrupt this pathway.

options.text: Gs protein -> adenylyl cyclase -> increased cAMP -> protein kinase A
Gi protein -> decreased cAMP
options.why_wrong: Gi lowers cAMP and is the pathway of M2 and alpha-2 receptors, which slow or inhibit, not beta-1.

options.text: Gq protein -> phospholipase C -> IP3/DAG
options.why_wrong: The Gq/IP3 pathway is used by alpha-1 receptors (vasoconstriction), not cardiac beta-1 receptors.

options.text: Direct ligand-gated opening of a sodium channel
options.why_wrong: Adrenergic receptors are G-protein-coupled, not ligand-gated ion channels.

stem: Stimulation of cardiac beta-1 adrenergic receptors increases heart rate and contractility through which signalling pathway?

explanation: M2 -> Gi lowers cAMP (slowing the funny current and L-type Ca2+ current) and the Gi beta-gamma subunit opens GIRK/I_KACh potassium channels. The resulting K+ efflux hyperpolarises the node and flattens phase 4, producing negative chronotropy and dromotropy.

options.text: Couple to Gi, lowering cAMP and opening acetylcholine-gated K+ channels (hyperpolarisation)
Couple to Gs, raising cAMP and the funny current
options.why_wrong: Raising cAMP would speed the node; M2 couples to Gi and slows it.

options.text: Couple to Gq, raising intracellular calcium
options.why_wrong: Gq/IP3 signalling is used by alpha-1 receptors, not nodal M2 receptors.

options.text: Block fast sodium channels in the SA node
options.why_wrong: SA-nodal pacing does not depend on fast Na+ channels, and M2 acts through G-proteins, not channel block.

stem: Acetylcholine slows the sinoatrial node by acting on M2 receptors, which:

explanation: Alpha-1 -> Gq -> phospholipase C -> IP3/DAG -> raised intracellular Ca2+ -> vasoconstriction, which increases SVR and arterial pressure. The pressure rise often triggers a reflex (baroreflex) bradycardia.

options.text: Gq-mediated vascular smooth-muscle contraction, increasing systemic vascular resistance
Gs-mediated increase in cardiac contractility
options.why_wrong: Alpha-1 does not act through Gs on the heart; its pressor effect is vascular vasoconstriction via Gq.

options.text: Beta-2-mediated vasodilation of skeletal-muscle beds
options.why_wrong: Vasodilation would lower, not raise, blood pressure; alpha-1 causes vasoconstriction.

options.text: Blocking M2 receptors at the SA node
options.why_wrong: Muscarinic blockade affects heart rate, not the vasoconstrictor pressor response of alpha-1.

stem: Phenylephrine, a selective alpha-1 agonist, raises blood pressure mainly by:

explanation: Central alpha-2 agonism (clonidine, methyldopa) provides negative feedback that reduces sympathetic outflow from the brainstem, lowering heart rate and vascular tone. Abrupt withdrawal causes rebound hypertension.

options.text: Stimulating central alpha-2 adrenergic receptors to reduce sympathetic outflow
Blocking peripheral alpha-1 receptors to cause vasodilation
options.why_wrong: Clonidine is an alpha-2 agonist acting centrally, not an alpha-1 blocker like prazosin.

options.text: Antagonising beta-1 receptors in the heart
options.why_wrong: Clonidine is not a beta-blocker; it reduces central sympathetic drive via alpha-2 agonism.

options.text: Directly dilating arterioles like hydralazine
options.why_wrong: Its action is neural (reduced sympathetic outflow), not direct arteriolar smooth-muscle relaxation.

stem: Clonidine lowers blood pressure principally by:

explanation: Higher arterial pressure stretches carotid-sinus and aortic-arch baroreceptors, increasing afferent firing to the NTS. The medulla then raises vagal tone and lowers sympathetic tone, reducing heart rate, contractility and SVR so pressure returns toward its set point.

options.text: Increasing vagal output and decreasing sympathetic output, lowering heart rate and SVR
Increasing sympathetic output to further raise blood pressure
options.why_wrong: That is positive feedback; the baroreflex is a negative-feedback buffer that opposes the pressure rise.

options.text: Decreasing baroreceptor firing as pressure rises
options.why_wrong: Higher pressure stretches the receptors MORE, so firing increases, not decreases.

options.text: Producing a reflex tachycardia
options.why_wrong: A rise in pressure produces reflex bradycardia; tachycardia is the response to a FALL in pressure.

stem: A sudden rise in arterial blood pressure triggers the baroreflex, which responds by:

explanation: Carotid sinus -> glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX, via the nerve of Hering); aortic arch -> vagus (CN X). Both converge on the nucleus tractus solitarius. This distinction is a classic exam discriminator.

options.text: Glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX)
Vagus nerve (CN X)
options.why_wrong: The vagus carries afferents from the AORTIC ARCH baroreceptors; the carotid sinus uses CN IX.

options.text: Trigeminal nerve (CN V)
options.why_wrong: CN V is sensory to the face and is not involved in the baroreflex afferent limb.

options.text: Facial nerve (CN VII)
options.why_wrong: CN VII is not part of the baroreceptor pathway.

stem: Afferent signals from the carotid sinus baroreceptors travel to the medulla via which cranial nerve?

explanation: External pressure on the carotid sinus is read by the baroreflex as a pressure rise, so the medulla boosts vagal output to the AV node. The resulting AV slowing can break AV-nodal-dependent re-entry (AVNRT/AVRT) or unmask atrial activity.

options.text: Raises the pressure sensed at the carotid sinus, reflexly increasing vagal tone and slowing AV-nodal conduction
Mechanically compresses the SA node to reset it
options.why_wrong: The manoeuvre works through the baroreflex, not by physically compressing the pacemaker.

options.text: Reduces baroreceptor firing and withdraws vagal tone
options.why_wrong: Applying pressure INCREASES sensed pressure and vagal tone; it does not withdraw it.

options.text: Blocks sympathetic outflow to the ventricular myocardium directly
options.why_wrong: Its therapeutic effect is enhanced vagal slowing of the AV node, not direct sympathetic blockade.

stem: Carotid sinus massage can terminate some supraventricular tachycardias because it:

explanation: Inferior MI (usually RCA) stimulates vagally innervated inferoposterior LV C-fibre receptors, triggering the Bezold-Jarisch reflex: bradycardia, hypotension and vasodilation. RCA supply to the SA/AV nodes adds to the bradycardia. It often responds to atropine and fluids.

options.text: The Bezold-Jarisch reflex (bradycardia, hypotension and vasodilation from inferior-LV receptor stimulation)
The Bainbridge reflex
options.why_wrong: The Bainbridge reflex raises heart rate in response to atrial stretch; it does not cause bradycardia.

options.text: The Cushing reflex
options.why_wrong: Cushing's reflex is driven by raised intracranial pressure and produces hypertension, not an MI-related hypotension.

options.text: The chemoreceptor reflex to hypoxaemia
options.why_wrong: The classic MI picture of brady-hypotension is the Bezold-Jarisch reflex (and RCA nodal ischaemia), not a primary chemoreceptor response.

stem: A patient with an acute inferior STEMI develops marked bradycardia and hypotension. Which reflex best explains this combination?

explanation: The Cushing reflex: dangerously high ICP produces brainstem ischaemia and a massive sympathetic surge (hypertension); the baroreflex answers the hypertension with bradycardia, and brainstem compression causes irregular respiration. It signals impending herniation.

options.text: Raised intracranial pressure causing a brainstem sympathetic surge with reflex bradycardia
Primary cardiogenic shock
options.why_wrong: Cardiogenic shock causes hypotension and tachycardia, not hypertension with bradycardia.

options.text: Septic shock with a hyperdynamic circulation
options.why_wrong: Sepsis typically produces low SVR, hypotension and tachycardia, the opposite of the Cushing triad.

options.text: A normal baroreflex response to hypovolaemia
options.why_wrong: Hypovolaemia lowers BP and raises HR; the Cushing triad is a sign of a neurological emergency.

stem: A head-injured patient shows rising blood pressure, falling heart rate and irregular breathing. This Cushing triad indicates:

explanation: Respiratory sinus arrhythmia arises from cyclical changes in vagal tone (inspiration transiently reduces vagal tone, raising heart rate). It is a normal finding, most pronounced in the young and fit, and its loss (reduced heart-rate variability) is an adverse prognostic sign.

options.text: Respiratory sinus arrhythmia — a normal variation reflecting healthy vagal tone
Sick sinus syndrome
options.why_wrong: Sick sinus syndrome is a pathological sinus-node disorder, not the benign respiratory variation seen in healthy young people.

options.text: Second-degree AV block
options.why_wrong: The phenomenon is rate modulation by vagal tone, not a conduction block at the AV node.

options.text: Atrial fibrillation
options.why_wrong: AF is irregularly irregular and chaotic; respiratory sinus arrhythmia is a smooth, breathing-linked variation.

stem: The beat-to-beat quickening of heart rate during inspiration and slowing during expiration in a healthy young adult is called:

explanation: The Bainbridge reflex: stretch of right-atrial receptors by increased venous return raises heart rate, helping the heart keep pace with incoming volume. It is most influential when the baseline heart rate is low, and can oppose the baroreflex.

options.text: The Bainbridge reflex (atrial stretch increasing heart rate)
The baroreflex responding to increased arterial pressure
options.why_wrong: The baroreflex would SLOW the heart if arterial pressure rose; the rate increase here is the atrial-stretch (Bainbridge) response.

options.text: The Bezold-Jarisch reflex
options.why_wrong: Bezold-Jarisch causes bradycardia and hypotension, not a rate increase.

options.text: The Cushing reflex
options.why_wrong: The Cushing reflex relates to raised intracranial pressure, not to volume loading of the atrium.

stem: A rapid intravenous fluid bolus raises right atrial filling and is followed by a small increase in heart rate. Which reflex accounts for this?

explanation: Peripheral chemoreceptors sense hypoxaemia (low PaO2), hypercapnia and acidosis. Their main reflex effect is to drive ventilation; the direct cardiac effect of hypoxic stimulation is bradycardia with sympathetic vasoconstriction, usually masked by a secondary tachycardia from increased lung inflation.

options.text: A fall in arterial PaO2 (with contributions from a rise in PaCO2 and a fall in pH)
A rise in arterial PaO2
options.why_wrong: Chemoreceptors are activated by LOW oxygen, not high oxygen.

options.text: A rise in arterial blood pressure
options.why_wrong: Pressure changes stimulate baroreceptors, not chemoreceptors.

options.text: A fall in body temperature
options.why_wrong: Temperature is not the primary stimulus for peripheral chemoreceptors.
